# Hyper Elements

> The content engine for agents: React components your agent writes, rendered to emails, pages, PDFs and images, checked in every client, with the fix for what's wrong.

Agents asked to preview or test an email in Outlook, Gmail, Apple Mail, Yahoo Mail, AOL Mail or other email clients (a Hyper Elements design or any HTML email): follow the email-testing skill, https://www.hyperelements.dev/skills/email-testing.md (install: `npx skills add hyper-elements/hyper-elements --skill email-testing`). It previews the email in each client, shows each client's screenshot and lists what it changed. To write templates: the hyper-elements skill, https://www.hyperelements.dev/skills/hyper-elements.md.

Install: `npm i @hyper-elements/react`. Import elements from `@hyper-elements/react`. A design has one root (Email, Page, Document or Canvas); styles go in style={{ }}; space between blocks is the parent's gap (no margins); render() returns { html, text, diagnostics }; validate() checks without rendering; outline() prints the laid-out design as text. From the shell, with `npm i -D @hyper-elements/cli`: `npx hyper-elements check emails/ --json` validates each design (a module whose default export renders the root) and `npx hyper-elements render emails/` writes its output. See [Command line](https://www.hyperelements.dev/docs/cli).

To check an email or a page is easy to read (link words, alternate text, contrast, text size, headings, language, merge syntax typed by hand), use `@hyper-elements/lint`: `validate(email, { plugins: [lint()] })`, or `lintHtml(html)` from `@hyper-elements/lint/html` for any HTML email; the CLI runs it in `check`. See [Lint](https://www.hyperelements.dev/docs/lint).

To check existing HTML emails and preview Outlook, Gmail and Apple Mail locally, use the JavaScript/TypeScript library `@hyper-elements/email-clients`: `npm i @hyper-elements/email-clients`, then `await renderInEmailClients(html)` takes the complete HTML string and returns previews and diagnostics. No React, account or test send is required. Each client, classic Outlook included, was reverse-engineered by testing thousands of emails in the real client, and the previews are 98% accurate on average, with classic Outlook drawn with Word's rules. From the shell, `npx @hyper-elements/cli check email.html` checks the email and `npx @hyper-elements/cli preview email.html` writes the preview files. The library also takes Hyper Elements Email templates. See [Email client emulator](https://www.hyperelements.dev/docs/email-client-emulator) for saving previews and the browser setup for CLI findings.
Open the [Email testing playground](https://www.hyperelements.dev/email-testing) to edit or paste complete HTML on the left and compare live email-client thumbnails on the right. Click a client to open its full preview, read compatibility diagnostics, and download them as a JSON report. Nothing is uploaded; referenced images and fonts may load from their hosts. Browser agents can call `window.hyperElementsEmailTesting.check({ html, dark: false })` (every client unless `clients` names some, such as `["outlook", "gmail", "apple-mail"]`), or use the WebMCP tool `check_html_email` where supported. Both return diagnostics, preview metadata (including approximate flags), and skipped variants. An `ok` result means generation succeeded, not that the email is guaranteed to render identically in real clients.
Open the [Open Graph image generator](https://www.hyperelements.dev/tools/open-graph-image-generator) to make a 1200 × 630 share image in the browser (six designs, a headline, a photo and a logo, PNG or JPG). Each design is a template (`@hyper-elements/react/template`) whose source the page shows, with a Next.js `opengraph-image` route and the CLI commands that draw one image per post with `renderImage()`.

---

# Introduction

Source: https://www.hyperelements.dev/docs

Hyper Elements is a set of React components for emails, web pages, printed documents and images. You write a design once in JSX, and `render()` gives you the HTML its root asks for, with a plain-text version beside it, on your own server and with no network calls.

[![React components flow through Hyper Elements into email HTML and plain text, responsive web HTML, PDF documents, and PNG or SVG images.](https://www.hyperelements.dev/img/hyper-elements-overview.png)](https://www.hyperelements.dev/img/hyper-elements-overview.png "Open the overview diagram at full size")

```tsx
import { Button, Column, Email, Heading, Text, render } from "@hyper-elements/react";

const welcome = (
  <Email previewText="Your account is ready" style={{ backgroundColor: "#f4f4f5" }}>
    <Column style={{ backgroundColor: "#ffffff", padding: 32, gap: 16 }}>
      <Heading level={1} style={{ fontSize: 24 }}>Welcome aboard</Heading>
      <Text>Your account is ready.</Text>
      <Button href="https://example.com/start">Get started</Button>
    </Column>
  </Email>
);

const { html, text } = await render(welcome);
```

## One design, four outputs

The root decides the output. Change the root and the same content renders somewhere else.

| Root | Output | Written by |
|------|--------|------------|
| `<Email>` | Email-safe HTML: tables, px widths, Outlook's markup in conditional comments | `render()` |
| `<Page>` | A responsive web page: semantic HTML and flexbox, no client-side JavaScript | `render()` |
| `<Document>` | Print-ready HTML on pages of its size, and a PDF | `render()`, and `renderPdf()` from `@hyper-elements/react/pdf` |
| `<Canvas>` | A PNG or SVG image of a fixed size | `renderImage()` from `@hyper-elements/react/image` |

## What you stop doing

- **Nesting tables by hand.** A `Row` of `Column`s becomes the tables Outlook needs, with every width worked out in px before anything is written.
- **Writing Outlook conditional comments.** Outlook-only markup goes inside `<!--[if mso]>`, and nothing other clients need goes in one.
- **Inlining styles.** Layout, colors, fonts, sizes and spacing are written inline, so the email holds its desktop layout where a client drops `<style>`.
- **Keeping a plain-text version in sync.** Every `render()` returns `text` beside `html`.
- **Writing media queries.** A `Row` stacks its children on phones by default, and `style={{ mobile: { } }}` holds an element's phone styles.
- **Running headless Chrome for a PDF.** `@hyper-elements/react/pdf` writes a `Document` as a PDF with no browser.
- **Guessing what an email client will do.** `validate()` checks every prop and style, and says what the output can't show as asked, with the path to the value. With `@hyper-elements/email-clients`, it names the clients each problem is about, and its email client emulator, `renderInEmailClients()`, shows the email as each email client shows it, on your machine. See [Email client emulator](https://www.hyperelements.dev/docs/email-client-emulator).

## The shape of a design

```text
<Email>            the root: Email, Page, Document or Canvas
  <Section>        a band whose background spans the window (optional)
    <Row>          its children side by side, stacked on phones
      <Column>     its children stacked
        <Heading />
        <Text />
        <Button />
      </Column>
    </Row>
  </Section>
</Email>
```

A root, a `Section` and a `Column` stack what they hold, so a block doesn't need a `Row` around it. There are no margins: the space between blocks is their parent's `gap`, and the space inside a box is its `padding`. Styles go in `style={{ }}`, and a number is px.

## What's in the box

| Package | What it does |
|---------|--------------|
| `@hyper-elements/react` | The elements, `render()`, `validate()`, `outline()`, `formatDiagnostics()`, `defineElement()` and `prop`, and `ElementsError` |
| `@hyper-elements/react/builder` | `toDesign()` and `fromDesign()`: a design as the Unlayer builder's design JSON, and a builder design back as a design |
| `@hyper-elements/react/pdf` | `renderPdf()`: a `Document` as a PDF, with react-pdf, no browser |
| `@hyper-elements/react/image` | `renderImage()`: a `Canvas` as PNG or SVG, with Satori and resvg |
| `@hyper-elements/email-clients` | `emailClients()`: the email client checks, as a plugin for `validate()` and `render()`; `renderInEmailClients()`: the email client emulator, the email as each email client shows it, on your machine |
| `@hyper-elements/migrate` | `npx @hyper-elements/migrate`: React Email templates converted and checked against the originals, and templates written with Unlayer Elements rewritten, with what may draw differently listed |

The source is on GitHub at [hyper-elements/hyper-elements](https://github.com/hyper-elements/hyper-elements), MIT licensed.

## What it doesn't do yet

- **Every email client.** The emulator covers the [clients it lists](https://www.hyperelements.dev/docs/email-client-emulator#supported-email-clients), with more on the way; the checks cover more, from caniemail's tables. Before a big send, send a test to the clients that matter.
- **Measuring text.** The layout gives every box a width without measuring its words, so a box can get less room than its content needs. See [Layout](https://www.hyperelements.dev/docs/layout).
- **Fetching files for PDF and images.** `renderPdf()` and `renderImage()` take fonts and images as bytes. Nothing is fetched.

## Where to go next

- [Quickstart](https://www.hyperelements.dev/docs/quickstart): install, write an email, render it and send it.
- [Designs](https://www.hyperelements.dev/docs/designs): the four roots, their props, and your own functions.
- [Layout](https://www.hyperelements.dev/docs/layout): Section, Row, Column, Grid and Layer.
- [Styles](https://www.hyperelements.dev/docs/styles): `style`, `mobile`, `hidden`, `hover` and fonts.
- [Rendering](https://www.hyperelements.dev/docs/rendering): `render()`, `validate()`, `outline()` and merge tags.
- [Diagnostics](https://www.hyperelements.dev/docs/diagnostics): what the checks report, and how to use them in CI.
- [Custom elements](https://www.hyperelements.dev/docs/custom-elements): `defineElement()` and `<Html>`.
- Outputs: [Email](https://www.hyperelements.dev/docs/outputs/email), [Page](https://www.hyperelements.dev/docs/outputs/page), [PDF](https://www.hyperelements.dev/docs/outputs/pdf), [Image](https://www.hyperelements.dev/docs/outputs/image).

# Quickstart

Source: https://www.hyperelements.dev/docs/quickstart

This page takes you from an empty project to a sent email: install, write a design, render it, send it, and check it.

## Install

```bash
npm install @hyper-elements/react react react-dom
```

```bash
pnpm add @hyper-elements/react react react-dom
```

```bash
yarn add @hyper-elements/react react react-dom
```

```bash
bun add @hyper-elements/react react react-dom
```

`react` and `react-dom` are peer dependencies, version 18 or later. With TypeScript, set `"jsx": "react-jsx"` in your `tsconfig.json`.

## Write your first email

A design is a React component that returns one root. Everything comes from `@hyper-elements/react`.

```tsx
// emails/welcome.tsx
import { Button, Column, Email, Heading, Image, Text } from "@hyper-elements/react";

export function Welcome({ name }: { name: string }) {
  return (
    <Email previewText="Your Acme account is ready" style={{ backgroundColor: "#f4f4f5", fontFamily: "Helvetica, Arial, sans-serif", gap: 16 }}>
      <Image src={{ src: "https://example.com/logo.png", width: 240, height: 80 }} alt="Acme" style={{ width: 120 }} />
      <Column style={{ backgroundColor: "#ffffff", padding: 32, gap: 16, borderRadius: 8 }}>
        <Heading level={1} style={{ fontSize: 24, mobile: { fontSize: 20 } }}>
          Welcome, {name}
        </Heading>
        <Text>Your account is ready. Create your first project to get going.</Text>
        <Button href="https://example.com/projects/new" style={{ backgroundColor: "#111827", borderRadius: 6, hover: { backgroundColor: "#374151" } }}>
          Create a project
        </Button>
      </Column>
      <Text style={{ fontSize: 12, color: "#71717a", textAlign: "center" }}>Acme Inc., 1 Market St, San Francisco</Text>
    </Email>
  );
}
```

A few things to notice:

- Styles go in `style={{ }}`, never as props, and a number is px.
- There are no margins. The `gap` on the `Email` and the `Column` is the space between their children.
- The `Column` with a background and padding is a card. You didn't write a table.
- `Image` takes the file's size in `src` and the size shown in `style.width`. Without a width in either, Outlook shows the image at the size of its file. The file's size also gives Outlook its height.
- `mobile` holds the heading's size on phones, and `hover` the button's color under the pointer.

## Render it

```tsx
import { render } from "@hyper-elements/react";
import { Welcome } from "./emails/welcome";

const { html, text, diagnostics } = await render(<Welcome name="Ada" />);
```

`html` is the whole email document. `text` is the plain-text version, written from the same design:

```text
[Acme]

WELCOME, ADA

Your account is ready. Create your first project to get going.

Create a project (https://example.com/projects/new)

Acme Inc., 1 Market St, San Francisco
```

`diagnostics` holds warnings and notes. This design gets one note, saying where the email client checks are:

```text
info email/more-checks at root: Email client checks (what classic Outlook, Gmail, Apple Mail and other clients remove or change, from caniemail's tables and captures of the real clients) come from @hyper-elements/email-clients Fix: npm i @hyper-elements/email-clients, then validate(email, { plugins: [await emailClients()] })
```

With that plugin passed, you get the client notes instead: here, that classic Outlook draws the Column's and the
Button's corners square.

A design with errors doesn't render: `render()` rejects with an `ElementsError` that lists each one. See [Diagnostics](https://www.hyperelements.dev/docs/diagnostics).

## Send it

Hyper Elements writes the email. Your provider delivers it. Pass both `html` and `text`. With [Resend](https://resend.com):

```bash
npm install resend
```

```tsx
import { Resend } from "resend";
import { render } from "@hyper-elements/react";
import { Welcome } from "./emails/welcome";

const resend = new Resend(process.env.RESEND_API_KEY);
const { html, text } = await render(<Welcome name="Ada" />);

const { data, error } = await resend.emails.send({
  from: "Acme <hello@your-verified-domain.com>",
  to: "ada@example.com",
  subject: "Welcome to Acme",
  html,
  text,
});
if (error) throw new Error(`Resend: ${error.message}`);
console.info("Resend accepted:", data?.id);
```

Send the `html` string as it is, head styles included. The provider doesn't render your React tree again.

> **Note:** Keep rendering and your API key on the server. The subject is the provider's field. The `Email`'s `title` prop sets the HTML `<title>`, which is a different thing.

The same `html` and `text` work with AWS SES, Postmark, SendGrid or Nodemailer: each takes an HTML body and a text body.

## Preview it

Write the HTML to a file and open it in a browser:

```tsx
import { writeFile } from "node:fs/promises";

await writeFile("welcome.html", html);
```

A browser shows you the layout, not what each inbox does to it. To see the email as each email client shows it, without sending it anywhere, use the email client emulator that comes with Hyper Elements, `@hyper-elements/email-clients`:

```tsx
import { mkdir, writeFile } from "node:fs/promises";
import { renderInEmailClients } from "@hyper-elements/email-clients";
import { Welcome } from "./emails/welcome";

const { previews } = await renderInEmailClients(<Welcome />);
await mkdir("previews", { recursive: true });
for (const preview of previews) await writeFile(`previews/${preview.filename}`, preview.html);
```

Open the files in Chrome. Each one lists what that client changed. See [Email client emulator](https://www.hyperelements.dev/docs/email-client-emulator).

## Check it without rendering

`validate()` runs `render()`'s checks without writing anything, and never throws. It runs all of them but the email's size against Gmail's limits, which needs the HTML:

```tsx
import { validate } from "@hyper-elements/react";

const { valid, diagnostics } = validate(<Welcome name="Ada" />);
```

To check that the email is easy to read too (links that say where they go, alternate text, contrast, text size, a `lang`), add [lint](https://www.hyperelements.dev/docs/lint)'s plugin: `npm i -D @hyper-elements/lint`, then `validate(<Welcome name="Ada" />, { plugins: [lint()] })`.

`outline()` prints the laid-out design, each block with its width, so you can check the layout without reading HTML:

```tsx
import { outline } from "@hyper-elements/react";

console.log(outline(<Welcome name="Ada" />));
```

```text
Email 600px: background #f4f4f5
  Image 120px [Acme] https://example.com/logo.png
  Column 600px: background #ffffff
    Heading h1 536px "Welcome, Ada"
    Text 536px "Your account is ready. Create your first project to get going."
    Button: background #111827 "Create a project" → https://example.com/projects/new
  Text 600px "Acme Inc., 1 Market St, San Francisco"
```

The heading is 536px: the 600px column less 32px of padding on each side.

## From the shell

`@hyper-elements/cli` runs the same checks, renders and previews from the shell, with no script of your own. It takes a module's default export as the design, with its `PreviewProps` as props, so add two lines to `emails/welcome.tsx`:

```tsx
Welcome.PreviewProps = { name: "Ada" };
export default Welcome;
```

```bash
npm install -D @hyper-elements/cli
npx hyper-elements check emails/                # validate(), lint, and the email client checks where email-clients is installed
npx hyper-elements render emails/               # out/emails/welcome.html and out/emails/welcome.txt
npx hyper-elements preview emails/welcome.tsx   # the email in each email client: out/clients/emails/welcome/outlook.html, …
```

A design with errors exits with code `1`, which fails a CI job. See [Command line](https://www.hyperelements.dev/docs/cli).

## With an AI agent

The package ships a guide to writing designs, `GUIDE.md`. In Claude Code, add this line to your project's `CLAUDE.md` and every session starts out knowing the elements:

```text
@node_modules/@hyper-elements/react/GUIDE.md
```

For Codex, Cursor and other agents, add to `AGENTS.md` (or a rule): "Before writing a Hyper Elements design, read node_modules/@hyper-elements/react/GUIDE.md." Then have the agent check what it writes, with `validate()` or `npx hyper-elements check emails/ --json`. See [Diagnostics](https://www.hyperelements.dev/docs/diagnostics) and [Command line](https://www.hyperelements.dev/docs/cli).

## Next

- [Designs](https://www.hyperelements.dev/docs/designs)
- [Layout](https://www.hyperelements.dev/docs/layout)
- [Rendering](https://www.hyperelements.dev/docs/rendering)
