# Designs

Source: https://www.hyperelements.dev/docs/designs

A design is JSX with one root. The root decides the output: an email, a web page, a PDF or an image.

<!-- example: designs/welcome.tsx -->
```tsx
import { Email, Heading, Text } from "@hyper-elements/react";

export default function Welcome() {
  return (
    <Email width={600} previewText="Thanks for signing up" lang="en">
      <Heading>Welcome</Heading>
      <Text>Thanks for signing up.</Text>
    </Email>
  );
}
```

That is a whole email. A root stacks its children down its content width, centered in the window, so you don't need a `Row`, a `Column` or a container to start.

To see it, `await render(<Welcome />)` gives its HTML ([Rendering](https://www.hyperelements.dev/docs/rendering)), and `npx hyper-elements dev` shows it in a browser as you edit ([Command line](https://www.hyperelements.dev/docs/cli)). New here? [Quickstart](https://www.hyperelements.dev/docs/quickstart) installs the package and sends a first email.

## The four roots

<div class="concept-grid">
<a class="concept" href="/docs/outputs/email"><img src="/generated/core-concepts/designs-email.svg" width="600" height="400" alt="An email in a mail window: from Orbit, subject The Weekly Signal, with a logo, a banner, a headline and the start of its text"><strong>Email</strong><span>Email-safe HTML and its plain text, from <code>render()</code>.</span></a>
<a class="concept" href="/docs/outputs/page"><img src="/generated/core-concepts/designs-page.svg" width="600" height="400" loading="lazy" alt="A web page in a browser window at orbit.example: a navigation bar, a large headline on a colored band, a button and a screenshot of the product"><strong>Page</strong><span>A responsive web page, from <code>render()</code>.</span></a>
<a class="concept" href="/docs/outputs/pdf"><img src="/generated/core-concepts/designs-document.svg" width="600" height="400" loading="lazy" alt="A document as a sheet of paper: an invoice with a letterhead, who it's billed to, a table of three lines and the total due"><strong>Document</strong><span>A PDF from <code>renderPdf()</code>, and print-ready HTML from <code>render()</code>.</span></a>
<a class="concept" href="/docs/outputs/image"><img src="/generated/core-concepts/designs-canvas.svg" width="600" height="400" loading="lazy" alt="An image, 1200 by 630: a social card with a large headline on indigo beside a grid of bright shapes in yellow, teal, coral and pink"><strong>Canvas</strong><span>A PNG or an SVG of a fixed size, from <code>renderImage()</code>.</span></a>
</div>

What's inside each frame is real output: a newsletter, a landing page, an invoice and a social card, all written with the same elements. Only the root differs.

| Root | Its width |
|------|-----------|
| [`Email`](https://www.hyperelements.dev/docs/elements/email) | `width`, 600 by default |
| [`Page`](https://www.hyperelements.dev/docs/elements/page) | `width`, 1200 by default: the widest the content gets |
| [`Document`](https://www.hyperelements.dev/docs/elements/document) | From its `size`, `orientation` and `margin` |
| [`Canvas`](https://www.hyperelements.dev/docs/elements/canvas) | `width` 1200 and `height` 630 by default |

A design has exactly one root, with nothing around it. A `<div>` around the root is an error.

## Root props

| Prop | Roots | What it does |
|------|-------|--------------|
| `width` | Email, Page, Canvas | The content width in px |
| `height` | Canvas | The image's height in px. What's past it is cut |
| `previewText` | Email | Shown after the subject in inbox lists, not in the email |
| `description` | Page | The page's meta description |
| `title` | all | The document's `<title>`, shown in a browser tab and by some email clients |
| `lang` | all | The language, as a BCP 47 tag (`"en"`, `"ar"`) |
| `dir` | all | `"ltr"`, `"rtl"` or `"auto"`. Text starts on that side unless you align it |
| `fonts` | all | The font files the design loads. See [Styles](https://www.hyperelements.dev/docs/styles#fonts) |
| `theme` | all | The brand's colors, fonts and defaults. See [Themes](https://www.hyperelements.dev/docs/themes) |
| `size` | Document | `"A3"`, `"A4"`, `"A5"`, `"Letter"`, `"Legal"` or `"Tabloid"`, `"A4"` by default |
| `orientation` | Document | `"portrait"` or `"landscape"`, `"portrait"` by default |
| `margin` | Document | Around each page's content, 48px on each side by default (96px to the inch) |

A root's width is a prop, not a style. An Email, a Page and a Document have no padding of their own: put padding on a `Column` (a card) or a `Section` (a band) inside:

```tsx
<Email width={640} style={{ backgroundColor: "#f4f4f5" }}>
  <Column style={{ backgroundColor: "#ffffff", padding: 32 }}>
    <Text>The card has the padding, not the root.</Text>
  </Column>
</Email>
```

The root's `style` takes the text styles every block inherits (`color`, `fontFamily`, `fontSize`, `lineHeight` and the rest), `backgroundColor`, `gap` and `alignItems`. A `Canvas`, which is one fixed box, also takes `padding` and `justifyContent`. See [Styles](https://www.hyperelements.dev/docs/styles).

## What goes inside

Everything in a design is an element. The ones a root, a Section or a Column stacks are called blocks: the layout elements, the text elements and the rest of the first four rows below. What goes inside text, or inside a List, a Table or an Svg, isn't a block.

| Kind | Elements |
|------|------------|
| Layout | [`Section`](https://www.hyperelements.dev/docs/elements/section), [`Row`](https://www.hyperelements.dev/docs/elements/row), [`Column`](https://www.hyperelements.dev/docs/elements/column), [`Grid`](https://www.hyperelements.dev/docs/elements/grid), [`Layer`](https://www.hyperelements.dev/docs/elements/layer) |
| Text | [`Heading`](https://www.hyperelements.dev/docs/elements/heading) (`level` 1 to 6), [`Text`](https://www.hyperelements.dev/docs/elements/text) |
| Inside text | [`Span`](https://www.hyperelements.dev/docs/elements/span), [`Link`](https://www.hyperelements.dev/docs/elements/link), [`LineBreak`](https://www.hyperelements.dev/docs/elements/linebreak), [`MergeTag`](https://www.hyperelements.dev/docs/elements/mergetag) |
| Other blocks | [`Button`](https://www.hyperelements.dev/docs/elements/button), [`Image`](https://www.hyperelements.dev/docs/elements/image), [`Divider`](https://www.hyperelements.dev/docs/elements/divider), [`List`](https://www.hyperelements.dev/docs/elements/list), [`Table`](https://www.hyperelements.dev/docs/elements/table), [`Video`](https://www.hyperelements.dev/docs/elements/video), [`Social`](https://www.hyperelements.dev/docs/elements/social), [`Menu`](https://www.hyperelements.dev/docs/elements/menu), [`Svg`](https://www.hyperelements.dev/docs/elements/svg) (not in an Email), [`Html`](https://www.hyperelements.dev/docs/elements/html) |
| Parts | [`ListItem`](https://www.hyperelements.dev/docs/elements/listitem) in a `List`; [`TableRow`](https://www.hyperelements.dev/docs/elements/tablerow) and [`TableCell`](https://www.hyperelements.dev/docs/elements/tablecell) in a `Table` |
| Shapes, in an `Svg` | [`Rect`](https://www.hyperelements.dev/docs/elements/rect), [`Circle`](https://www.hyperelements.dev/docs/elements/circle), [`Ellipse`](https://www.hyperelements.dev/docs/elements/ellipse), [`Line`](https://www.hyperelements.dev/docs/elements/line), [`Polygon`](https://www.hyperelements.dev/docs/elements/polygon), [`Path`](https://www.hyperelements.dev/docs/elements/path) |
| Document parts | [`Document.Page`](https://www.hyperelements.dev/docs/elements/document-page), [`PageBreak`](https://www.hyperelements.dev/docs/elements/pagebreak), [`PageHeader`](https://www.hyperelements.dev/docs/elements/pageheader), [`PageFooter`](https://www.hyperelements.dev/docs/elements/pagefooter), [`PageNumber`](https://www.hyperelements.dev/docs/elements/pagenumber) |

[Layout](https://www.hyperelements.dev/docs/layout) covers the first row. Each element's page lists its props and styles.

### Text is elements, not HTML

Words go in a `Heading` or a `Text`. Inside one, a `Span` styles a run, a `Link` links one, a `LineBreak` breaks the line and a `MergeTag` writes a merge tag (a placeholder your sending service fills in, such as a first name):

```tsx
<Text>
  Order <Span style={{ fontWeight: 700 }}>#10482</Span> ships tomorrow.
  <LineBreak />
  <Link href="https://example.com/orders/10482">Track it</Link>
</Text>
```

`<b>`, `<br>`, `<div>` and other HTML elements in a design are errors (`jsx/markup`), and so are words straight in a root or a Column. For markup no element says, there's [`<Html>`](https://www.hyperelements.dev/docs/custom-elements#html-markup-as-it-is).

### Images

An `Image` takes its file's size along with its address, `src={{ src, width, height }}`, in the file's own px. Its `style.width` is the size it's shown at:

```tsx
<Image
  src={{ src: "https://example.com/logo.png", width: 240, height: 80 }}
  alt="Acme"
  style={{ width: 120 }}
/>
```

### Ids

Every element takes an `id`. It starts with a letter, holds letters, digits, `_` and `-`, and is used once in a design. It's written as the HTML `id`, and it's how [templates](https://www.hyperelements.dev/docs/templates) and tools name one part of a design.

## Your own functions

A function that returns elements is a part of your own, to use wherever those elements can go. It's a React component, so write designs the way you write the rest of your React app:

```tsx
import { Column, Email, Heading, Text } from "@hyper-elements/react";

function Footer({ company }: { company: string }) {
  return (
    <Text style={{ fontSize: 12, color: "#71717a", textAlign: "center" }}>
      {company}
    </Text>
  );
}

interface Order {
  name: string;
  items: string[];
}

export function OrderShipped({ name, items }: Order) {
  return (
    <Email previewText="Your order is on its way" style={{ gap: 16 }}>
      <Column style={{ gap: 8 }}>
        <Heading level={1}>On its way, {name}</Heading>
        {items.map((item) => (
          <Text key={item}>{item}</Text>
        ))}
      </Column>
      <Footer company="Acme Inc." />
    </Email>
  );
}
```

`render()` runs your functions with React, so props, hooks, Context, Fragments, arrays and conditions work as they do in React.

A function that's async or suspends is an error (`jsx/async`): `render()` doesn't wait for it. Fetch your data first and pass it in as props.

Data you pass as children or props is escaped when the output is written, so a customer's name can't add markup.

For a part with typed props that are checked like a built-in element's, see [Custom elements](https://www.hyperelements.dev/docs/custom-elements).

## Share content between roots

Write the content once, as a function:

<!-- example: designs/_parts/receipt.tsx -->
```tsx
export function ReceiptContent({ receipt }: { receipt: Receipt }) {
  return (
    <Column style={{ backgroundColor: "#ffffff", padding: 32, gap: 16 }}>
      <Heading level={1} style={{ fontSize: 28 }}>Payment receipt</Heading>
      <Text>
        Invoice <Span style={{ fontWeight: 700 }}>{receipt.number}</Span>
      </Text>
      <Text>
        Thank you, {receipt.customer}. You paid {receipt.total}.
      </Text>
      <Button href={receipt.url}>View invoice</Button>
    </Column>
  );
}
```

Then give each output its root:

```tsx
const content = <ReceiptContent receipt={receipt} />;

const email = await render(<Email>{content}</Email>);
const page = await render(<Page width={600}>{content}</Page>);
const printed = await render(<Document size="A4">{content}</Document>);
```

<figure class="diagram"><img src="/generated/core-concepts/designs-shared.svg" width="880" height="226" alt="One receipt three times: as an email, as a web page, and at the top of a document's first page"></figure>

`render()` needs no mode: the root says what to write. `email.html` is email HTML, `page.html` a web page and `printed.html` print HTML. For the PDF itself, pass the same `Document` to `renderPdf()`. See [Rendering](https://www.hyperelements.dev/docs/rendering).

Shared content doesn't mean identical pixels. An email is written as tables, a page with flexbox, and a document on pages of a fixed size. Each output's page says what it does differently: [Email](https://www.hyperelements.dev/docs/outputs/email), [Web pages](https://www.hyperelements.dev/docs/outputs/page), [Documents and PDF](https://www.hyperelements.dev/docs/outputs/pdf), [Images](https://www.hyperelements.dev/docs/outputs/image).

## Next

- [Layout](https://www.hyperelements.dev/docs/layout): arrange blocks with Section, Row, Column, Grid and Layer.
- [Styles](https://www.hyperelements.dev/docs/styles): `style`, phone styles and fonts.
- [Rendering](https://www.hyperelements.dev/docs/rendering): turn a design into its output.

---

# Layout

Source: https://www.hyperelements.dev/docs/layout

Five elements arrange blocks: `Section`, `Row`, `Column`, `Grid` and `Layer`. None is required, since a root stacks its children. Reach for them when you want bands, columns, cards or words over an image.

<figure class="diagram"><img src="/generated/core-concepts/layout-row.svg" width="880" height="308" alt="A Row of three Columns on desktop, 180px, 259px and 129px wide with 16px gaps between them, and the same Row on a phone, its Columns stacked at full width"></figure>

That is this Row, in a 600px email:

<!-- example: layout/row.tsx -->
```tsx
const box = {
  backgroundColor: "#eef2ff",
  padding: [16, 0],
  borderRadius: 8,
  textAlign: "center",
} as const;

<Email width={600}>
  <Row style={{ gap: 16 }}>
    <Column style={{ ...box, width: 180 }}>
      <Text>Fixed</Text>
    </Column>
    <Column style={{ ...box, flex: 2 }}>
      <Text>Two shares</Text>
    </Column>
    <Column style={box}>
      <Text>One share</Text>
    </Column>
  </Row>
</Email>
```

The fixed Column takes 180px and the two gaps take 32px. The other two share the 388px left, two to one. On a phone, the Row stacks its Columns at full width.

You don't need a browser to see the widths. [`outline()`](https://www.hyperelements.dev/docs/rendering#outline) prints them:

<!-- output: rowOutline -->
```text
Email 600px
  Row 600px: 3 side by side, stacked on phones
    Column 180px: background #eef2ff
      Text 180px "Fixed"
    Column 259px: background #eef2ff
      Text 259px "Two shares"
    Column 129px: background #eef2ff
      Text 129px "One share"
```

## Which one to use

| You want | Use |
|----------|-----|
| A background across the whole window | [`Section`](#section) |
| Blocks side by side | [`Row`](#row) |
| A card, or a group of blocks with its own spacing | [`Column`](#column) |
| Equal columns, row after row | [`Grid`](#grid) |
| Words over an image | [`Layer`](#layer) |

## Gap and padding

There are no margins. Space between blocks is their parent's `gap`. Space inside a box is its `padding`.

<figure class="diagram"><img src="/generated/core-concepts/layout-spacing.svg" width="720" height="287" alt="A card with its padding shaded on all four sides, 32px, and the gap between its heading, text and button shaded, 16px each"></figure>

<!-- example: layout/spacing.tsx -->
```tsx
<Column style={{ backgroundColor: "#ffffff", padding: 32, gap: 16 }}>
  <Heading level={2}>Your order</Heading>
  <Text>Ships tomorrow.</Text>
  <Button href="https://example.com/orders/10482">Track it</Button>
</Column>
```

A `gap` is the same between every child. Where one space should differ, either group the blocks that belong together in a Column with its own `gap`, or give a block `padding` on that side:

```tsx
<Column style={{ gap: 24 }}>
  <Column style={{ gap: 4 }}>
    <Heading level={2}>Your order</Heading>
    <Text>Ships tomorrow.</Text>
  </Column>
  <Button href="https://example.com/orders/10482">Track it</Button>
</Column>
```

`marginBottom` and the other margins are errors, and the message says to use the parent's `gap`, or `padding`. In an email, both are written as table cell padding, which holds up in classic Outlook (the Windows desktop app, which draws email with Word's engine and drops a good deal of CSS).

`padding` takes one number for every side, or a value for each: `[12, 24]` is 12px top and bottom, 24px left and right. [Styles](https://www.hyperelements.dev/docs/styles#values) lists every form.

## Section

A [`Section`](https://www.hyperelements.dev/docs/elements/section) is a band across the whole window. Its background spans the window, and its children are stacked at the content width.

<figure class="diagram"><img src="/generated/core-concepts/layout-section.svg" width="880" height="321" alt="An email in a window wider than its content: the Section's dark background spans the whole window, and its heading and the card below sit inside the 600px content width"></figure>

<!-- example: layout/section.tsx -->
```tsx
<Email width={600} style={{ backgroundColor: "#f4f4f5" }}>
  <Section
    style={{ backgroundColor: "#15132e", padding: [24, 40], color: "#ffffff" }}
  >
    <Heading level={2}>Acme weekly</Heading>
  </Section>
  <Section style={{ padding: [32, 40] }}>
    <Column style={{ backgroundColor: "#ffffff", padding: 24, gap: 8 }}>
      <Heading level={3}>This week</Heading>
      <Text>A Section is a band. A Column with a background is a card.</Text>
    </Column>
  </Section>
</Email>
```

The heading is 520px wide: the 600px content width less 40px of padding on each side.

A Section goes directly in a root, never inside a Column, a Row or another Section. For a background that stops at the content width, use a Column.

## Row

A [`Row`](https://www.hyperelements.dev/docs/elements/row) puts its children side by side. Each child takes its `width`, or a share of what's left: its `flex`, 1 by default.

```tsx
// Equal shares.
<Row style={{ gap: 16 }}>
  <Column>{/* content */}</Column>
  <Column>{/* content */}</Column>
</Row>

// A set width, and what's left.
<Row style={{ gap: 16 }}>
  <Column style={{ width: 180 }}>{/* content */}</Column>
  <Column>{/* content */}</Column>
</Row>

// Shares of two to one.
<Row style={{ gap: 16 }}>
  <Column style={{ flex: 2 }}>{/* content */}</Column>
  <Column>{/* content */}</Column>
</Row>
```

- `width` takes px, or a percentage of the Row's width: `"25%"` of a 600px Row is 150px.
- `flex: "none"` makes a child take its own size.
- `minWidth` and `maxWidth` hold a child's width where its share would go past them.

A Row's children don't have to be Columns. A Text, a Button or an Image can sit in a Row itself. Use a Column where one side holds more than one block.

### Stacking on phones

In an Email or a Page, a Row stacks its children at full width on phones. To keep them side by side, set `stackOnMobile={false}`:

```tsx
<Row stackOnMobile={false} style={{ gap: 12 }}>
  <Column><Text>Subtotal</Text></Column>
  <Column><Text style={{ textAlign: "right" }}>$48.00</Text></Column>
</Row>
```

Stacked, each child is as wide as the Row, whatever its `width` or `flex`, and the Row's `gap` is the space between them, as in the picture at the top of this page.

A phone is a window up to 20px wider than an email's content (620px for a 600px email), or up to 480px wide on a page. [Styles](https://www.hyperelements.dev/docs/styles#where-phones-start) has the details.

`flexWrap: "wrap"` lets children that don't fit go onto another line. In an email, it works only in a Row with `stackOnMobile={false}`.

## Column

A [`Column`](https://www.hyperelements.dev/docs/elements/column) stacks its children, with its own `gap`, `padding` and box. With a background, it's a card.

```tsx
<Column
  style={{
    backgroundColor: "#ffffff",
    padding: 24,
    gap: 12,
    border: "1px solid #e4e4e7",
    borderRadius: 8,
  }}
>
  <Heading level={3}>Pro plan</Heading>
  <Text>$12 a month</Text>
</Column>
```

Anything that stacks its children (a root, a Section, a Column) gives each child its full width. The exceptions are a child with a `width`, and a Button or an Image, which take their own size.

## Grid

A [`Grid`](https://www.hyperelements.dev/docs/elements/grid) puts its children in columns of equal width, row after row. On phones, they go one under another unless `stackOnMobile={false}`.

<figure class="diagram"><img src="/generated/core-concepts/layout-grid.svg" width="880" height="310" alt="A Grid of four cards in three columns on desktop, the fourth starting a second row, and the same Grid on a phone, one card under another"></figure>

<!-- example: layout/grid.tsx -->
```tsx
const card = { backgroundColor: "#eef2ff", padding: 16, borderRadius: 8 };

<Grid columns={3} style={{ gap: 16, rowGap: 24 }}>
  <Column style={card}><Text>One</Text></Column>
  <Column style={card}><Text>Two</Text></Column>
  <Column style={card}><Text>Three</Text></Column>
  <Column style={card}><Text>Four</Text></Column>
</Grid>
```

`columns` is 1 to 12, 2 by default. `gap` is the space across and down, and `rowGap` the space between rows where it differs. Every output draws a Grid, since it's laid out as Rows of Columns.

## Layer

A [`Layer`](https://www.hyperelements.dev/docs/elements/layer) puts its children over each other, in one box as tall as the tallest. Use it for words on an image.

<figure class="diagram"><img src="/generated/core-concepts/layout-layer.svg" width="720" height="312" alt="A Layer 240px tall: a photo covering it, and a heading over the photo at its bottom left"></figure>

<!-- example: layout/layer.tsx -->
```tsx
const photo = {
  src: "https://hyperelements.dev/img/gradient.png",
  width: 1200,
  height: 500,
};

<Layer style={{ height: 240, alignItems: "end" }}>
  <Image src={photo} alt="" />
  <Column style={{ padding: 32 }}>
    <Heading level={2} style={{ color: "#ffffff" }}>Spring collection</Heading>
  </Column>
</Layer>
```

With a `height`, the image under the other children covers the Layer, cut at its sides or at its top and bottom. `alignItems` places the children down the box (`"start"` by default), and `justifyItems` across it (`"stretch"` by default).

> **Note:** An email draws one shape of Layer: an Image as wide as the Layer with one child over it, as above. Any other shape is an error in an Email (`email/layer`).

## Alignment

`alignItems` places children across the layout's direction: vertically in a Row, horizontally in a Column. `justifyContent` places them along it. The values are CSS's: `"start"`, `"center"`, `"end"`, plus `"stretch"` for `alignItems` and `"space-between"` for `justifyContent`.

<figure class="diagram"><img src="/generated/core-concepts/layout-alignment.svg" width="720" height="240" alt="A Row whose logo and two lines of text are centered on each other vertically, and a Column whose heading and button are centered across it"></figure>

<!-- example: layout/alignment.tsx -->
```tsx
const logo = {
  src: "https://hyperelements.dev/img/orbit-logo.png",
  width: 252,
  height: 128,
};

<Row style={{ gap: 16, alignItems: "center" }}>
  <Column style={{ width: 128 }}>
    <Image src={logo} alt="Orbit" style={{ width: 128 }} />
  </Column>
  <Column>
    <Text style={{ fontWeight: 700 }}>Ada Lovelace</Text>
    <Text>Commented on your design</Text>
  </Column>
</Row>
<Column style={{ alignItems: "center", textAlign: "center", gap: 12 }}>
  <Heading level={2}>Centered by textAlign</Heading>
  <Button href="https://example.com">Centered by alignItems</Button>
</Column>
```

In a Column, `alignItems` moves the blocks that take their own size: a Button, an Image, a block with a `width`. A Heading or a Text fills the Column's width, so `alignItems` leaves its words where they were. Center those with `textAlign: "center"`.

A Button can place itself with `alignSelf` (`"start"`, `"center"` or `"end"`), whatever its parent's `alignItems`, and somewhere else on phones with `style={{ mobile: { alignSelf } }}`.

> **Note:** `justifyContent: "space-between"` isn't possible in a Row in an email. Its children start at the left, and `validate()` warns (`email/unsupported`).

## How widths are worked out

Before any HTML is written, Elements works out every box's width in px, from the root's width down. Every output is written from those widths, so an email (which needs px widths for Outlook's tables) and a page agree.

A Row's widths follow CSS flexbox: each child starts from its `width` or its own size, what's left is shared by `flex`, and a child that reaches its `minWidth` or `maxWidth` keeps it. Widths that don't fit are narrowed as a browser narrows them, with a warning (`layout/shrunk`). Minimum widths that can't fit are reported too (`layout/overflow`).

> **Warning:** Text isn't measured. A box can get less room than its words need: text in a few px, a label wider than its button. A page then overflows the box, while an email's table cell widens to its longest word and its neighbors give way. No diagnostic says so yet, so give boxes room for their words.

---

# Styles

Source: https://www.hyperelements.dev/docs/styles

Every element takes its styles in `style={{ }}`, with CSS's property names and values wherever CSS has one for the job. Inside it, the `mobile` block holds its styles on phones and the `hover` block its styles under the pointer.

<figure class="diagram"><img src="/generated/core-concepts/styles-mobile.svg" width="880" height="240" alt="A card on desktop, its heading 32px at the left inside 32px of padding, and the same card on a phone, its heading 24px and centered inside 16px of padding"></figure>

<!-- example: styles/mobile.tsx -->
```tsx
<Column style={{ padding: 32, gap: 8, mobile: { padding: 16 } }}>
  <Heading
    level={1}
    style={{ fontSize: 32, mobile: { fontSize: 24, textAlign: "center" } }}
  >
    Welcome
  </Heading>
  <Text>Your account is ready.</Text>
</Column>
```

| You want | Use |
|----------|-----|
| A style | [`style={{ fontSize: 32 }}`](#style) |
| Another value on phones | [`style={{ mobile: { fontSize: 24 } }}`](#mobile) |
| A block on desktop only, or on phones only | [`hidden={{ mobile: true }}`](#hidden) |
| Another color under the pointer | [`style={{ hover: { backgroundColor } }}`](#hover) |

## style

Styles go in `style`, never as props. `<Email backgroundColor="#fff">` is an error whose message tells you to write `style={{ backgroundColor: "#fff" }}`.

- **A number is px.** `padding: 16` is 16px, `fontSize: 15` is 15px.
- **Names are CSS's** where the meaning is the same: `alignItems`, `justifyContent: "space-between"`, `textTransform`, `borderRadius`. Where a behavior isn't CSS, it's a prop (`<Row stackOnMobile={false}>`).
- **Each element takes its own list.** A style an element doesn't take is an error (`style/unknown`), which names what to use instead where there's an equivalent. Each element's page lists its styles, with their defaults.
- **A value may be a theme's token**, `color: token("colors.primary")`, and `apply` merges a theme's named styles under the rest: `style={{ apply: ["card"], gap: 16 }}`. See [Themes](https://www.hyperelements.dev/docs/themes).

### Values

| Kind | What it takes |
|------|---------------|
| Color | `"#0879a1"`, `"rgb(…)"`, `"rgba(…)"` or a CSS name |
| Font family | A stack, as CSS writes it: `"Inter, Arial, sans-serif"` |
| Font weight | 100 to 900 in hundreds, `"normal"` or `"bold"` |
| Line height | A multiple of the font size (`1.5`), a percentage (`"150%"`), px (`"24px"`) or `"normal"` |
| Insets (`padding`, a Document's `margin`) | `16` for every side, `[v, h]`, `[top, h, bottom]`, `[top, right, bottom, left]`, `"8px 16px"` (1 to 4 values) or `{ top, right, bottom, left }` |
| Border | `"1px solid #ccc"`, `{ width, style, color }` for every side, or `{ top, right, bottom, left }` with one of those each |
| Radius | px for every corner, `[topLeft, topRight, bottomRight, bottomLeft]` or `{ topLeft, topRight, bottomRight, bottomLeft }` |
| Flex | A share of the free width (0 or more), or `"none"` |

<!-- example: styles/values.tsx -->
```tsx
<Column
  style={{
    padding: [24, 32],
    backgroundColor: "#ffffff",
    border: { width: 1, style: "solid", color: "#a1a1aa" },
    borderRadius: [16, 16, 0, 0],
  }}
>
  <Heading
    level={2}
    style={{
      fontWeight: "bold",
      lineHeight: "120%",
      textTransform: "uppercase",
    }}
  >
    Title
  </Heading>
  <Text style={{ lineHeight: "24px", border: { bottom: "1px solid #ccc" } }}>
    E = mc<Span style={{ verticalAlign: "super" }}>2</Span>
  </Text>
</Column>
```

<figure class="diagram"><img src="/generated/core-concepts/styles-values.svg" width="720" height="176" alt="A card with a 1px border, its top corners rounded and its bottom corners square, holding a title in capitals and a line of text with a rule under it and a superscript 2"></figure>

### Text styles are inherited

`color`, `fontFamily`, `fontSize`, `fontWeight`, `fontStyle`, `lineHeight`, `letterSpacing`, `textAlign` and `textTransform` pass down from the root to everything inside. Set your type once on the root:

```tsx
<Email
  style={{
    color: "#111827",
    fontFamily: "Inter, Arial, sans-serif",
    fontSize: 15,
    lineHeight: 1.6,
  }}
>
  {/* every block inherits these */}
</Email>
```

The root's defaults are `color: "#000000"`, `fontFamily: "Arial, Helvetica, sans-serif"`, `fontSize: 16`, `fontWeight: 400`, `lineHeight: 1.5` and `textAlign: "left"`. Some elements have their own: a Heading is bold at a line height of 1.25, a Button is white 14px text on `#0879a1`, a Link is `#0000ee` and underlined.

In an email, every text style is written on the text itself, since Outlook doesn't pass styles down through tables. That's done for you.

Box styles (`width`, `padding`, `backgroundColor`, `border`, `borderRadius` and the rest) aren't inherited.

A [theme](https://www.hyperelements.dev/docs/themes) sets the root's text styles for every design that takes it, with its roles: `colors.foreground`, `fonts.body`, `fontSizes.body` and `lineHeights.body`.

### No margins

Space between blocks is their parent's `gap`, and space inside a box is its `padding`. A margin is an error. See [Layout](https://www.hyperelements.dev/docs/layout#gap-and-padding).

## mobile

The `mobile` block of an element's `style` holds its styles on phones, in an Email or a Page. On a phone, they replace the element's own, as in the picture at the top of this page:

```tsx
<Heading style={{ fontSize: 32, mobile: { fontSize: 24 } }}>Welcome</Heading>
```

Phone styles are sizes, spacing and alignment: `fontSize`, `lineHeight`, `letterSpacing`, `textAlign`, `width`, `maxWidth`, `padding`, `border`, `gap`, `rowGap` and `alignSelf`. Each element takes the ones on its own list.

- **Colors and fonts stay the same on phones.** `mobile: { color: "#ff0000" }` is an error (`mobile/not-allowed`), and a type error in TypeScript, since the block is typed to the element's list.
- **A Document and a Canvas have no phone width.** Phone styles in one are an error (`mobile/not-supported`).
- **A Row stacks on phones without any phone styles.** See [Layout](https://www.hyperelements.dev/docs/layout#stacking-on-phones).

A few phone styles are accepted but not shown, and `validate()` warns about each:

- A Page root's own phone text styles. Set them on its Sections or Columns.
- A stacking Grid's phone `rowGap`. Its children are its phone `gap` apart.
- In an email, an Image's or a TableCell's phone `border`, and a phone `lineHeight` of `"normal"`.

### Where phones start

There is one breakpoint: a window is a phone or it isn't. In an email, it's one up to 20px wider than the content: 620px for a 600px email. On a page, it's one up to 480px wide, or up to the page's own `breakpoints.mobile`:

<figure class="diagram"><img src="/generated/core-concepts/styles-phones.svg" width="880" height="250" alt="Window widths from 0 to 1000px. A 600px Email takes its phone styles up to 620px wide, its width plus 20px. A Page takes them up to 480px wide, or up to its own breakpoints.mobile."></figure>

```tsx
<Page width={1200} breakpoints={{ mobile: 600 }}>
  <Column style={{ padding: 32, mobile: { padding: 16 } }}>…</Column>
</Page>
```

Phone styles and `hidden={{ mobile: true }}` apply at that width and below. `breakpoints.mobile` is a whole number of px from 240. One as wide as the page's content or wider is a warning (`page/phone-width`), since phone styles would then apply where the content is at full width.

An email's breakpoint follows its width and can't be set. Its phone styles are rules in its stylesheet, so they apply in the email clients that keep the stylesheet. A few drop it. There, a Row still stacks, once the window is too narrow to hold its children side by side, but `mobile` styles and `hidden` don't apply. See [Email](https://www.hyperelements.dev/docs/outputs/email#rows-that-stack-without-media-queries).

## hidden

`hidden` shows a block on one size only:

<figure class="diagram"><img src="/generated/core-concepts/styles-hidden.svg" width="880" height="199" alt="A card on desktop showing its desktop detail and not its phone detail, and the same card on a phone showing its phone detail and not its desktop detail"></figure>

<!-- example: styles/hidden.tsx -->
```tsx
<Text>Your order has shipped.</Text>
<Text hidden={{ mobile: true }}>Desktop detail: track it on the web.</Text>
<Text hidden={{ desktop: true }}>Phone detail: track it in the app.</Text>
```

Hidden on both, a block never shows, and `validate()` warns (`hidden/everywhere`).

## hover

The `hover` block holds a link's or a button's styles under the pointer:

```tsx
<Button
  href="https://example.com/buy"
  style={{ backgroundColor: "#111827", hover: { backgroundColor: "#374151" } }}
>
  Buy
</Button>

<Text>
  <Link
    href="https://example.com/help"
    style={{
      color: "#2563eb",
      textDecoration: "none",
      hover: { textDecoration: "underline" },
    }}
  >
    Help
  </Link>
</Text>
```

A Button takes `color` and `backgroundColor` on hover. A Link takes `color`, `textDecoration` and `backgroundColor`. Other elements take no `hover` block. Keyboard focus gets the same styles, so a link or button reached with Tab shows its hover colors.

In an email, `validate()` notes that hover doesn't show everywhere: classic Outlook for Windows and some apps and webmail leave the colors as they are. A PDF and an image can't show hover, and say so.

## Fonts

The root's `fonts` lists the font files the design loads, one face each:

```tsx
const fonts = [
  { family: "Inter", src: "https://example.com/400.woff2", weight: 400 },
  { family: "Inter", src: "https://example.com/700.woff2", weight: "bold" },
  { family: "Inter", src: "https://example.com/400i.woff2", style: "italic" },
];

<Email fonts={fonts} style={{ fontFamily: "Inter, Arial, sans-serif" }}>
```

A face is `{ family, src, format, weight, style }`. The format comes from the file's extension where you don't give it, and a variable font's weight is a range (`"100 900"`). Name the family in a `fontFamily` stack, before the fonts to show where it can't load. The browser picks the face for each weight and style.

- **On a page**, each face is an `@font-face` rule with `font-display: swap`.
- **In an email**, Apple Mail and iOS Mail load web fonts. Gmail and classic Outlook don't, and show the next font in the stack, so end each stack on a font every client has. `@hyper-elements/email-clients`' checks name the clients that don't load web fonts, and warn when a stack ends on one.
- **In a PDF or an image**, you pass the font files as bytes. See [PDF](https://www.hyperelements.dev/docs/outputs/pdf#fonts-and-images) and [Image](https://www.hyperelements.dev/docs/outputs/image#fonts-and-images).

## Text direction

A root's `dir` and a text block's own `dir` (Text, Heading, ListItem, TableCell, and a Row) set the direction. Text starts on that side unless you align it: a right-to-left email is right-aligned by default, and an Arabic paragraph in an English email sits on the right.

```tsx
<Email lang="ar" dir="rtl">
  <Text>مرحبا بك</Text>
</Email>
```

## What each output can't show

A familiar CSS name doesn't promise every output can show it. For each style, Elements knows whether each output shows it as asked, partly, or not at all, and `validate()` reports what your design's output can't do: a hover in a PDF, `justifyContent: "space-between"` in an email's Row.

What each email client does with the HTML is a separate set of checks, from the `@hyper-elements/email-clients` plugin: `validate(email, { plugins: [await emailClients()] })`. Rounded corners are the common case. Classic Outlook draws them square, and the plugin notes it:

```text
info email/outlook-degraded at root.children[0].style.borderRadius: borderRadius on this Column in classic Outlook: square corners
```

See [Diagnostics](https://www.hyperelements.dev/docs/diagnostics).

---

# Rendering

Source: https://www.hyperelements.dev/docs/rendering

`render()` turns a design into the output its root asks for. `validate()` runs the same checks without writing anything, and `outline()` prints the layout as text.

```tsx
import { render } from "@hyper-elements/react";

const { html, text } = await render(<Receipt />);
```

<figure class="diagram"><img src="/generated/core-concepts/rendering-flow.svg" width="880" height="318" alt="A design goes through four steps: it is collected in one React render, checked, laid out, and written. validate() and outline() stop after the layout: one returns what is wrong, the other prints the layout. render(), renderPdf() and renderImage() go on to write the output."></figure>

| You want | Call | From |
|----------|------|------|
| An Email's or a Page's HTML, and its plain text | [`render()`](#render) | `@hyper-elements/react` |
| A Document as a PDF | [`renderPdf()`](#renderpdf) | `@hyper-elements/react/pdf` |
| A Canvas as a PNG or an SVG | [`renderImage()`](#renderimage) | `@hyper-elements/react/image` |
| What's wrong with a design, without writing it | [`validate()`](#validate) | `@hyper-elements/react` |
| The layout, as text | [`outline()`](#outline) | `@hyper-elements/react` |

The examples on this page use one receipt email:

<figure class="diagram"><img src="/generated/core-concepts/rendering-receipt.svg" width="880" height="559" alt="The receipt email on desktop, its two columns side by side under the table, and on a phone, the columns stacked and the heading smaller"></figure>

<details>
<summary>The receipt's source</summary>

<!-- example: rendering/receipt.tsx -->
```tsx
import {
  Button,
  Column,
  Email,
  Heading,
  Image,
  LineBreak,
  Link,
  List,
  ListItem,
  MergeTag,
  Row,
  Span,
  Table,
  TableCell,
  TableRow,
  Text,
} from "@hyper-elements/react";

const logo = {
  src: "https://hyperelements.dev/img/orbit-logo.png",
  width: 252,
  height: 128,
};

export default function Receipt() {
  return (
    <Email
      lang="en"
      previewText="Order #10482 has shipped. Here is your receipt."
      style={{ backgroundColor: "#f4f4f5", gap: 16 }}
    >
      <Image src={logo} alt="Orbit" style={{ width: 96 }} />
      <Column
        style={{
          backgroundColor: "#ffffff",
          padding: 32,
          gap: 16,
          borderRadius: 8,
        }}
      >
        <Heading
          level={1}
          style={{ fontSize: 24, mobile: { fontSize: 20 } }}
        >
          Thanks for your order, <MergeTag name="first_name" />
        </Heading>
        <Text>
          Order <Span style={{ fontWeight: 700 }}>#10482</Span> shipped.
          <LineBreak />
          <Link href="https://example.com/orders/10482">Track it</Link>
        </Text>
        <Table
          style={{ cellPadding: [8, 0], rowBorder: "1px solid #e4e4e7" }}
        >
          <TableRow header>
            <TableCell>Item</TableCell>
            <TableCell style={{ textAlign: "right" }}>Price</TableCell>
          </TableRow>
          <TableRow>
            <TableCell>Linen shirt</TableCell>
            <TableCell style={{ textAlign: "right" }}>$48.00</TableCell>
          </TableRow>
        </Table>
        <Row style={{ gap: 16 }}>
          <Column>
            <Text style={{ fontWeight: 700 }}>Shipping to</Text>
            <Text>Ada Lovelace, London</Text>
          </Column>
          <Column>
            <Text style={{ fontWeight: 700 }}>Next steps</Text>
            <List type="number">
              <ListItem>We pack it</ListItem>
              <ListItem>You track it</ListItem>
            </List>
          </Column>
        </Row>
        <Button
          href="https://example.com/orders/10482"
          style={{ backgroundColor: "#15132e", borderRadius: 6 }}
        >
          View your order
        </Button>
      </Column>
      <Text style={{ fontSize: 14, color: "#52525b", textAlign: "center" }}>
        Orbit Inc., 1 Market St, San Francisco
      </Text>
    </Email>
  );
}
```

</details>

## render()

`render(element, options?)` is async. It resolves to:

| Field | What it is |
|-------|------------|
| `html` | The whole document, with no React hydration markers and no client-side JavaScript |
| `text` | The plain-text version, from the same design |
| `head` | What goes in `<head>`: meta tags, the title, the stylesheet |
| `body` | What goes in `<body>` |
| `bodyStyle` | The body's own inline style |
| `diagnostics` | Warnings and notes (severity `warning` and `info`). Errors aren't here: they make `render()` reject |

`head`, `body` and `bodyStyle` are for embedding the output in a page of your own. See [Web pages](https://www.hyperelements.dev/docs/outputs/page#embed-it-in-your-own-page).

A design with errors doesn't render. `render()` rejects with an `ElementsError`, whose `diagnostics` give each problem's `code`, `message` and `path`:

```tsx
import { ElementsError, render } from "@hyper-elements/react";

try {
  await render(<Receipt />);
} catch (error) {
  if (error instanceof ElementsError) {
    for (const { code, message, path } of error.diagnostics) {
      console.error(code, path, message);
    }
  }
  throw error;
}
```

### The plain-text version

`text` is written from the same design, so it never drifts from the HTML. Headings are in capitals, links and buttons show their URL in brackets, list items get their numbers (or a `-`), a table's cells are joined with `|`, and an image shows its alt text. The receipt's:

<!-- output: receiptText -->
```text
[Orbit]

THANKS FOR YOUR ORDER, {{first_name}}

Order #10482 shipped.
Track it (https://example.com/orders/10482)

Item | Price
Linen shirt | $48.00

Shipping to

Ada Lovelace, London

Next steps

1. We pack it
2. You track it

View your order (https://example.com/orders/10482)

Orbit Inc., 1 Market St, San Francisco
```

The preview text isn't in it.

### Options

| Option | Default | What it does |
|--------|---------|--------------|
| `pretty` | `false` | Indents the HTML, for reading it. For sending, keep the compact HTML: white space may change how some email clients show it |
| `mergeTag` | `` (name) => `{{name}}` `` | A function from a merge tag's name to how it's written |
| `plugins` | None | Packages that add checks, such as `@hyper-elements/email-clients`. `validate()` takes them too. See [validate()](#validate) |
| `classPrefix` | `"e"` | What every class name in the stylesheet starts with, for HTML embedded where other CSS is. A Document's page boxes keep the class `elements-page` |
| `hideBelow` | Where the phone styles start | In an Email, the window width in px at and below which what's hidden on phones is hidden |
| `blockMap` | `false` | For tools that preview a design: also returns `blocks`, the UTF-8 byte offset of each block in `html` with its place in the design, for every root. The HTML stays the same. Not with `pretty` ([REFERENCE.md](https://github.com/hyper-elements/hyper-elements/blob/main/packages/react/REFERENCE.md#for-tools-where-each-block-is-in-the-html)) |

```tsx
const { html } = await render(<Receipt />, {
  pretty: true,
  classPrefix: "acme-",
});
```

## renderPdf()

A `Document` becomes a PDF with `renderPdf()`, from `@hyper-elements/react/pdf`. It needs `@react-pdf/renderer` installed, and no browser. This is the receipt from [Designs](https://www.hyperelements.dev/docs/designs#share-content-between-roots), as a Document:

<!-- example: rendering/_scripts/pdf.tsx -->
```tsx
import { writeFile } from "node:fs/promises";
import { renderPdf } from "@hyper-elements/react/pdf";
import ReceiptDocument from "../../designs/receipt-document";

const { pdf, diagnostics } = await renderPdf(<ReceiptDocument />);
for (const { code, message } of diagnostics) console.warn(code, message);
await writeFile("receipt.pdf", pdf);
```

<figure class="diagram"><img src="/generated/core-concepts/rendering-pdf.svg" width="720" height="409" alt="The top of the PDF's first page: the receipt inside the A4 page's margins"></figure>

`render()` of the same Document writes print-ready HTML, for a browser to print. [Documents and PDF](https://www.hyperelements.dev/docs/outputs/pdf) covers pages, headers, footers, fonts and images.

## renderImage()

A `Canvas` becomes a PNG with `renderImage()`, from `@hyper-elements/react/image`, or an SVG with its `format: "svg"` option. It needs `satori` and `@resvg/resvg-js` installed, and no browser. You give it the font files as bytes:

<!-- example: rendering/_scripts/image.tsx -->
```tsx
import { readFile, writeFile } from "node:fs/promises";
import { renderImage } from "@hyper-elements/react/image";
import Card from "../../designs/card";

const regular = await readFile("fonts/Inter-Regular.ttf");
const bold = await readFile("fonts/Inter-Bold.ttf");

const { image, width, height } = await renderImage(<Card />, {
  fonts: [
    { family: "Inter", src: regular },
    { family: "Inter", src: bold, weight: 700 },
  ],
});
console.log(`${width}×${height}`);
await writeFile("card.png", image);
```

<figure class="diagram"><img src="/generated/core-concepts/rendering-image.svg" width="720" height="423" alt="The image: a social card 1200 by 630, with a name, a large headline and a line of text"></figure>

<details>
<summary>The card's source</summary>

<!-- example: designs/card.tsx -->
```tsx
import {
  Canvas,
  Circle,
  Column,
  Heading,
  Path,
  Rect,
  Row,
  Svg,
  Text,
} from "@hyper-elements/react";

const fonts = [
  { family: "Inter", src: "../fonts/Inter-Regular.ttf", weight: 400 },
  { family: "Inter", src: "../fonts/Inter-Bold.ttf", weight: 700 },
];
const INK = "#15132e";
const SUN = "#ffc93c";
const TEAL = "#2dd4bf";
const CORAL = "#ff6b57";
const PINK = "#f9a8d4";
const MIST = "#e0e7ff";

// Six tiles, two across: each a ground, and a shape drawn on it.
const T = 210;
const tiles = [
  [TEAL, "quarter", SUN],
  [CORAL, "dot", MIST],
  [SUN, "ring", INK],
  [INK, "quarter", PINK],
  [PINK, "dot", CORAL],
  [MIST, "quarter", TEAL],
] as const;

function Tile({ at }: { at: number }) {
  const [ground, shape, color] = tiles[at];
  const [x, y] = [(at % 2) * T, Math.floor(at / 2) * T];
  const [cx, cy] = [x + T / 2, y + T / 2];
  const quarter = `M${x} ${y}h${T}a${T} ${T} 0 0 1 ${-T} ${T}z`;
  const ring = { fill: "transparent", stroke: color, strokeWidth: 30 };
  return (
    <>
      <Rect x={x} y={y} width={T} height={T} style={{ fill: ground }} />
      {shape === "quarter" && <Path d={quarter} style={{ fill: color }} />}
      {shape === "dot" && (
        <Circle cx={cx} cy={cy} r={64} style={{ fill: color }} />
      )}
      {shape === "ring" && <Circle cx={cx} cy={cy} r={62} style={ring} />}
    </>
  );
}

export default function Card() {
  return (
    <Canvas
      width={1200}
      height={630}
      fonts={fonts}
      style={{
        backgroundColor: "#4f46e5",
        color: "#ffffff",
        fontFamily: "Inter",
      }}
    >
      <Row style={{ height: 630 }}>
        <Column
          style={{
            height: 630,
            padding: 64,
            justifyContent: "space-between",
          }}
        >
          <Text style={{ fontSize: 32, fontWeight: 700 }}>Orbit</Text>
          <Heading level={1} style={{ fontSize: 80, lineHeight: 1.05 }}>
            Release notes that write themselves
          </Heading>
          <Text style={{ fontSize: 28, fontWeight: 700, color: SUN }}>
            Out now at orbit.example
          </Text>
        </Column>
        <Svg width={2 * T} height={3 * T} style={{ flex: "none" }}>
          {tiles.map((tile, at) => (
            <Tile key={tile.join()} at={at} />
          ))}
        </Svg>
      </Row>
    </Canvas>
  );
}
```

</details>

[Images](https://www.hyperelements.dev/docs/outputs/image) covers fonts, pictures, fitting text and what a Canvas can't draw.

## Merge tags

A [`MergeTag`](https://www.hyperelements.dev/docs/elements/mergetag) is a value your sending service fills in, written in that service's syntax:

```tsx
<Text>
  Hi <MergeTag name="first_name" />, your order has shipped.
</Text>
```

By default it's written as `{{first_name}}`, in the HTML and in the plain text. For another syntax, pass `mergeTag`:

```tsx
// Mailchimp-style: *|FIRST_NAME|*
await render(<Receipt />, { mergeTag: (name) => `*|${name.toUpperCase()}|*` });

// Liquid with spaces: {{ first_name }}
await render(<Receipt />, { mergeTag: (name) => `{{ ${name} }}` });
```

What `mergeTag` returns goes into the HTML as it is, with the name in it escaped, so a syntax with `<` in it (`<%= name %>`) works there too.

A link can be a merge tag as well: `href` takes a URL or a tag, so `<Link href="{{unsubscribe_url}}">` writes `href="{{unsubscribe_url}}"`.

### Tags typed into your text

Prefer `MergeTag`: it follows the `mergeTag` option, so a design moves to another sending service without edits. [Lint](https://www.hyperelements.dev/docs/lint), the checks for what makes an email hard to read, warns where merge syntax is typed into the text instead (`email/lint-merge-syntax`).

Typed tags still work where you need them, for what `MergeTag` doesn't write, such as a condition. Text you write is escaped, and tags without `<`, `>` or `&` in them pass through unchanged: `{{code}}`, `*|FNAME|*` and `{% if vip %}` reach the HTML and the plain text as you wrote them. A tag with `<` in it, typed as text, is escaped in the HTML (`&lt;%= name %&gt;`).

## validate()

`validate(element, options?)` runs the checks `render()` runs, all but one, without writing anything. It's synchronous. What's wrong with the design comes back in `diagnostics`, not as an error:

```tsx
import { validate } from "@hyper-elements/react";

const { valid, diagnostics } = validate(<Receipt />);
```

`valid` is `false` when there's an error. Warnings and notes leave it `true`.

It checks props, styles, children and ids, lays the design out, and reports what the output can't show as asked. The one check it leaves to `render()` needs the written HTML: an email's size against Gmail's limit.

Email client checks aren't built in. They come from a plugin, which `validate()` and `render()` both take:

```tsx
import { emailClients } from "@hyper-elements/email-clients";

const { diagnostics } = validate(<Receipt />, {
  plugins: [await emailClients()],
});
```

See [Diagnostics](https://www.hyperelements.dev/docs/diagnostics).

## outline()

`outline(element)` prints the laid-out design: each block on a line under what holds it, with its width on desktop and what it shows (a heading's words, a link's URL, an image's alt text), and whether a Row stacks on phones. Use it to check a layout without reading HTML, in a test or from an AI coding agent.

```tsx
import { outline } from "@hyper-elements/react";

console.log(outline(<Receipt />));
```

<!-- output: receiptOutline -->
```text
Email 600px: background #f4f4f5
  Image 96px [Orbit] https://hyperelements.dev/img/orbit-logo.png
  Column 600px: background #ffffff
    Heading h1 536px "Thanks for your order, {{first_name}}"
    Text 536px "Order #10482 shipped. / Track it (https://example.com/orders/10482)"
    Table 536px
      TableRow 536px
        TableCell 268px "Item"
        TableCell 268px "Price"
      TableRow 536px
        TableCell 268px "Linen shirt"
        TableCell 268px "$48.00"
    Row 536px: 2 side by side, stacked on phones
      Column 260px
        Text 260px "Shipping to"
        Text 260px "Ada Lovelace, London"
      Column 260px
        Text 260px "Next steps"
        List 260px
          ListItem 236px "We pack it"
          ListItem 236px "You track it"
    Button: background #15132e "View your order" → https://example.com/orders/10482
  Text 600px "Orbit Inc., 1 Market St, San Francisco"
```

Like `render()`, it throws an `ElementsError` when the design has errors.

## The same input, the same output

A design renders the same every time. Rules that inline styles can't express (phone styles, hiding, hover) go in a stylesheet under short classes named after the rule's content, like `.e3k9fa`. The same rule always gets the same class, and the HTML gets no generated ids, only the `id`s you write. Snapshot tests stay stable, and diffs show real changes.

`renderPdf()` and `renderImage()` hold to the same rule: the same design writes the same bytes.

## Where it runs

`render()` runs on your server, with no network calls. It works in plain Node.js, and in Next.js route handlers, Server Components and Client Components' server render. Elements keeps none of its own state in React context, which Server Components don't have, so it renders there too.

`@hyper-elements/react/pdf` and `@hyper-elements/react/image` run in Node.js only.

Fetch your data before you render, and pass it in as props: `render()` doesn't wait for a component that's async or suspends (`jsx/async`).

---

# Themes

Source: https://www.hyperelements.dev/docs/themes

A theme is the brand, written once. Give it to a root, and the design needs almost no styles of its own:

<!-- example: themes/welcome.tsx -->
```tsx
<Email theme={brand} lang="en" previewText="Your Acme account is ready.">
  <Section style={{ apply: ["card"] }}>
    <Heading level={1}>Welcome to Acme</Heading>
    <Text>Your account is ready.</Text>
    <Button href="https://example.com/start">Get started</Button>
    <Button href="https://example.com/docs" variant="secondary">
      Read the docs
    </Button>
  </Section>
  <Section
    tokens={{ colors: { background: "#15132e", foreground: "#ffffff" } }}
    style={{ padding: [24, 32] }}
  >
    <Text style={{ fontSize: token("fontSizes.small") }}>
      Acme Inc., 1 Market St, San Francisco
    </Text>
  </Section>
</Email>
```

<figure class="diagram"><img src="/generated/core-concepts/themes-welcome.svg" width="987" height="360" alt="The welcome email, each part labeled with what in the theme styles it: the card by a named style, the heading and text by roles, the buttons by a role and a variant, the dark band by a scope, and its small text by a token."></figure>

The design names no font, and no color but the band's. Each label in the picture is one part of the theme:

| Part | What it is |
|------|------------|
| [Tokens](#tokens) | The brand's values, by name: `colors.primary`, `spacing.lg` |
| [Roles](#roles) | The tokens built-in elements read by themselves: a Button's background is `colors.primary` |
| [Element defaults and variants](#element-defaults-and-variants) | How every Button looks, and its named versions |
| [Named styles](#named-styles) | A set of styles any element applies by name: a card |
| [Scopes](#scopes) | Other token values for one part of a design: a dark band |

The rest of this page writes that theme, a part at a time. A theme takes any root: the same one styles an Email, a Page, a Document and a Canvas. A design without a theme renders as it always did, and a theme changes only what it defines.

## Tokens

`defineTheme()`, from `@hyper-elements/react` like `token()`, takes the brand's values by name. These are its tokens:

<!-- example: themes/brand.ts -->
```tsx
export const brand = defineTheme({
  colors: {
    background: "#f4f4f5",
    foreground: "#15132e",
    primary: "#4f46e5",
    primaryForeground: "#ffffff",
    muted: "#e0e7ff",
    border: "#e4e4e7",
  },
  fonts: { body: "Helvetica, Arial, sans-serif", heading: "Georgia, serif" },
  fontSizes: { body: 16, small: 13 },
  lineHeights: { body: 1.6 },
  spacing: { md: 16, lg: 32 },
```

There are six groups of tokens: `colors`, `spacing`, `fontSizes`, `lineHeights`, `fonts` and `radii`. A token's value is what the same style takes, so a number is px.

In a design, `token("colors.primary")` stands for a token's value wherever a style takes one:

```tsx
<Text style={{ color: token("colors.primary") }}>Paid</Text>
```

Inside the theme, one token refers to another as `"{colors.primary}"`. That form is for the theme only. In a design it's a plain string, and the error for it says to write `token("colors.primary")`.

## Roles

Some token names are roles. Where the theme defines one, the built-in elements read it without the design naming it. That's why the welcome email's heading is in Georgia and its button is indigo.

| Token | Is |
|-------|----|
| `colors.background` | The root's background, and a scope's |
| `colors.foreground` | Body text's color, in the root and in a scope |
| `fonts.body` | Body text's font |
| `fontSizes.body` | Body text's size, and a Button's |
| `lineHeights.body` | Body text's line height |
| `fonts.heading` | A Heading's font |
| `colors.primary` | A Button's background, and a Link's color |
| `colors.primaryForeground` | A Button's text color |
| `colors.border` | A Divider's color |

Any other name (`muted`, `small`, `lg`) is yours, to use with `token()`.

Body text's styles are set on the root, and Text, table cells and list items inherit them. So set body text with these roles, not with a default for `Text`, which would miss table cells and list items.

## Element defaults and variants

`elements` holds each built-in element's default styles, written as in `style`, and its `variants`: named versions picked with the `variant` prop.

<!-- example: themes/brand.ts -->
```tsx
elements: {
  Heading: {
    by: {
      level: {
        1: { fontSize: 32, mobile: { fontSize: 26 } },
        2: { fontSize: 22 },
      },
    },
  },
  Button: {
    borderRadius: 8,
    variants: {
      secondary: {
        backgroundColor: "{colors.muted}",
        color: "{colors.foreground}",
      },
    },
  },
},
```

- **Every Button** gets `borderRadius: 8`.
- **`<Button variant="secondary">`** also gets the variant's colors. A list of variants merges in order: `variant={["secondary", "small"]}`.
- **`by`** sets a default by one of the element's props. Here it's a type scale: a Heading's size by its `level`.

A variant the theme doesn't give that element is an error that lists the ones it has.

## Named styles

`styles` holds sets of styles that any element applies by name, with `apply` in its `style`:

<!-- example: themes/brand.ts -->
```tsx
styles: {
  card: {
    backgroundColor: "#ffffff",
    padding: "{spacing.lg}",
    gap: "{spacing.md}",
    mobile: { padding: "{spacing.md}" },
  },
},
```

```tsx
<Section style={{ apply: ["card"] }}>…</Section>
<Column style={{ apply: ["card"], gap: 8 }}>…</Column>
```

The element's own styles go beside `apply` and win over it: the Column above has the card's padding and background, and its own `gap`.

Use a variant for a version of one element (a secondary Button), and a named style for a look several elements share (a card).

## Scopes

`tokens` on a Section, Row, Column or Grid changes token values for itself and everything inside it. It's called a scope. A scope that sets `colors.background` or `colors.foreground` takes them as its own background and text color, so the welcome email's dark band is one prop:

```tsx
<Section tokens={{ colors: { background: "#15132e", foreground: "#ffffff" } }}>
  <Text>White text on a dark band</Text>
  <Button href="https://example.com">Still the primary color</Button>
</Section>
```

Scopes nest, and they work in a design that has no theme.

## Which wins

An element's style is merged from these, each over the one before:

1. Its roles
2. Its element's defaults, then its defaults by a prop's value (`by`)
3. Its variants, in order
4. Its named styles, in order
5. Its own `style`

So a style written on the element always wins.

## Next

[Theme reference](https://www.hyperelements.dev/docs/themes/reference) has the rest: every part of `defineTheme()`, which tokens each style takes, overrides for one kind of root (`formats`), `extendTheme()`, tokens in your own elements, typed names, and what each output writes.

---

# Custom elements

Source: https://www.hyperelements.dev/docs/custom-elements

There are three ways to add something of your own to a design. Start with the first, and move down only when you need what the next one adds.

| You want | Use |
|----------|-----|
| To reuse some elements in your own code: a footer, a layout | [A function](#a-function-for-most-things) |
| A block of your own with typed props that are checked like a built-in element's, and that tools see by name | [`defineElement()`](#defineelement) |
| Markup no element writes | [`<Html>`](#html-markup-as-it-is) |

## A function, for most things

A function that returns elements is enough for most designs. It's a React component: use it anywhere the elements it returns can go.

```tsx
function Footer({ company }: { company: string }) {
  return (
    <Text style={{ fontSize: 12, color: "#71717a", textAlign: "center" }}>
      {company}
    </Text>
  );
}

<Email>
  {/* … */}
  <Footer company="Acme Inc., 1 Market St, San Francisco" />
</Email>
```

Elements never sees the function, only the elements it returns. So a wrong prop is yours to catch, with TypeScript. [Designs](https://www.hyperelements.dev/docs/designs#your-own-functions) has what functions can do.

## defineElement()

`defineElement()` makes a custom element: a block with a name and props of its own. Here is a product card, used twice:

<figure class="diagram"><img src="/generated/core-concepts/custom-cards.svg" width="800" height="332" alt="Two product cards side by side, each a photo, a name and a button: the first with a price and an indigo Buy button, the second with a larger name and a gray Sold out button"></figure>

<!-- example: custom/product-card.tsx -->
```tsx
import {
  Button,
  Column,
  Heading,
  Image,
  Text,
  defineElement,
  prop,
} from "@hyper-elements/react";

export const ProductCard = defineElement({
  type: "acme.ProductCard",
  label: "Product card",
  props: {
    name: prop.text({ label: "Name", required: true }),
    photo: prop.image({ label: "Photo", required: true }),
    href: prop.link({ label: "Link", required: true }),
    price: prop.text({ label: "Price" }),
    accent: prop.color({ label: "Accent", default: "#4f46e5" }),
    size: prop.choice(["compact", "large"], {
      label: "Size",
      default: "compact",
    }),
    soldOut: prop.boolean({ label: "Sold out", default: false }),
  },
  render: ({ name, photo, href, price, accent, size, soldOut }) => (
    <Column style={{ gap: 8 }}>
      <Image src={photo} alt={name} />
      <Heading level={3} style={{ fontSize: size === "large" ? 22 : 16 }}>
        {name}
      </Heading>
      {price ? <Text>{price}</Text> : null}
      <Button
        href={href}
        style={{ backgroundColor: soldOut ? "#a1a1aa" : accent }}
      >
        {soldOut ? "Sold out" : "Buy"}
      </Button>
    </Column>
  ),
});
```

Use it like any element:

<!-- example: custom/shop.tsx -->
```tsx
<Row style={{ gap: 16 }}>
  <ProductCard
    name="Night poster"
    photo={poster}
    href="https://example.com/p/1"
    price="$48.00"
  />
  <ProductCard
    name="The Weekly Signal"
    photo={weekly}
    href="https://example.com/p/2"
    size="large"
    soldOut
  />
</Row>
```

### What it adds to a function

- **Its props are checked when the design is read**, not only by TypeScript. A wrong value is a diagnostic with a path, like a built-in element's, so it's caught when the value comes from data, a JSON file or an AI agent:

  <!-- part-of: customRefused -->
  ```text
  error prop/invalid at root.children[0].props.size: size: expected one of "compact", "large", not "huge"
  ```

- **Its defaults are filled in** before `render` runs: `accent` is `"#4f46e5"` where an instance gives none.
- **It stays one named block in the design.** The command line's [`inspect`](https://www.hyperelements.dev/docs/cli/reference#commands) lists it by its `type`, with the props each instance gave:

  <!-- part-of: customInspect -->
  ```text
  root.children[0].children[0] acme.ProductCard: props.name, props.photo, props.href, props.price
  ```

- **Every output renders it.** It's replaced by the built-in elements its `render` returns before the layout is worked out.
- **Its props take a theme's tokens**: `<ProductCard accent={token("colors.primary")} />`.

### The spec

| Field | What it is |
|-------|------------|
| `type` | A namespace, a dot and a capitalized name: `"acme.ProductCard"`. The namespace keeps it from clashing with built-in elements |
| `label` | Its name for people |
| `description` | Optional: what it's for |
| `props` | Its props, made with `prop.*` |
| `placement` | `"block"` (the default) goes where a block goes. `"section"` goes where a Section goes, and renders a Section |
| `render` | The block as built-in elements, from its props with defaults applied |

`render` is a pure function of its props: no hooks, and nothing read from outside its props, so it renders anywhere. It returns one element, which takes your element's place.

Its second argument is `{ theme }`: the [theme](https://www.hyperelements.dev/docs/themes)'s tokens as values where the instance is, scopes around it included (`theme.colors.primary`), for values `render` works out itself. It's empty without a theme.

### Props

| Helper | Takes |
|--------|-------|
| `prop.text()` | Text |
| `prop.color()` | A color |
| `prop.image()` | An image: a URL, or `{ src, width, height }` |
| `prop.link()` | A link: a URL or a merge tag, or `{ href, target }` |
| `prop.boolean()` | `true` or `false` |
| `prop.number()` | A number, with optional `min`, `max` and `integer` |
| `prop.length()` | A length, px by default |
| `prop.choice(values, …)` | One of `values` |
| `prop.fontFamily()` | A font stack |
| `prop.fontWeight()` | A font weight |

Each takes `label`, and optionally a `description`, `required: true` or a `default`. Their types carry through to `render`'s props and to the JSX. A color, length or font prop also takes a theme's token in JSX, and `render` gets its value where the instance is.

### On each instance

Beside its own props, an instance takes `id`, `hidden`, and `style={{ flex }}` for its share of a Row. Its `flex` and `hidden` go onto the element it renders. It takes no `variant` or named styles: apply those in what it renders.

An `id` inside a custom element is written after its instance's: an `id="photo"` in the card is `first-photo` in `<ProductCard id="first" />`. Without an instance `id`, ids inside are left out (with an `id/dropped` note), so two instances never share an id.

### A section-level element

With `placement: "section"`, a custom element goes where a Section goes, and renders one:

```tsx
import { Text, Section, defineElement, prop } from "@hyper-elements/react";

export const Banner = defineElement({
  type: "acme.Banner",
  label: "Banner",
  placement: "section",
  props: {
    text: prop.text({ label: "Text", required: true }),
    background: prop.color({ label: "Background", default: "#111827" }),
  },
  render: ({ text, background }) => (
    <Section
      style={{
        backgroundColor: background,
        padding: [16, 40],
        color: "#ffffff",
        textAlign: "center",
      }}
    >
      <Text>{text}</Text>
    </Section>
  ),
});
```

## Html: markup as it is

`Html` is a built-in element, and the escape hatch: for markup no element writes, it writes yours as it is, in an email and on a page.

```tsx
import { Email, Html } from "@hyper-elements/react";

<Email>
  <Html
    html={'<p style="margin:0">Written <b>as it is</b>.</p>'}
    text="Written as it is."
  />
</Email>
```

Or give the markup as JSX inside the block, which React writes:

```tsx
<Html text="Written as JSX.">
  <p style={{ margin: 0 }}>Written <b>as JSX</b>.</p>
</Html>
```

`text` is what the block reads as in the plain-text version. Without it, the markup's words are used. A Document's PDF and a Canvas's image can't draw markup, so they draw that plain text, and say so.

> **Warning:** Nothing in an `Html` block is checked or escaped. Put only markup you wrote there, never a customer's data. Everywhere else, values you pass as children or props are escaped for you.

Inside an `Html` block, you're back to writing email HTML yourself: tables for Outlook, inline styles, and testing in each client. Reach for it last.

---

# Command line

Source: https://www.hyperelements.dev/docs/cli

`@hyper-elements/cli` is the `hyper-elements` command. It previews, checks and renders your designs from the shell, with no script of your own.

| You want | Run |
|----------|-----|
| A live page of your designs while you write them | [`npx hyper-elements dev emails/`](#dev) |
| What's wrong with them, with the email client checks | [`npx hyper-elements check emails/`](#check) |
| Their HTML, PDFs and images, as files | [`npx hyper-elements render emails/`](#render) |
| An email as Outlook, Gmail and Apple Mail draw it | [`npx hyper-elements preview emails/welcome.tsx`](#preview) |
| A design's layout, as text | [`npx hyper-elements outline emails/welcome.tsx`](#outline) |

<figure class="diagram"><img src="/generated/core-concepts/cli-dev.png" width="1200" height="760" alt="The page dev serves: a list of the designs on the left, and on the right the receipt email's diagnostics and the email itself, drawn at desktop width"></figure>

Other readers of this page:

- **You have an HTML email, not a design.** `check` and `preview` take it as it is, with nothing installed. See [Any HTML email](#any-html-email).
- **You make designs from a template.** See [Templates in the command line](https://www.hyperelements.dev/docs/templates/cli).
- **You're an agent, or writing for one.** See [With an agent](https://www.hyperelements.dev/docs/cli/reference#with-an-agent).

## Install

```bash
npm install -D @hyper-elements/cli
```

Install it beside `@hyper-elements/react` 0.4 or 0.5 (0.5 for [templates](https://www.hyperelements.dev/docs/templates)), in the project that holds your designs, and run it as `npx hyper-elements`. It renders with your project's own versions of Elements and React. It runs on Node.js 20.6 or later, and on Bun 1.3 or later as `bunx --bun hyper-elements`.

Some of what it does needs a package you install only if you want it:

| For | Install |
|-----|---------|
| The email client checks and `preview`, for your designs | `@hyper-elements/email-clients` |
| A Document's PDF | `@react-pdf/renderer` |
| A Canvas's image | `satori` and `@resvg/resvg-js` |

## A design file

A design file is a module whose default export is a component that renders an `<Email>`, a `<Page>`, a `<Document>` or a `<Canvas>`:

<!-- example: cli/emails/welcome.tsx -->
```tsx
import { Button, Column, Email, Heading, Text } from "@hyper-elements/react";

export default function Welcome({ name }: { name: string }) {
  return (
    <Email
      lang="en"
      previewText="Your Acme account is ready. Create your first project."
      style={{ backgroundColor: "#f4f4f5" }}
    >
      <Column
        style={{
          backgroundColor: "#ffffff",
          padding: 32,
          gap: 16,
          borderRadius: 8,
        }}
      >
        <Heading level={1} style={{ fontSize: 24 }}>
          Welcome, {name}
        </Heading>
        <Text>Your account is ready.</Text>
        <Button href="https://example.com/new">Create a project</Button>
      </Column>
    </Email>
  );
}
Welcome.PreviewProps = { name: "Ada" };
```

Its props come from `--props file.json`, else the component's `PreviewProps`, else `{}`.

Give the commands files or folders. A folder is searched for designs, leaving out `node_modules`, build output, and folders whose name starts with `.` or `_`, so shared parts can live in `emails/_parts/`. TypeScript, path aliases and workspace packages work as they do in your project.

## dev

```bash
npx hyper-elements dev emails/
```

`dev` prints a URL on `127.0.0.1` and serves the page whose top is pictured above. It lists the designs and shows the one you pick: an Email or a Page at desktop width and at 375px, a Document's PDF, a Canvas's image, its diagnostics, and an Email's previews in each email client. It renders every design again when the project's source changes. It writes nothing in the project, and runs until Ctrl-C.

## check

```bash
npx hyper-elements check emails/
```

<!-- output: cliCheck -->
```text
✓ emails/receipt.tsx (Email)
    info email/outlook-degraded at root.children[1].style.borderRadius: borderRadius on this Column in classic Outlook: square corners [outlook] See: https://www.caniemail.com/features/css-border-radius/
    info email/outlook-degraded at root.children[1].children[4].style.borderRadius: borderRadius on this Button in classic Outlook: square corners [outlook] See: https://www.caniemail.com/features/css-border-radius/
    info email/phone-styles at root: On phones, the email's phone styles don't apply: it keeps its desktop styles (Rows still stack) [gmail-app-other] See: https://www.caniemail.com/features/css-at-media/
✓ emails/welcome.tsx (Email)
    info email/outlook-degraded at root.children[0].style.borderRadius: borderRadius on this Column in classic Outlook: square corners [outlook] See: https://www.caniemail.com/features/css-border-radius/
2 designs: 0 errors, 0 warnings, 0 skipped
```

`check` runs every check [`validate()`](https://www.hyperelements.dev/docs/rendering#validate) runs, and writes nothing. It adds two sets of checks `validate()` doesn't run by itself:

- **The email client checks**, where the project has `@hyper-elements/email-clients`. Each names the clients it's about, as `[outlook]` above: classic Outlook, the Windows desktop app.
- **[Lint](#lint)**, on each Email and Page.

An error fails the run (exit code 1). Warnings and notes (`info`, as above) don't, unless you pass `--max-warnings 0`, which fails it on any warning.

## render

```bash
npx hyper-elements render emails/welcome.tsx
```

<!-- output: cliRender -->
```text
✓ emails/welcome.tsx (Email) → out/emails/welcome.html, out/emails/welcome.txt
    info email/outlook-degraded at root.children[0].style.borderRadius: borderRadius on this Column in classic Outlook: square corners [outlook] See: https://www.caniemail.com/features/css-border-radius/
1 design: 0 errors, 0 warnings, 0 skipped
```

`render` writes each design's output under `out/`, at the design's path from the current folder:

| Root | Files |
|------|-------|
| Email | `name.html` and `name.txt` |
| Page | `name.html` |
| Document | `name.pdf` (and its print HTML with `--html`) |
| Canvas | `name.png` (or `name.svg` with `--format svg`) |

It prints the same diagnostics as `check`. A design with errors writes nothing. `--out <dir>` writes somewhere else, and `--base emails` leaves `emails/` out of the paths: `out/welcome.html`.

For a Document or a Canvas, the CLI loads the fonts and images the design names and hands them to the PDF or image engine. See [PDFs and images](https://www.hyperelements.dev/docs/cli/reference#pdfs-and-images).

## preview

```bash
npx hyper-elements preview emails/welcome.tsx
```

<!-- output: cliPreview -->
```text
✓ emails/welcome.tsx (Email)
    info email/outlook-degraded at root.children[0].style.borderRadius: borderRadius on this Column in classic Outlook: square corners [outlook] See: https://www.caniemail.com/features/css-border-radius/
  outlook: out/clients/emails/welcome/outlook.html
  outlook-com: out/clients/emails/welcome/outlook-com.html
  outlook-com.mac: out/clients/emails/welcome/outlook-com.mac.html
  gmail: out/clients/emails/welcome/gmail.html
  gmail.mac: out/clients/emails/welcome/gmail.mac.html
  apple-mail: out/clients/emails/welcome/apple-mail.html
  apple-mail.iphone: out/clients/emails/welcome/apple-mail.iphone.html
1 design: 0 errors, 0 warnings, 0 skipped
```

`preview` writes each Email as the email clients draw it: one self-contained HTML file per client. Open one in a browser. It draws the email, and lists what that client removed or changed:

<figure class="diagram"><img src="/generated/core-concepts/cli-preview.svg" width="880" height="481" alt="The welcome email's preview file for classic Outlook: a note that it removed border-radius, and the email drawn with square corners"></figure>

Nothing is sent anywhere to be drawn. To have the CLI open the files and report what each client changed, add `--findings`. See [preview](https://www.hyperelements.dev/docs/cli/reference#preview) in the reference, and the [email client emulator](https://www.hyperelements.dev/docs/email-client-emulator).

## outline

```bash
npx hyper-elements outline emails/welcome.tsx
```

<!-- output: cliOutline -->
```text
Email 600px: background #f4f4f5
  Column 600px: background #ffffff
    Heading h1 536px "Welcome, Ada"
    Text 536px "Your account is ready."
    Button: background #0879a1 "Create a project" → https://example.com/new
```

`outline` prints one design laid out, each block with its width, as [`outline()`](https://www.hyperelements.dev/docs/rendering#outline) does.

## Lint

`check`, `render` and `dev` run [lint](https://www.hyperelements.dev/docs/lint) on each Email and Page: links that don't say where they go, images without alternate text, faint or small text, and more. Its findings are warnings and notes, so they change the exit code only past `--max-warnings`. `--no-lint` leaves them out. Its options go in `package.json`. See [Lint](https://www.hyperelements.dev/docs/cli/reference#lint) in the reference.

## Any HTML email

`check` and `preview` also take an HTML email however it was made (MJML, React Email, by hand, an email builder's export). No design's code runs, so neither React nor Elements is needed, and the CLI brings the email client checks with it. Run the package by its name, with nothing installed:

```bash
npx @hyper-elements/cli check email.html
npx @hyper-elements/cli preview email.html
```

See [Any HTML email](https://www.hyperelements.dev/docs/cli/reference#any-html-email) in the reference. To try it in a browser first, open the [email testing playground](https://www.hyperelements.dev/email-testing).

## JSON and exit codes

Every command takes `--json`: one JSON line per design, then a summary line. And every command exits with one of three codes:

| Exit code | Means |
|-----------|-------|
| `0` | Every design rendered, checked or previewed without errors |
| `1` | A design has errors, failed to load, or the run passed `--max-warnings` |
| `2` | The run couldn't do what it was asked: a usage error, no designs found, Elements not installed |

In CI, fail the build on any problem in your designs:

```bash
npx hyper-elements check emails/ --max-warnings 0
```

[JSON and exit codes](https://www.hyperelements.dev/docs/cli/reference#json-and-exit-codes) in the reference has the JSON's fields and every case of each code.

## Next

- [Command line reference](https://www.hyperelements.dev/docs/cli/reference): every command and option, how fonts and images are loaded, and how the CLI runs your designs.
- [Templates in the command line](https://www.hyperelements.dev/docs/templates/cli): `describe`, `design new`, `design set` and values files.

# Email

Source: https://www.hyperelements.dev/docs/outputs/email
