| `extract/no-design`, `extract/no-root` | A default export that isn't a component written in the file, or no root in its JSX | `1` |

---

# Diagnostics

Source: https://www.hyperelements.dev/docs/diagnostics

Every check Hyper Elements runs ends up as a diagnostic: a stable code, a severity, a message that says what to do instead, and the path to the value. Errors stop a render. Warnings and notes tell you what an output can't show as you asked.

```tsx
import { Email, Text, validate } from "@hyper-elements/react";

const { valid, diagnostics } = validate(
  <Email>
    <Text style={{ marginBottom: 16 }}>Hi</Text>
  </Email>
);
// valid: false
// diagnostics[0].code: "style/unknown"
// diagnostics[0].path: "root.children[0].style.marginBottom"
// diagnostics[0].message: "\"marginBottom\" isn't a style a Text takes: use the parent's gap, or padding. …"
```

Props and styles are typed from each element's definition, so in TypeScript a margin like this one is a type error before it's a diagnostic. `validate()` catches it at runtime too, with the path and the fix, for JavaScript, generated designs and agents.

## A diagnostic

```ts
interface Diagnostic {
  code: string;                              // stable, for tools to match on: "style/unknown"
  severity: "error" | "warning" | "info";
  message: string;                           // what's wrong, and what to do instead
  path: string;                              // where: "root.children[1].style.padding"
  nodeId?: string;                           // the node's id, where it has one
  clients?: readonly string[];               // the email clients it's about (from email-clients' checks)
  fix?: string;                              // what to change
  see?: string;                              // where to see more about it (an https URL)
}
```

`formatDiagnostics(diagnostics)` prints each on a line, with its clients, fix and where to see it where it has them.

## Email client checks

`@hyper-elements/react` checks the design, and what Elements' own writers can't write. What each email client
removes or changes in the HTML comes from a separate package, `@hyper-elements/email-clients`, through a plugin:

```tsx
import { emailClients } from "@hyper-elements/email-clients";

validate(<Welcome />, { plugins: [await emailClients()] });                          // the clients most email is read in
validate(<Welcome />, { plugins: [await emailClients({ clients: ["gmail", "outlook"] })] });   // only these clients
```

Its diagnostics name the clients they're about in `clients`, with a `fix`. Without the plugin, an Email gets one note,
`email/more-checks`, saying where the client checks are; `plugins: []` leaves it out.

The same package is the email client emulator: it shows the email as each email client shows it, on your machine, with
what each client changed. See [Email client emulator](https://www.hyperelements.dev/docs/email-client-emulator).

Before 0.4, the client checks were part of this package, with an `emailClients` option and `EMAIL_CLIENTS` (now
exported by `@hyper-elements/email-clients`). Passing `emailClients` now gives an `email/clients-moved` note with the
replacement, until 0.5. Where WebAssembly isn't available, the plugin runs only the checks from caniemail's tables, and
says so first (`email/captured-checks`).

### Plugins

A plugin is `{ name, api: PLUGIN_API, check?, checkOutput? }`. `check` sees a frozen copy of the laid-out design,
`checkOutput` the written HTML and the root's type (`render()` only). What a plugin returns is checked: a diagnostic that doesn't fit (a
code for another kind of root, an error, a path that isn't in the design) is left out, with a `plugin/invalid`
warning. Another root's code is taken only as a note ending in `-ignored`, saying that what the plugin was given
doesn't apply to this root (`email/clients-ignored` on a Page). A plugin that throws, or returns something that can't
be read, gives a `plugin/failed` warning; the render still completes.

The path walks the design from the root: `root.children[2].style.justifyContent` is the third child's `justifyContent` style.

## Severities

| Severity | Means | `render()` | `validate()` |
|----------|-------|------------|--------------|
| `error` | The design can't be rendered as written | Rejects with an `ElementsError` | `valid: false` |
| `warning` | It renders, but not as you asked: an output can't show something, a width doesn't fit | In `diagnostics` | `valid: true` |
| `info` | A note: shown as asked, except somewhere (classic Outlook's square corners) | In `diagnostics` | `valid: true` |

## ElementsError

A design with errors makes `render()` reject, and `outline()` throw, with an `ElementsError`. Its `diagnostics` hold everything found, and its message lists the errors, one per line:

```text
[Elements] The template has 1 error:
error style/unknown at root.children[0].style.marginBottom: "marginBottom" isn't a style a Text takes: use the parent's gap, or padding. …
```

`formatDiagnostics(diagnostics)` writes any list in that one-line form, for logs.

```tsx
import { ElementsError, formatDiagnostics, render } from "@hyper-elements/react";

try {
  const { html, diagnostics } = await render(<Receipt />);
  if (diagnostics.length) console.warn(formatDiagnostics(diagnostics));
} catch (error) {
  if (error instanceof ElementsError) console.error(formatDiagnostics(error.diagnostics));
  throw error;
}
```

## Codes you'll meet

### Errors: how the design is written

| Code | What triggers it |
|------|------------------|
| `jsx/markup` | An HTML element in a design (`<b>`, `<br>`, `<div>`), or around the root |
| `jsx/root` | Something beside the root, such as two roots |
| `jsx/async` | A component that's async or suspends. Load its data first and pass it in as props |
| `jsx/error` | A component that threw inside a `<Suspense>` |
| `prop/unknown` | A prop the element doesn't take, often a style written as a prop: `<Email backgroundColor="#fff">` |
| `prop/required` | A required prop is missing: a Button's `href`, an Image's `src` |
| `prop/invalid` | A prop's value isn't one it takes, such as a `javascript:` link |
| `style/unknown` | A style the element doesn't take: a margin, a root's `padding`, an old name like `align` (the message names the new one) |
| `style/invalid` | A style's value isn't one it takes: `justifyContent: "around"`, `fontWeight: 650` |
| `mobile/not-allowed` | A phone style the element doesn't take on phones |
| `mobile/not-supported` | Phone styles in a Document or a Canvas, which have no phone width |
| `hidden/not-supported` | `hidden` in a Document or a Canvas |
| `hover/not-allowed` | A hover style the element doesn't take |
| `children/not-allowed` | A child the element can't hold: a Heading in a Text, a root inside a root |
| `children/text-not-allowed` | Loose text where it can't go, such as straight in a Row. Put it in a Text or Heading |
| `children/one-only` | A second `PageHeader` or `PageFooter` in a Document |
| `id/duplicate` | Two elements with one `id` |
| `id/invalid` | An `id` that doesn't start with a letter |
| `mobile/invalid`, `hover/invalid`, `hidden/invalid` | A `mobile`, `hover` or `hidden` value that isn't one they take |
| `target/unsupported` | An element the output can't draw: an `Svg` or a `PageNumber` in an email (Gmail and classic Outlook drop inline SVG) |
| `document/page-number` | A `PageNumber` in a Page or a Canvas, which have no pages |
| `element/not-supported` | An element under a root that doesn't take it. The message names the roots that do |
| `prop/not-supported` | A prop for some roots only (a `defineElement()`'s, made with `roots`), under another |
| `style/not-supported` | A style for some roots only, under another, in `style` or in its `mobile` or `hover` block |
| `theme/schema` | A theme that isn't one: a token name that isn't letters and digits (`gray-900`: nest it as `gray.900`) or is `__proto__`, `constructor` or `prototype`, a value its group doesn't take, a `{ base, dark }` value (modes come later), a second `by` prop or a `by` value its prop never has, `variants` on a root, a group that isn't one yet (`shadows`), or a theme given both at a document's top level and on its root |
| `theme/missing-token` | A token that doesn't exist (the message suggests the one meant), or a token in a design with no theme |
| `theme/value` | A token from another group than the place takes: a `spacing` token as a color |
| `theme/cycle` | Tokens, or named styles, that refer to each other in a loop |
| `variant/unknown` | A `variant` the theme doesn't give that element (the message lists those it does) |
| `style/unknown-name` | A named style in `apply` the theme doesn't have |
| `style/apply-place` | `apply` inside `mobile` or `hover`, or on a custom element |
| `email/layer` | A Layer email can't draw: in an email it's an Image as wide as the Layer with one child over it |
| `custom/render` | Your own element's `render` throws, or returns something other than one element |
| `custom/depth` | Your own elements expanding into each other too deep, as when one contains itself |
| `custom/duplicate` | Two different `defineElement()` definitions with one `type` |

### Warnings and notes: what an output can't show

| Code | Severity | What triggers it |
|------|----------|------------------|
| `email/unsupported` | warning | A style or prop email can't show. The message says what it shows instead: `justifyContent: "space-between"` starts children at the left |
| `email/degraded` | info | Not quite as the Email writer can write it: a wrapped Row's gap between its lines, or `overflow: "hidden"` on a Column or Grid without a box of its own |
| `email/video-thumbnail` | warning | A Vimeo Video with no `thumbnail`, which can't be found without the network |
| `email/more-checks` | info | An Email checked without email-clients' plugin: where the email client checks are (`plugins: []` leaves it out) |
| `email/clients-moved` | info | `emailClients` passed: the option moved to email-clients' plugin (until 0.5) |
| `plugin/invalid` | warning | An entry of `plugins` that isn't a plugin (a Promise: `emailClients()` not awaited), or diagnostics a plugin returned that don't fit |
| `plugin/unsupported` | warning | A plugin written for another plugin `api` |
| `plugin/duplicate` | warning | Two plugins with one `name`; the second is ignored |
| `plugin/failed` | warning | A plugin's hook threw, or returned something other than a list |
| `web/unsupported` | warning | The same, for a page |
| `layout/shrunk` | warning | A Row's children's widths add up to more than it has. They're narrowed to fit, as a browser does |
| `layout/overflow` | warning | Content wider than the space it has: a Row's children at their minimum widths, a box wider than its parent, a Table's columns wider than the Table |
| `style/ignored` | warning | A style that does nothing where it is, such as `flex` on a child that isn't in a Row |
| `email/layer-phone` | info | On phones, an email keeps a Layer's height and cuts its image at the sides |
| `hidden/everywhere` | warning | Hidden on phones and on desktop, so it never shows |
| `theme/inherited` | warning | A theme's default for an element (`elements.Text.color`) replaces the body text's color, font, size or line height a box sets for what it holds. Set them with the roles `colors.foreground`, `fonts.body`, `fontSizes.body` and `lineHeights.body` |
| `id/dropped` | info | An `id` inside one of your own elements used without one of its own is left out |
| `mobile/not-shown` | warning | Your own element's `mobile` style that nothing it renders has a phone version of |
| `jsx/compat` | warning | A `compat` prop on a root, which is left out |
| `document/overflow` | warning | A page's content looks taller than the page (an estimate) |
| `canvas/overflow` | warning | A Canvas's content looks taller than the Canvas (an estimate) |

`renderPdf()` and `renderImage()` add codes of their own (`pdf/…`, `image/…`). See [PDF](https://www.hyperelements.dev/docs/outputs/pdf#diagnostics) and [Image](https://www.hyperelements.dev/docs/outputs/image#diagnostics).

## Where support data comes from

Each style and prop of each element declares how each output shows it: `full`, `partial`, or `none` (with what it shows instead). One pass reads those declarations for the styles and props you set, and turns each into a diagnostic. A test keeps the declarations true: every style and prop, at every value, either changes the output or gives a diagnostic. Nothing is dropped silently.

Each declaration names its evidence: the writer's own output checked in Chromium, or plain CSS. Some are marked as not checked yet: those are only ever notes, and say so. What email clients do with the HTML isn't declared here: it's `@hyper-elements/email-clients`' to check.

## Use it in CI and with agents

`validate()` is synchronous, writes nothing, and returns what's wrong rather than throwing it, so it fits in a unit test:

```tsx
import { expect, test } from "vitest";
import { validate } from "@hyper-elements/react";
import { Welcome } from "./emails/welcome";

test("the welcome email is valid and has no warnings", () => {
  const { valid, diagnostics } = validate(<Welcome name="Ada" />);
  expect(valid).toBe(true);
  expect(diagnostics.filter((d) => d.severity === "warning")).toEqual([]);
});
```

Match on `code`, which is stable for tools to match on, and show people the `message`.

For an agent, `validate()` is the feedback loop. Each message says what to use instead and where, so an agent that writes a design, validates it and reads the messages can fix its own mistakes: a margin becomes the parent's `gap`, a style written as a prop goes into `style`. Pair it with [`outline()`](https://www.hyperelements.dev/docs/rendering#outline) to check the layout as text, without reading HTML.

Before it writes, an agent can ask what a root takes. `@hyper-elements/react/inspect` says it as data: `describeElements({ root: "Email" })` lists the elements an Email takes, each prop and style with its kind and the roots that take it, and `inspect(element)` lists each element of a design with whether its root takes it (`allowed`), what it's given and the diagnostics on it.

```tsx
import { describeElement, inspect } from "@hyper-elements/react/inspect";

describeElement("Svg", { root: "Email" });   // undefined: an Email doesn't take one
inspect(<Welcome />).nodes.filter((node) => !node.allowed || node.problems.length);   // what's wrong, and where
```

> **Tip:** Point your agent at the package's guide, `node_modules/@hyper-elements/react/GUIDE.md`, before it writes a design. It lists every element on a line, and the mistakes that most often fail a first try.

---

# Test emails in Outlook and Gmail locally

Source: https://www.hyperelements.dev/docs/email-client-emulator

`@hyper-elements/email-clients` is a free JavaScript and TypeScript library for checking existing HTML emails and previewing Outlook, Gmail and Apple Mail locally. It takes a Hyper Elements email, or complete HTML from MJML, React Email, an email builder or a hand-written email; the HTML needs no React. Use the library in your code or [`@hyper-elements/cli`](#test-an-email-from-the-shell) from the shell. No account, API key or test send is needed, and the email is never uploaded.

`renderInEmailClients()` returns a preview per client: a self-contained HTML page that opens in a browser and lists what the client changed.

## Supported email clients

[Try the email testing playground](https://www.hyperelements.dev/email-testing) to paste an existing HTML email, select clients, and inspect previews and compatibility findings in your browser.

We reverse-engineered each of these email clients, classic Outlook included, by testing thousands of emails in the real client and measuring what it does to them. The emulator is a model of each one, 98% accurate on average:

| Client | ID | Accuracy |
|--------|------|----------|
| Classic Outlook for Windows | `outlook` | 97% |
| Outlook.com and new Outlook | `outlook-com`, `outlook-com.mac` | 99% |
| Outlook for Mac, light and dark | `outlook-mac`, `outlook-mac.dark` | 98% |
| Gmail on the web | `gmail`, `gmail.mac` | 99% |
| Gmail app on Android and an iPhone | `gmail-app`, `gmail-app-other`, `gmail-app.iphone` | 98% |
| Apple Mail on a Mac and an iPhone, light and dark | `apple-mail`, `apple-mail.dark`, `apple-mail.iphone`, `apple-mail.iphone.dark` | 98% |
| Yahoo Mail, light and dark | `yahoo`, `yahoo.mac`, `yahoo.dark`, `yahoo.mac.dark` | 99% |
| AOL Mail | `aol`, `aol.mac` | 99% |

More email clients are on the way.

Name the clients you want with `emailClients: ["outlook", "gmail-app"]`; without it you get the default set (see [Options](#options)). `apple-mail` is previewed on a Mac and on an iPhone, 393px wide, and `gmail-app` on Android and on an iPhone, 345px wide. `gmail-app-other` is a non-Gmail account in the Gmail app, which drops the email's `<style>`. `yahoo` and `aol` are drawn in their message panes, 758px and 869px wide. AOL Mail's dark mode leaves the email as it is, so `aol.dark` matches `aol`.

## How accurate it is

The emulator isn't a guess from a table of supported CSS. We tested thousands of emails in each real client, measured what it removes, rewrites and how it lays out the rest, and reverse-engineered a model of it. Every release is tested against the real clients again, on emails the models weren't built from.

- **Classic Outlook is drawn as Word draws it.** Classic Outlook lays email out with Word, and the emulator follows Word's rules, so spacing, line wrapping, tables and what Outlook ignores come out as Outlook draws them.
- **Dark mode too.** Apple Mail, Outlook for Mac, Yahoo Mail and AOL Mail are previewed in dark mode, reverse-engineered the same way, with more clients' dark modes on the way.

Classic Outlook's engine runs only on Windows with Office installed. The emulator runs anywhere your code does, on a Mac or Linux, in CI and in an agent's loop, in milliseconds, with the same result every time.

## Test a Hyper Elements email

```bash
npm i @hyper-elements/email-clients
```

```tsx
import { Button, Column, Email, Heading, Text } from "@hyper-elements/react";
import { renderInEmailClients } from "@hyper-elements/email-clients";

const welcome = (
  <Email previewText="Your account is ready" style={{ backgroundColor: "#f4f4f5" }}>
    <Column style={{ backgroundColor: "#ffffff", padding: 32, gap: 16, borderRadius: 12 }}>
      <Heading level={1} style={{ fontSize: 24 }}>Welcome aboard</Heading>
      <Text>Your account is ready.</Text>
      <Button href="https://example.com/start" style={{ borderRadius: 999 }}>Get started</Button>
    </Column>
  </Email>
);

const { previews, skipped, diagnostics } = await renderInEmailClients(welcome, { dark: true });

previews.map((preview) => preview.id);
// ["outlook", "outlook-com", "outlook-com.mac", "gmail", "gmail.mac",
//  "apple-mail", "apple-mail.iphone", "apple-mail.dark", "apple-mail.iphone.dark"]

const outlook = previews.find((preview) => preview.id === "outlook");
// { id: "outlook", client: "outlook", variant: "desktop", dark: false, width: 820,
//   filename: "outlook.html", html: "<!doctype html>…" }

skipped[0];
// { client: "outlook", dark: true, reason: "Classic Outlook's dark mode isn't measured" }

diagnostics[0].message;
// "borderRadius on this Column in classic Outlook: square corners"
```

What happens next is up to you or your agent: write `outlook.html` to a file and open it, load it in Playwright and take a screenshot, or read what the client changed (see [What a preview tells you](#what-a-preview-tells-you)). Opened in Chromium, the Outlook preview shows the card and the button with square corners, as classic Outlook draws them.
