## Test any HTML email

An email built another way (MJML, React Email, by hand, an email builder's export) can be tested as it is: `renderInEmailClients()` takes its HTML as a string too. React and `@hyper-elements/react` aren't needed for that: `npm i @hyper-elements/email-clients` is enough.

```bash
npm install @hyper-elements/email-clients
```

Save this as `preview-email.mjs` beside your complete `welcome.html` email:

```js
import { mkdir, readFile, writeFile } from "node:fs/promises";
import { renderInEmailClients } from "@hyper-elements/email-clients";

const html = await readFile("welcome.html", "utf8");
const { previews } = await renderInEmailClients(html, { emailClients: ["outlook", "gmail-app"] });
await mkdir("out", { recursive: true });
for (const preview of previews) await writeFile(`out/${preview.filename}`, preview.html);
```

Run `node preview-email.mjs`, then open `out/outlook.html` in Chromium or Chrome. You can also screenshot it or read what the client changed.

It takes the whole email, from `<html>` to `</html>`, exactly as you send it, and the preview options: `emailClients`, `dark`, `fonts`, `widths` and `computers`.

Its `diagnostics` list what each client previewed removes or changes in the HTML, each with its line:

```ts
const { diagnostics } = await renderInEmailClients(html, { emailClients: ["outlook", "gmail", "gmail-app"] });
// [{ code: "email/html-css", severity: "info", line: 5, excerpt: "<style>", clients: ["outlook"],
//    message: "This email may have an @media in a <style>: the client applies no media query, …", fix: "…" }]
```

## Test an email from the shell

[`@hyper-elements/cli`](https://www.hyperelements.dev/docs/cli) checks and previews an existing HTML email with no script or React installation:

```bash
npx @hyper-elements/cli check email.html
npx @hyper-elements/cli preview email.html
```

The preview command writes `out/clients/email/outlook.html` and the other client previews. To draw them and collect findings automatically, install the CLI and `playwright-core` together, and have Chrome, Edge or Playwright's Chromium installed:

```bash
npm install -D @hyper-elements/cli playwright-core
npx hyper-elements preview email.html --findings
```

If you need Chromium, download it once with `npx hyper-elements preview --install-browser`. For Hyper Elements designs, [install the CLI in your project](https://www.hyperelements.dev/docs/cli#install) and run `npx hyper-elements preview emails/welcome.tsx`.

For an agent or a CI job that wants what each client changed as data, there are three ways, by what it has:

1. **A Chromium the CLI finds.** `npx hyper-elements preview emails/welcome.tsx --findings --json` opens each preview in Chromium, with `playwright-core` (install it beside the CLI): the browser `CHROME_PATH` names, else Playwright's Chromium (`npx hyper-elements preview --install-browser` downloads it), else an installed Chrome or Edge. Its JSON line gives each preview's `ready` (`ok`; `incomplete` where a font or an image didn't load; `error`) and its `findings`: what the client removed, what was missing, the fonts and the findings listed under [What a preview tells you](#what-a-preview-tells-you).
2. **A browser of its own.** Where the CLI finds none, the run exits `2` with `"browser": null, "reason": "no-browser"` (`"no-playwright-core"` where that isn't installed), and the files are written all the same. Open each file, or the URLs `preview --serve` prints for a browser that can't open `file://` paths, wait for `<html data-email-client-ready>`, and read the JSON in `#email-client-findings`.
3. **No browser at all.** `npx hyper-elements check emails/welcome.tsx --json` gives the email client checks: each problem with the clients it's about and what to change. That's what's known without drawing the email.

## Why it matters

- **No send-and-wait loop.** A preview takes as long as a render, so you can check every change, not only the last one before a campaign.
- **Free, with no API.** There's no account to make, no key to keep, and no limit on how many previews you make.
- **Nothing leaves your machine.** The email isn't sent anywhere or uploaded to a screenshot service, which matters for customer data, unreleased products and regulated content.
- **It runs where your code runs.** In a test, in CI, or in an agent's loop: an agent with a browser can open a preview, read what the client changed, and fix the design.
- **The same answer every time.** The same email gives the same preview, so a preview can be a snapshot in a test.

## Compared with screenshot services

| | Email client emulator | Screenshot services |
|---|---|---|
| Cost | Free | Paid, per test or per seat |
| Setup | `npm i` | An account and an API key |
| Where it runs | Your machine, your CI, your agent | Their servers, with your email uploaded |
| Speed | Milliseconds | Minutes per test |
| What you get | A preview per client, and what each one changed | A screenshot per client |
| Clients | The clients above, with more on the way | Dozens, on real devices |

The emulator checks every change in the clients above; a screenshot service covers the clients it doesn't yet, such as the Outlook app and Samsung Email. [Litmus alternatives](https://www.hyperelements.dev/alternatives/litmus) compares Hyper Elements with Litmus, Parcel and Mailosaur.

## Options

| Option | What it does |
|--------|--------------|
| `emailClients` | The clients to emulate (default: `outlook`, `outlook-com`, `gmail`, `apple-mail`) |
| `dark` | Also a dark-mode preview, for the clients that have one (Apple Mail on a Mac and an iPhone, Outlook for Mac, Yahoo Mail and AOL Mail, today) |
| `widths` | The width a client's preview draws the email at, where it isn't the client's own: `{ "outlook-com": 540 }` for Outlook.com's reading pane beside the message list. Webmail matches media queries at the browser window's width, not the pane's, so a narrow pane keeps the email's desktop styles, as it does for its readers |
| `computers` | Webmail draws with the reader's computer's fonts. Outlook.com, Gmail, Yahoo Mail and AOL Mail on the web are each previewed on Windows (`outlook-com`, `gmail`, `yahoo`, `aol`) and on a Mac (`outlook-com.mac`, `gmail.mac`, `yahoo.mac`, `aol.mac`). `computers: ["windows"]` keeps one |
| `fonts` | `"url"` (the default) loads the open fonts the previews draw with from a CDN; `"inline"` puts them in each preview, so it draws offline |
| `plugins`, and `render()`'s other options | Passed to `render()`. The email client checks for the clients emulated are added for you |

`renderInEmailClients()` returns:

- `previews`: `{ id, client, model, computer, variant, dark, width, filename, html, approximate }` for each client and variant, light before dark;
- `skipped`: what wasn't emulated, and why (a client with no dark mode);
- `diagnostics`: `render()`'s, with the email client checks for the clients emulated.

A preview isn't the email you send: that's `render()`'s `html`.

## What a preview tells you

Each preview lists, at its top, what the client changed and anything it couldn't draw as the client does:

- **Removed:** what the client removed or rewrote, and how often (rounded corners, `rgba()` colors, a `<style>` rule).
- **Missing:** a font the machine opening the preview doesn't have, the email's own web font where it didn't load, an image that didn't load.
- **Fonts:** the system fonts it drew with.
- **Findings:** a Heading or Button that a client draws on more lines, text that doesn't read in dark mode, and where Gmail clips the email.

## Checks and the emulator

The same package checks a design without drawing it: `emailClients()` is a plugin for `validate()` and `render()`, and names the clients each problem is about, with the fix. See [Diagnostics](https://www.hyperelements.dev/docs/diagnostics).

```tsx
import { validate } from "@hyper-elements/react";
import { emailClients } from "@hyper-elements/email-clients";

const { diagnostics } = validate(welcome, { plugins: [await emailClients()] });
// info email/outlook-degraded … borderRadius on this Column in classic Outlook: square corners [outlook]
```

The checks cover more clients than the emulator (the Outlook app, Samsung Email and others, from caniemail's tables).

## Common questions

### How do I test an email in Outlook without sending it?

Render it with `renderInEmailClients()` from `@hyper-elements/email-clients` and open its `outlook` preview in Chromium: it shows the email as classic Outlook for Windows draws it, and lists what Outlook changed. There's no test send, no Outlook to install and no account. For Outlook.com and the new Outlook, open the `outlook-com` preview.

### Can I trust a preview of classic Outlook?

Yes. We reverse-engineered classic Outlook by testing thousands of emails in it, and the emulator draws email as Outlook does: its spacing, line wrapping, tables and what it removes. See [How accurate it is](#how-accurate-it-is).

### How do I preview an email in Gmail?

Open the `gmail` preview for Gmail on the web, or name `gmail-app` in `emailClients` for the Gmail app at a phone's width. Each preview lists, at its top, what Gmail removed or changed in the email.

### Can I test an email I didn't build with Hyper Elements?

Yes. Pass its HTML to `renderInEmailClients()` as a string; React and Hyper Elements aren't needed for that (see [Test any HTML email](#test-any-html-email)). To bring a React Email template over to Hyper Elements instead, use `npx @hyper-elements/migrate` (see [From React Email](https://www.hyperelements.dev/docs/migrate/react-email)).

### Is it free?

Yes. `@hyper-elements/email-clients` is free and runs on your machine: no API key, no account, no cost per preview, and the email isn't sent or uploaded anywhere.

### Can my coding agent use it?

Yes. An agent can run `npx hyper-elements preview emails/welcome.tsx --findings --json` (or call `renderInEmailClients()` after rendering), read what each client changed, and fix the design. See [Test an email from the shell](#test-an-email-from-the-shell) and [AI agents](https://www.hyperelements.dev/docs/guides/ai-agents).

---

# Lint

Source: https://www.hyperelements.dev/docs/lint

`@hyper-elements/lint` checks an email or a page for what makes it hard to read or use: links that don't say where they go, images without alternate text, text too faint or too small, headings out of order, merge syntax typed into the copy by hand. Elements' own checks say whether a design is correct, and the [email client emulator](https://www.hyperelements.dev/docs/email-client-emulator) what each email client does to it; lint says whether it's good.

```bash
npm i -D @hyper-elements/lint
```

It's a plugin, so it runs wherever `validate()` and `render()` do: in a test, on a server, in the browser. For HTML made any other way, there's [`lintHtml()`](#any-html-email).

```tsx
import { render, validate } from "@hyper-elements/react";
import { lint } from "@hyper-elements/lint";

const { html, diagnostics } = await render(<Welcome />, { plugins: [lint()] });
diagnostics[0];
// { code: "email/lint-link-text", severity: "warning", path: "root.children[2]",
//   message: 'The Button says "Click here": a screen reader lists links by their words alone',
//   fix: 'say where it goes ("Confirm your email"), or give it an aria-label',
//   see: "https://www.hyperelements.dev/docs/lint#link-text" }
```

Its findings are [diagnostics](https://www.hyperelements.dev/docs/diagnostics) like Elements' own: warnings and notes, never errors, so lint never stops a render. On an Email they're `email/lint-<rule>`, on a Page `page/lint-<rule>`; a Document and a Canvas get none. Each says where in the design it is, what to do, and links to its rule below.

## It reads the design, not the HTML

Lint reads the laid-out design, as each output writes it, so it knows what a reader gets:

- **At desktop and at phone width.** A block hidden on phones isn't checked there, and text gets the size it's shown at on each: 16px on desktop and 12px on phones is small on phones. A finding names the width it's found at where it's only one.
- **What's behind the text.** Contrast is checked against the nearest background, with see-through ones mixed in, as WCAG does. Text over a `Layer`'s image isn't checked where the image is drawn.
- **What each link says.** A `Button`'s words or `aria-label`, a `Link`'s words, or the `alt` of the images it holds.

## Options

```tsx
lint({
  rules: { "text-size": "off", contrast: "info" }, // a rule's severity, or off
  kind: "marketing",                               // a marketing email needs a way to unsubscribe
});
```

`rules` sets a rule's severity, `"off"`, `"info"` or `"warning"`, by its id. `kind` is `"marketing"` or `"transactional"`: `"marketing"` turns on [`unsubscribe`](#unsubscribe). A rule, severity or kind lint doesn't know throws a `TypeError` when `lint()` is called.

`rules` lists every rule with its default severity, the roots it runs on, what it checks, its fix and its docs link, for a tool that shows them:

```ts
import { rules } from "@hyper-elements/lint";
rules.find((rule) => rule.id === "contrast");
// { id: "contrast", severity: "warning", roots: ["Email", "Page"], summary: "…", fix: "…", see: "…#contrast" }
```

## From the command line

[`@hyper-elements/cli`](https://www.hyperelements.dev/docs/cli#lint) runs lint in `check`, `render` and `dev`, with its options from `package.json`:

```json
{ "hyperElements": { "lint": { "rules": { "text-size": "off" }, "kind": "marketing" } } }
```

```bash
npx hyper-elements check emails/                   # lint's findings with the other checks
npx hyper-elements check emails/ --max-warnings 0  # fail CI on any warning
npx hyper-elements check email.html                # lintHtml() on any HTML email
```

## Any HTML email

`lintHtml()`, from `@hyper-elements/lint/html`, runs the rules HTML can show on any HTML email, however it was made (MJML, React Email, by hand). It needs nothing else installed: no Elements, no React.

```ts
import { lintHtml } from "@hyper-elements/lint/html";

const { diagnostics } = lintHtml(html, { rules: { title: "off" } });
diagnostics[0];
// { code: "lint/image-alt", severity: "warning", line: 42, column: 7,
//   message: 'This image has no alt attribute: a screen reader reads out its file name instead (src "hero.png")',
//   fix: "…", see: "https://www.hyperelements.dev/docs/lint#image-alt" }
```

Its findings are `lint/<rule>`, each with its line and column. It takes the same options as `lint()`. On HTML with an `<html>` or a `<body>`, a whole document, it also checks the heading order, one `<h1>`, the language and the title. Outlook's conditional comments (`<!--[if mso]>`) are skipped: what's in them is Outlook's copy of what's outside them. An `Html` block's markup in a design gets the same rules, at the block's `html`, with its line.

HTML can't say what a design can. `lintHtml()` doesn't check contrast or text size (that needs the CSS cascade), and doesn't check merge syntax: in HTML, a hand-typed `{{name}}` and a `MergeTag`'s output look the same.

## Rules

<!-- rules:start (written from the package's rules by its docs test: UPDATE_LINT_DOCS=1 pnpm --filter @hyper-elements/lint test docs) -->

### `image-alt`

A link holds only images with no alternate text, so a screen reader has nothing to read out for it. In HTML, any link with nothing to name it, and an image with no alt attribute at all.

A warning by default, on an Email and a Page, and on HTML (an `Html` block's and `lintHtml()`'s). **Fix:** give the image an alt that says where the link goes, or the link an aria-label.

### `alt-text`

An image's alternate text is a file name, a URL or a word like "image" or "logo", which says nothing about it.

A note by default, on an Email and a Page. **Fix:** say what the image shows ("Tarn's logo", "A blue bowl"), or leave alt empty if it's only decoration.

### `link-text`

A link or button says only "click here", "read more" or the like: screen readers list links by their words alone.

A warning by default, on an Email and a Page, and on HTML (an `Html` block's and `lintHtml()`'s). **Fix:** say where it goes ("Confirm your email"), or give it an aria-label.

### `link-empty`

A link or button has no words, alternate text, aria-label or title: nothing names it.

A warning by default, on an Email and a Page. **Fix:** give it words, or an aria-label.

### `link-target`

A link goes nowhere (empty, #, a mailto: or tel: with no address or number), over http: rather than https:, or (in HTML) runs a script.

A warning by default, on an Email and a Page, and on HTML (an `Html` block's and `lintHtml()`'s). **Fix:** link to the page it's for, over https:.

### `heading-order`

A heading is more than one level below the heading before it (an h2 followed by an h4).

A warning by default, on an Email and a Page, and on a whole HTML document (`lintHtml()`'s). **Fix:** use the next level down, and style it as you want it to look.

### `heading-one`

There's more than one level-1 heading.

A note by default, on an Email and a Page, and on a whole HTML document (`lintHtml()`'s). **Fix:** keep one level-1 heading, the title, and use level 2 for the rest.

### `heading-empty`

A heading has no words.

A warning by default, on an Email and a Page, and on HTML (an `Html` block's and `lintHtml()`'s). **Fix:** give it words, or take it out.

### `contrast`

Text is too faint against its background to read easily: under WCAG AA's 4.5:1, or 3:1 for large text.

A warning by default, on an Email and a Page. **Fix:** darken the text or lighten the background (or the reverse) until it reaches the ratio.

### `text-size`

Body text is under 14px, hard to read on a phone.

A note by default, on an Email and a Page. **Fix:** make it 14px or larger, on phones at least (style.mobile.fontSize).

### `lang`

The email or page doesn't say its language, so a screen reader may read it in the wrong one.

A warning by default, on an Email and a Page, and on a whole HTML document (`lintHtml()`'s). **Fix:** give the root a lang ("en", "fr") (in HTML, give <html> a lang ("en", "fr")).

### `dir`

The language is written right to left, but the root doesn't say so.

A warning by default, on an Email and a Page. **Fix:** give the root dir="rtl".

### `title`

The page has no title for the browser's tab and for screen readers.

A note by default, on a Page, and on a whole HTML document (`lintHtml()`'s). **Fix:** give the root a title (in HTML, give the email a <title> in its <head>).

### `preview-text`

The email has no preview text, or a very short one: inboxes show its first words instead.

A note by default, on a Email. **Fix:** give the Email a previewText of 30 characters or more.

### `merge-syntax`

Merge syntax ({{name}}, *|NAME|*, %%name%%) is typed into the text, where a MergeTag would write it.

A warning by default, on an Email and a Page. **Fix:** use <MergeTag name="…" />, which writes your sending service's syntax (the mergeTag option).

### `unsubscribe`

A marketing email (kind: "marketing") has no unsubscribe link.

A warning by default, on a Email. **Fix:** add a link to unsubscribe or manage preferences, or the service's MergeTag for one.

### `video-title`

A video's title is the default, "Video": the alternate text of its thumbnail in an email.

A note by default, on an Email and a Page. **Fix:** give it a title that says what the video is.

### `role-button`

A link has role="button": screen readers announce a button, which a link in an email isn't.

A warning by default, on HTML (an `Html` block's and `lintHtml()`'s). **Fix:** take the role off: a link is a link, however it looks.

<!-- rules:end -->

---

# Theme reference

Source: https://www.hyperelements.dev/docs/themes/reference

[Themes](https://www.hyperelements.dev/docs/themes) introduces a theme with one example. This page lists everything a theme takes and the rules it follows.

## defineTheme()

`defineTheme()` takes the theme's parts and returns it as frozen data. Every part is optional.

| Part | What it holds |
|------|---------------|
| `colors` | Colors: `primary: "#0f766e"` |
| `spacing` | Lengths for padding, gaps and borders: `md: 16` |
| `fontSizes` | Font sizes: `body: 16` |
| `lineHeights` | Line heights: `body: 1.6` |
| `fonts` | Font stacks: `body: "Inter, Arial, sans-serif"` |
| `radii` | Corner radii: `card: 8`, or `card: { topLeft: 8, topRight: 8 }` |
| `elements` | Each built-in element's defaults, its defaults by one prop's value (`by`), and its `variants` |
| `styles` | Named styles, applied with `style={{ apply: [...] }}` |
| `formats` | Overrides for one kind of root: `email`, `page`, `document`, `canvas` |

The first six are tokens.

## Tokens

A token's value is what the same style takes (a number is px). It's checked when the design is read, whether a design uses it or not.

- **Names are letters and digits**, so each token is also a CSS custom property's name. To group tokens, nest them: `colors: { gray: { 100: "#f3f4f6", 900: "#111827" } }` makes `colors.gray.100` and `colors.gray.900`. `gray-900` is an error that says to nest it.
- **One token refers to another** as `"{colors.primary}"`, the [W3C Design Tokens](https://www.designtokens.org/) format's alias: `link: "{colors.primary}"`. That works only inside a theme. A reference to a token that doesn't exist, to one in another group, or a loop of references, is an error.
- **A token has one value.** `{ base, dark }` values are an error until dark mode comes, as are groups Elements doesn't take yet (`shadows`, `keyframes`).

### token()

In a design, `token("colors.primary")` stands for a token's value, where a style or part of one takes it:

```tsx
<Column
  style={{
    padding: token("spacing.lg"),
    border: { width: 1, style: "solid", color: token("colors.border") },
  }}
>
  <Text style={{ color: token("colors.primary") }}>Paid</Text>
</Column>
```

A style takes tokens from the groups of its kind:

| Style | Takes tokens from |
|-------|-------------------|
| A color (`color`, `backgroundColor`, a border's `color`) | `colors` |
| A length (`fontSize`, `width`, `gap`, …) | `spacing`, `fontSizes` |
| `padding`, a border's `width` | `spacing` |
| `borderRadius` | `radii` |
| `fontFamily` | `fonts` |
| `lineHeight` | `lineHeights` |

A token from another group is an error (`theme/value`), and so is one that doesn't exist (`theme/missing-token`), which names the token meant where it's a typo away. `brand.tokens.colors.primary` is the same as `token("colors.primary")`.

### Roles

Nine token names are roles: the built-in elements read them by themselves.

| Token | Is |
|-------|----|
| `colors.background` | The root's background, and a scope's |
| `colors.foreground` | Body text's color, in the root and in a scope |
| `fonts.body` | Body text's font |
| `fontSizes.body` | Body text's size, and a Button's |
| `lineHeights.body` | Body text's line height |
| `fonts.heading` | A Heading's font |
| `colors.primary` | A Button's background, and a Link's color |
| `colors.primaryForeground` | A Button's text color |
| `colors.border` | A Divider's color |

Where a theme's default for an element replaces the color, font, size or line height a box sets for what it holds, `validate()` warns (`theme/inherited`).

## Element defaults

`elements.Button: { … }` is every Button's default style. Styles inside it are written as in `style`, with `mobile` and `hover` blocks, and may refer to tokens.

```ts
elements: {
  Button: {
    borderRadius: 8,
    padding: [12, 24],
    hover: { backgroundColor: "#115e59" },
  },
  Divider: {
    borderTop: { width: 2, style: "solid", color: "{colors.border}" },
  },
}
```

`by` sets a default by one of the element's props, a choice or a boolean. A type scale is a Heading's style by its level:

```ts
elements: {
  Heading: {
    by: {
      level: {
        1: { fontSize: 36, mobile: { fontSize: 28 } },
        2: { fontSize: 24 },
        3: { fontSize: 20 },
      },
    },
  },
}
```

A value the prop never has (a level 7) is an error. Other differences are variants.

## Variants

`variants` are an element's named versions, picked with its `variant` prop. A list merges in order:

```tsx
const brand = defineTheme({
  elements: {
    Button: {
      variants: {
        secondary: { backgroundColor: "#f3f4f6", color: "#111827" },
        small: { padding: [6, 12], fontSize: 13 },
      },
    },
  },
});

<Button href="https://example.com" variant="secondary">Learn more</Button>
<Button href="https://example.com" variant={["secondary", "small"]}>
  Later
</Button>
```

Every built-in element but the roots takes `variant`. A variant the theme doesn't give that element is an error that lists the ones it has.

## Named styles

`styles` are named styles any element can apply, in order, with `apply` at the top of its `style`:

```tsx
const brand = defineTheme({
  styles: {
    card: {
      backgroundColor: "#ffffff",
      padding: 32,
      borderRadius: 8,
      mobile: { padding: 16 },
    },
    quiet: { color: "#6b7280", fontSize: 13 },
  },
});

<Column style={{ apply: ["card"], gap: 16 }}>
  <Text style={{ apply: ["quiet"] }}>Ships in 2 days</Text>
</Column>
```

A named style, a variant or an element default may apply named styles too. Named styles that apply each other in a loop are an error. A custom element takes no named styles: apply them in what it renders.

## The merge order

An element's style is merged from, lowest first:

1. Its roles
2. Its element's defaults, then its defaults by its prop's value (`by`)
3. Its variants, in order
4. Its named styles, in order
5. Its own `style`

Each `mobile` and `hover` block merges key by key the same way. A style the element sets itself, outside a block, also replaces the theme's phone and hover values for it: `style={{ padding: 8 }}` stays 8 on phones, whatever the theme's `mobile` says.

## Scopes

`tokens` on a Section, Row, Column or Grid changes tokens for itself and everything it holds. A scope that sets `colors.background` or `colors.foreground` takes them as its own background and text color.

- **Scopes nest.** The nearest one around an element wins.
- **A reference in the theme follows them.** With `link: "{colors.primary}"`, a scope that changes `colors.primary` changes `link` inside it too.
- **A scope can refer to the tokens around it** with `token()`.
- **Scopes work without a theme.**

## formats

`formats` overrides the theme for one kind of root, merged over the rest:

```ts
const brand = defineTheme({
  fontSizes: { body: 16 },
  formats: {
    document: { fontSizes: { body: 11 }, fonts: { body: "Georgia, serif" } },
    email: { elements: { Button: { borderRadius: 4 } } },
  },
});
```

What a root can't show is left out of the theme there: a theme's phone and hover styles do nothing in a Document. Every root's overrides are checked whichever root reads the theme.

## extendTheme()

`extendTheme(base, overrides)` makes a theme from another, for a brand over a shared base or a customer over a brand. Objects merge key by key at every depth, and anything else (a value, a list) is replaced:

```ts
const customer = extendTheme(brand, {
  colors: { primary: "#b91c1c" },
  fonts: { body: "Helvetica, Arial, sans-serif" },
});
```

## Your own elements

A [custom element](https://www.hyperelements.dev/docs/custom-elements#defineelement)'s color, length and font props take a token like a style does. Its `render` gets the theme's tokens where the instance is, scopes included, as values in its second argument:

```tsx
const Badge = defineElement({
  type: "acme.Badge",
  label: "Badge",
  props: { tint: prop.color({ label: "Tint" }) },
  render: ({ tint }, { theme }) => {
    const muted = String(theme.colors?.muted ?? "#f3f4f6");
    const style = { backgroundColor: tint ?? muted, padding: [2, 8] } as const;
    return <Text style={style}>New</Text>;
  },
});

<Badge tint={token("colors.primary")} />
```

## Typed names

Register your theme, once in your app, to type every token, variant and named style:

```ts
declare module "@hyper-elements/react" {
  interface Register {
    theme: typeof brand;
  }
}
```

Then `token("colors.primry")`, `variant="tertiary"` and `apply: ["crad"]` are type errors. Without a registered theme they're strings, checked when the design is read. A theme made with `extendTheme()` can be registered too.

## What's written

A theme's values are written into each output as values, as if the design had set them: an email, a PDF and an image hold no theme.

- **A Page** also writes its tokens as CSS custom properties (`--colors-primary`, `--fontSizes-body`) on its root, and a scope's where they differ, for your own CSS and `Html` blocks.
- **A builder design** gets the values each block has. `toDesign()`, which writes a design for the [visual editor](https://www.hyperelements.dev/docs/guides/visual-editor), notes that it keeps no theme.
- **`inspect()`**, from `@hyper-elements/react/inspect`, lists the theme: its tokens and their values, the roles it defines, its named styles and each element's variants.

Every theme problem is a [diagnostic](https://www.hyperelements.dev/docs/diagnostics) with the path to the token, style or variant it's about: `root.theme.elements.Button.variants.ghost`.

---

# Command line reference

Source: https://www.hyperelements.dev/docs/cli/reference

[Command line](https://www.hyperelements.dev/docs/cli) introduces the commands with one project. This page has every command and the details of each.

## Commands

| Command | What it does |
|---------|--------------|
| `render <files or folders…>` | Writes each design's output under `--out` (default `out/`): an Email's `name.html` and `name.txt`, a Page's `name.html`, a Document's `name.pdf`, a Canvas's `name.png` |
| `check <files or folders…>` | Runs `validate()` with the email client checks and lint, and writes nothing |
| `outline <file>` | Prints the design laid out, each block with its width, as [`outline()`](https://www.hyperelements.dev/docs/rendering#outline) does |
| `preview <files or folders…>` | Writes each Email as the email clients show it, one file per client, with the [email client emulator](https://www.hyperelements.dev/docs/email-client-emulator) |
| `dev <files or folders…>` | Serves a page on `127.0.0.1` that shows each design, rendered again when the project changes |
| `inspect <files or folders…>` | Lists each element of a design, what it's given, whether its root takes it and the problems found on it |
| `describe [Element \| template.tsx]` | Lists the elements a design can use, with their props and styles; `--root Email` narrows it to what that root takes. Given a template module, what the template takes: its formats, fields, image regions and rules |
| `design new <template> -o <name.values.json>` | Writes a design made from a [template](https://www.hyperelements.dev/docs/templates), as a values file, once the template has checked its values |
| `design set <name.values.json> <field=value>…` | Changes some of a values file's values, checked by the template; the file is left as it was if they fail |
| `template extract <design> --id <id> --field <id>… -o <file>` | Writes a template from an approved design: each `--field` names an `id` in it, whose literal text or image becomes a field |
| `migrate …` | Runs [`@hyper-elements/migrate`](https://www.hyperelements.dev/docs/migrate/react-email) with the arguments given |

## Options

| Option | Commands | What it does |
|--------|----------|--------------|
| `--out <dir>` | `render`, `preview` | Where files are written, `out` by default |
| `--base <dir>` | `render`, `preview` | Outputs keep their path from this folder, the current one by default |
| `--props <file.json>` | all | Props for every design given, in place of its `PreviewProps` |
| `--json` | all | One JSON line per design, then a summary line |
| `--clients <a,b>` | `render`, `check`, `preview`, `dev` | The email clients to check for, or to preview |
| `--no-lint` | `render`, `check`, `dev` | Leaves out lint's checks |
| `--max-warnings <n>` | `check` | Fails the run (exit 1) with more than `n` warnings |
| `--rendered` | `check` | Also renders, for the check only the written HTML has |
| `--stdout` | `render` | Writes the one design's HTML, PDF or image to stdout |
| `--pretty` | `render` | Indents the HTML |
| `--html` | `render` | Also writes a Document's print HTML |
| `--format <png\|svg>` | `render` | A Canvas's image format, `png` by default |
| `--scale <n>` | `render`, `check` | A Canvas's pixels per px, 1 by default |
| `--public <dir>` | `render`, `check`, `dev` | Where `/paths` are read from |
| `--refresh`, `--offline` | `render`, `check` | Fetch remote fonts and images again, or fetch nothing |
| `--dark` | `preview`, `dev` | Also the dark previews |
| `--fonts <url\|inline>` | `preview`, `dev` | Where a preview's stand-in fonts come from |
| `--findings`, `--screenshots` | `preview` | Draw each preview in Chromium and report what it found, or save a PNG of it |
| `--serve` | `preview` | Serves the previews on `127.0.0.1` until Ctrl-C |
| `--port <n>` | `dev` | The port to serve on |
| `--timeout <seconds>` | all | How long a process rendering designs may run, 60 by default |

The options for templates (`--template-format`, `--require-template`, and those of `design` and `template extract`) are in [Templates in the command line](https://www.hyperelements.dev/docs/templates/cli). `npx hyper-elements --help` prints all of them.

## render

`render` writes each output at the design's path from the current folder: `render emails/` writes `out/emails/welcome.html` and `out/emails/welcome.txt`. `--out <dir>` replaces `out`, and `--base emails` makes the paths start inside `emails/`: `out/welcome.html`.

It prints each design's diagnostics, with the email client checks where the project has `@hyper-elements/email-clients`, as `check` runs them. `--clients` picks the clients. `--pretty` indents the HTML, and `--stdout` writes one design's HTML, PDF or image to stdout. A design with errors writes nothing.

### PDFs and images

A Document is drawn with [`renderPdf()`](https://www.hyperelements.dev/docs/outputs/pdf) and a Canvas with [`renderImage()`](https://www.hyperelements.dev/docs/outputs/image), so install their engines beside Elements: `@react-pdf/renderer` for PDFs, `satori` and `@resvg/resvg-js` for images. `--html` also writes a Document's print HTML. `--format svg` writes a Canvas as SVG, and `--scale 2` with twice the pixels.

Neither engine loads a font or an image itself. The CLI loads the ones the design names and hands them over:

| Source | Read from |
|--------|-----------|
| `fonts/Inter.ttf`, `./logo.png` | The design's folder |
| `/logo.png` | `--public <dir>`; by default the first `public/` beside a `package.json`, from the design's folder up |
| `data:` | The URI itself |
| `https://…` | Fetched once and cached in `node_modules/.cache/hyper-elements/`; `--refresh` fetches again, `--offline` fetches nothing |

Give fonts as TTF, OTF or WOFF files: neither engine draws WOFF2, Google Fonts' default. A source that can't be loaded is left out with a `cli/asset` warning that says why. A Document's PDF is written on Node.js only: on Bun, `render` refuses a Document (`cli/bun`).

## check

`check` runs every check `validate()` runs, without writing anything.

- **Email client checks** run where the project has `@hyper-elements/email-clients` (`npm i -D @hyper-elements/email-clients`), naming the clients each problem is about. `--clients gmail,outlook` picks the clients.
- **[Lint](#lint)** runs on each Email and Page.
- **`--rendered`** also renders each design, for the one check that needs the written HTML: an email's size against Gmail's limit.
- **`--max-warnings 0`** fails the run on any warning.

## Lint

`check`, `render` and `dev` run [lint](https://www.hyperelements.dev/docs/lint) on each Email and Page: links that don't say where they go, images without alternate text, faint or small text, headings out of order, a missing `lang`, merge syntax typed into the text. Its findings are warnings and notes (`email/lint-<rule>`, `page/lint-<rule>`), so they change the exit code only past `--max-warnings`. `check` of an HTML email runs its HTML rules (`lint/<rule>`, each at its line). `--no-lint` leaves them out.

Its options go in the `package.json` nearest the current folder, read once when the run (or `dev`) starts:

```json
{
  "hyperElements": {
    "lint": { "rules": { "text-size": "off" }, "kind": "marketing" }
  }
}
```

[Lint](https://www.hyperelements.dev/docs/lint) lists the rules and what `kind` does. An option of the wrong shape, or a rule, severity or kind lint doesn't know, exits 2 before anything is checked. Lint is the project's copy where the design resolves one (`npm i -D @hyper-elements/lint` picks its version), else the CLI's own, with an `info` note, `cli/lint-copy`.

## preview

`preview` writes each Email as the email clients show it, with the project's `@hyper-elements/email-clients` (`renderInEmailClients()`): one self-contained HTML file per client and variant, under `out/clients/<its path>/<name>/` (`out/clients/emails/welcome/` for `emails/welcome.tsx`). `--clients`, `--dark` and `--fonts inline` are [its options](https://www.hyperelements.dev/docs/email-client-emulator#options). A design whose root isn't an Email is skipped.

A preview file draws the email when a browser opens it, and lists what the client changed.

- **`--findings`** has the CLI read those findings for you. It needs `playwright-core` installed beside the CLI (`npm install -D playwright-core`); nothing else does. It opens each file in Chromium and reports what it found. It uses the first of these that starts: the browser `CHROME_PATH` names, Playwright's own Chromium (`npx hyper-elements preview --install-browser` downloads it), then an installed Chrome or Edge.
- **`--screenshots`** also writes a PNG of each preview beside it.
- **`--serve`** serves the previews on `127.0.0.1` and prints each one's URL, for a browser that can't open `file://` paths. It runs until Ctrl-C.

Nothing is sent anywhere to be drawn: the requests a preview makes are its stand-in fonts from jsDelivr (`--fonts inline` puts them in each file) and the email's own images and web fonts.

## Any HTML email

`check` and `preview` also take an HTML email however it was made (MJML, React Email, by hand, an email builder's export): an `.html` or `.htm` file given by name, or `-` to read one from stdin. No design's code runs, so neither React nor Elements is needed:

```bash
npx @hyper-elements/cli check email.html
cat email.html | npx @hyper-elements/cli preview -
```

To draw the previews and collect findings automatically, install the CLI and `playwright-core` together, and have Chrome, Edge or Playwright's Chromium installed:

```bash
npm install -D @hyper-elements/cli playwright-core
npx hyper-elements preview email.html --findings
```

If you need Chromium, download it once with `npx hyper-elements preview --install-browser`.

Each diagnostic has the `line` in the file and an excerpt of it. `check` runs [lint](#lint)'s HTML rules on it too. A folder's HTML files aren't picked up, since a folder of designs often holds the HTML rendered from them: give them by name (`check emails/*.html`).

To try the client previews before installing anything, open the [email testing playground](https://www.hyperelements.dev/email-testing), which runs the email-clients package in your browser.

## dev

```bash
npx hyper-elements dev emails/ docs/
```

`dev` prints a URL on `127.0.0.1` and serves a page that lists the designs and shows the one you pick: an Email or a Page at desktop width and at 375px, a Document's PDF, a Canvas's image, its diagnostics, and, for an Email with `@hyper-elements/email-clients`, links to its previews in each email client.

It renders every design again when the project's source, or a workspace package it depends on, changes. It writes nothing in the project, and runs until Ctrl-C. It serves on a free port; `--port <n>` picks one, to forward from a container or a remote machine (the path still starts with a random token).

## Templates

A [template](https://www.hyperelements.dev/docs/templates) is a design with fields: what may change, and the rules each value must meet. A design made from one is a values file, `name.values.json`, or a TSX file whose root is the template.

`render`, `check`, `inspect` and `outline` run such a design once per format, each with its own line and file. A value the template refuses exits `1`, and `render` writes nothing for a format that fails. `--require-template` fails anything a template didn't check.

[Templates in the command line](https://www.hyperelements.dev/docs/templates/cli) has every command and flag, values files, trusted templates and the diagnostics. [Template examples](https://www.hyperelements.dev/docs/templates/examples) runs them on real ones.

## JSON and exit codes

With `--json`, stdout holds one JSON line per design, then a summary line, and nothing else. What designs print goes to stderr. A design's line, laid out here to read:

<!-- json: cliJson -->
```json
{
  "version": 1,
  "command": "check",
  "file": "drafts/broken.tsx",
  "input": "template",
  "root": "Email",
  "status": "error",
  "outputs": [],
  "diagnostics": [
    {
      "code": "style/unknown",
      "severity": "error",
      "message": "\"marginBottom\" isn't a style a Text takes: use the parent's gap, or padding. See Text in @hyper-elements/react/GUIDE.md",
      "path": "root.children[0].style.marginBottom"
    }
  ]
}
```

And the summary line:

<!-- part-of: cliJson -->
```json
{"version":1,"summary":{"templates":1,"errors":1,"warnings":0,"skipped":0,"late":[]},"exitCode":1}
```

The field names are older than the docs' words: `templates` counts the designs given, and `input` is `"template"` for a design file, `"html"` for an HTML email and `"values"` for a values file.

Each diagnostic is the one [`validate()`](https://www.hyperelements.dev/docs/diagnostics) gives: `code`, `severity`, `message`, `path`, and the `clients` and `fix` where there are some.

A design that doesn't load has no diagnostics but an `error`, which says why in one line. For a syntax error, in the design or a module it imports, that's the file, line, column and reason:

```text
emails/welcome.tsx:3:34: Unexpected closing "Emal" tag does not match opening "Email" tag
```

`preview --json` adds each preview's `path`, `ready` and `findings`, and the `browser` it drew in.

| Exit code | Means |
|-----------|-------|
| `0` | Every design rendered, checked or previewed without errors |
| `1` | A design has errors, failed to load or threw; a values file is wrong, a draft, or its values fail its template; a design ran past `--timeout`; a PDF or image engine isn't installed; a preview failed in the browser; or the run passed `--max-warnings` |
| `2` | The run couldn't do what it was asked: a usage error, `render` of a template module, templates with an Elements before 0.5, no designs (none found, or no input that turned out to be one, such as a file whose default export isn't a component: each is still listed, as skipped), Elements missing, a Document's PDF on Bun, `preview` without `@hyper-elements/email-clients`, or `--findings` with no browser found |

In CI, fail the build on any problem in your designs:

```bash
npx hyper-elements check emails/ --max-warnings 0
```

## With an agent

An agent that can run commands needs no script to check its work. A loop from the shell:

1. `npx hyper-elements check emails/welcome.tsx --json`: fix each error, by its `path` and `message`, until the exit code is `0`.
2. `npx hyper-elements outline emails/welcome.tsx`: compare the layout with what was asked.
3. `npx hyper-elements preview emails/welcome.tsx --findings --json`: each preview's `findings` say what that email client removed or changed, what was missing, and text it draws on more lines.

Where no Chromium is found, `preview --findings` still writes the files, gives each preview `"findings": null` and the line `"browser": null, "reason": "no-browser"`, and exits `2`. Where `playwright-core` isn't installed, the reason is `"no-playwright-core"`, and stderr says how to install it.

An agent with a browser of its own opens each file (or the URLs `--serve` prints), waits for `<html data-email-client-ready>`, and reads the JSON in `#email-client-findings`. With no browser at all, `check`'s diagnostics are what it has. See [AI agents](https://www.hyperelements.dev/docs/guides/ai-agents) and [Email client emulator](https://www.hyperelements.dev/docs/email-client-emulator#test-an-email-from-the-shell).

## How it runs designs

The CLI loads Elements, React and `@hyper-elements/email-clients` the way each design does, so it renders with your versions. Designs run in child processes, one per package and tsconfig. Each is loaded through a small module the CLI writes beside it for a moment, so the design's folder must be writable.

`--timeout` (60 seconds by default) ends a design that loops or hangs: it fails, and the designs after it in its group run in a new process.

On Bun, the CLI gives the same output as on Node.js, byte for byte, except a Document's PDF, which it refuses there (Bun's zlib compresses the PDF's streams differently): render Documents with Node.js. `check`, `outline` and `preview` work on Bun for every root.

---

# Sending email

Source: https://www.hyperelements.dev/docs/guides/sending

Hyper Elements renders. Your email provider delivers. You render once on your server, get two strings, and pass them to any provider's SDK. The provider never sees React, and you never write a second plain-text version by hand.

## Render once

```tsx
import { Button, Column, Email, Heading, MergeTag, Text, render } from "@hyper-elements/react";

const Welcome = ({ plan }: { plan: string }) => (
  <Email width={600} previewText="Your workspace is ready" style={{ backgroundColor: "#f4f4f5", gap: 16 }}>
    <Column style={{ backgroundColor: "#ffffff", padding: 32, gap: 16 }}>
      <Heading level={1} style={{ fontSize: 24 }}>
        Welcome, <MergeTag name="first_name" />
      </Heading>
      <Text>Your {plan} workspace is ready.</Text>
      <Button href="https://example.com/dashboard" style={{ backgroundColor: "#111827" }}>
        Open your dashboard
      </Button>
    </Column>
  </Email>
);

const { html, text, diagnostics } = await render(<Welcome plan="Pro" />);
```

- `html` is the complete document, from its doctype to `</html>`, with the email shell and its head styles. Send that string as the HTML body. Keep the head styles.
- `text` is the plain-text alternative. Send it as the text body.
- `diagnostics` holds warnings. A design with errors rejects with an `ElementsError` that lists them, so a broken design never reaches a send call.

`render()` is async, so everything that calls it awaits it. The `Email`'s `title` prop sets the HTML `<title>`. That's separate from the subject line, which you give the provider.

## A provider-ready message

Put rendering in one function and reuse it for every provider. This is the shape the examples below import as `../message`:

```ts
import { render } from "@hyper-elements/react";
import { invoiceTemplate, sampleInvoice, type InvoiceData } from "./invoice";

export async function renderInvoiceEmail(data: InvoiceData = sampleInvoice) {
  const { html, text } = await render(invoiceTemplate(data, "email"));
  return {
    subject: `Receipt for invoice ${data.number}`,
    html,
    text,
  };
}

export function requireEnv(name: string): string {
  const value = process.env[name];
  if (!value?.trim()) throw new Error(`Set ${name} before sending email`);
  return value;
}

export async function deliveryMessage() {
  return {
    ...(await renderInvoiceEmail()),
    from: requireEnv("EMAIL_FROM"),
    to: requireEnv("EMAIL_TO"),
  };
}
```

`invoiceTemplate` is a plain synchronous function that returns the root element. Fetch your data before you call it: a component that is async or suspends is an error.

Every snippet below sends one real email. Set a verified sender and a recipient you control, and keep credentials on the server, never in browser code:

```bash
export EMAIL_FROM='receipts@your-verified-domain.com'
export EMAIL_TO='your-test-inbox@example.com'
```

## Resend

```bash
npm install resend
```

Set `RESEND_API_KEY`. Resend needs an API key and a verified sending domain.

```ts
import { Resend } from "resend";
import { deliveryMessage, requireEnv } from "../message";

const client = new Resend(requireEnv("RESEND_API_KEY"));
const { data, error } = await client.emails.send(await deliveryMessage());
if (error) throw new Error(`Resend: ${error.message}`);
console.info("Resend accepted:", data?.id);
```

## AWS SES

```bash
npm install @aws-sdk/client-sesv2
```

Set `AWS_REGION` to the region that holds your verified identity. Credentials come from the AWS SDK's default chain (an IAM role or `AWS_PROFILE`) with permission to send through SES. In the SES sandbox, recipients need verifying too.

```ts
import { SESv2Client, SendEmailCommand } from "@aws-sdk/client-sesv2";
import { deliveryMessage, requireEnv } from "../message";

const client = new SESv2Client({ region: requireEnv("AWS_REGION") });
const { from, to, subject, html, text } = await deliveryMessage();
try {
  const result = await client.send(new SendEmailCommand({
    FromEmailAddress: from,
    Destination: { ToAddresses: [to] },
    Content: {
      Simple: {
        Subject: { Data: subject, Charset: "UTF-8" },
        Body: {
          Html: { Data: html, Charset: "UTF-8" },
          Text: { Data: text, Charset: "UTF-8" },
        },
      },
    },
  }));
  console.info("SES accepted:", result.MessageId);
} finally {
  client.destroy();
}
```

## Postmark

```bash
npm install postmark
```

Set `POSTMARK_SERVER_TOKEN`. Use a server token and a confirmed sender signature or domain. The `outbound` message stream is for transactional mail.

```ts
import { ServerClient } from "postmark";
import { deliveryMessage, requireEnv } from "../message";

const client = new ServerClient(requireEnv("POSTMARK_SERVER_TOKEN"));
const { from, to, subject, html, text } = await deliveryMessage();
const result = await client.sendEmail({
  From: from,
  To: to,
  Subject: subject,
  HtmlBody: html,
  TextBody: text,
  MessageStream: "outbound",
});
console.info("Postmark accepted:", result.MessageID);
```

## SendGrid

```bash
npm install @sendgrid/mail
```

Set `SENDGRID_API_KEY`. Use an API key with Mail Send permission and an authenticated sender.

```ts
import sendgrid from "@sendgrid/mail";
import { deliveryMessage, requireEnv } from "../message";

sendgrid.setApiKey(requireEnv("SENDGRID_API_KEY"));
const [response] = await sendgrid.send(await deliveryMessage());
console.info("SendGrid accepted:", response.statusCode, response.headers["x-message-id"]);
```

## Nodemailer (SMTP)

```bash
npm install nodemailer
npm install --save-dev @types/nodemailer
```

Set `SMTP_HOST`, `SMTP_PORT`, `SMTP_USER` and `SMTP_PASSWORD`, with credentials from your SMTP service. Port 465 uses implicit TLS. Submission ports such as 587 require STARTTLS here. Keep certificate verification on.

```ts
import nodemailer from "nodemailer";
import { deliveryMessage, requireEnv } from "../message";

const port = Number(requireEnv("SMTP_PORT"));
if (!Number.isInteger(port) || port < 1 || port > 65535) {
  throw new Error("SMTP_PORT must be an integer between 1 and 65535");
}
const transport = nodemailer.createTransport({
  host: requireEnv("SMTP_HOST"),
  port,
  secure: port === 465,
  requireTLS: port !== 465,
  auth: { user: requireEnv("SMTP_USER"), pass: requireEnv("SMTP_PASSWORD") },
});
try {
  const result = await transport.sendMail(await deliveryMessage());
  if (result.rejected.length) throw new Error("SMTP rejected the recipient");
  console.info("SMTP accepted:", result.messageId);
} finally {
  transport.close();
}
```

## Merge tags

Some values are filled in by the sending service, not by you: a first name in a bulk send, an unsubscribe link. Write those with `MergeTag`:

```tsx
<Heading level={1}>
  Welcome, <MergeTag name="first_name" />
</Heading>
```

By default a merge tag is written as `{{name}}`, in the HTML and in the plain text:

```text
WELCOME, {{first_name}}
```

If your provider uses another syntax, pass `mergeTag` to `render()`. It takes the tag's name and returns what to write. For a service that writes `*|FIRST_NAME|*`:

```tsx
const { html, text } = await render(<Welcome plan="Pro" />, {
  mergeTag: (name) => `*|${name.toUpperCase()}|*`,
});
```

What the function returns goes into the HTML as it is, with the name in it escaped.

A link's target can be a merge tag too. Write it in your provider's syntax: `mergeTag` changes `MergeTag` elements, not the `href` strings you write.

```tsx
<Link href="*|UNSUB|*">Unsubscribe</Link>
```

> **Tip:** Values you know at render time don't need merge tags. Pass them as props and children, as `plan` is above. Elements escapes text passed as children.

## Before you send

- Keep rendering and provider credentials on the server.
- Use absolute HTTPS URLs for links and for images, and give each `Image` its file's size: `src={{ src, width, height }}`.
- Keep customer data out of an `Html` block's `html` prop. It is written as it is, unescaped.
- Use a verified sender. Add deduplication to your jobs, so a retry doesn't send a second receipt.
- A provider's "accepted" response is not inbox delivery. Record the message ID and use the provider's delivery and bounce events for the final status.
- Check the result in the email clients you care about.

> **Note:** The builder design from `toDesign()` is for the [visual editor](https://www.hyperelements.dev/docs/guides/visual-editor), not an email body. Send `html` and `text`.

---

# Next.js

Source: https://www.hyperelements.dev/docs/guides/nextjs

Hyper Elements runs on the server, so it fits the App Router as it is. No client bundle, no extra build step, and for emails, pages and PDFs no entry in `next.config.ts`: Next.js bundles it into your server code like any other package. Images (`@hyper-elements/react/image`) need one, as their engines can't be bundled: `serverExternalPackages: ["@resvg/resvg-js", "satori"]` (see [Image output](https://www.hyperelements.dev/docs/outputs/image#install)). Only the HTML and text strings ever reach the browser.

## A design

A design is a plain component. Nothing in it is specific to Next.js, so the same tree renders from a route handler, a Server Component, a background job or a test.

```tsx
// src/emails/welcome-email.tsx
import { Button, Column, Email, Heading, Text, Span } from "@hyper-elements/react";

export interface WelcomeEmailProps {
  name: string;
  plan: string;
  dashboardUrl: string;
}

export default function WelcomeEmail({ name, plan, dashboardUrl }: WelcomeEmailProps) {
  return (
    <Email width={560} title={`Welcome, ${name}`} previewText={`Your ${plan} workspace is ready, ${name}.`} style={{ backgroundColor: "#f4f4f5", gap: 20 }}>
      <Column style={{ backgroundColor: "#ffffff", padding: [32, 40], gap: 24 }}>
        <Heading level={1} style={{ fontSize: 26 }}>Welcome, {name}</Heading>
        <Text>
          Your <Span style={{ fontWeight: 700 }}>{plan}</Span> workspace is ready.
        </Text>
        <Button href={dashboardUrl} style={{ backgroundColor: "#18181b", borderRadius: 8 }}>
          Open your dashboard
        </Button>
      </Column>
    </Email>
  );
}
```

Props like `name` come from outside: a database row, a webhook, a form. Text passed as children is escaped when Elements writes the HTML. Elements refuses links that run scripts (`javascript:`), but a URL from outside deserves a stricter check of your own, such as allowing absolute `http:` and `https:` URLs only.

## A route handler

Return the rendered HTML from a GET handler. `render()` is async, so the handler is too.

```tsx
// src/app/email-preview/raw/route.ts
import React from "react";
import { render } from "@hyper-elements/react";
import WelcomeEmail from "@/emails/welcome-email";

export async function GET() {
  const { html } = await render(
    React.createElement(WelcomeEmail, {
      name: "Ada",
      plan: "Pro",
      dashboardUrl: "https://example.com/dashboard",
    })
  );

  return new Response(html, {
    headers: { "Content-Type": "text/html; charset=utf-8" },
  });
}
```

This is the shape production code usually takes. Swap the `Response` for a call to your provider and you have a send endpoint: see [Sending email](https://www.hyperelements.dev/docs/guides/sending).

## A Server Component

An async Server Component awaits `render()` and passes the strings on. The design never ships to the browser.

```tsx
// src/app/email-preview/page.tsx
import { render } from "@hyper-elements/react";
import WelcomeEmail from "@/emails/welcome-email";
import PreviewDashboard from "./PreviewDashboard";

export default async function EmailPreviewPage() {
  const { html, text } = await render(
    <WelcomeEmail name="Ada" plan="Pro" dashboardUrl="https://example.com/dashboard" />
  );

  return <PreviewDashboard initialHtml={html} initialText={text} />;
}
```

`PreviewDashboard` here is your own Client Component. It receives strings, not React elements.

## A builder design from a route

`toDesign()` from `@hyper-elements/react/builder` works in the same places. It's synchronous:

```ts
// src/app/design/route.ts
import React from "react";
import { toDesign } from "@hyper-elements/react/builder";
import WelcomeEmail from "@/emails/welcome-email";

export function GET() {
  const { design } = toDesign(
    React.createElement(WelcomeEmail, { name: "Ada", plan: "Pro", dashboardUrl: "https://example.com/dashboard" })
  );
  return Response.json(design);
}
```

See [Visual editing](https://www.hyperelements.dev/docs/guides/visual-editor) for what to do with it.

## An edge route

On the edge runtime, a render either works or rejects with an error that tells you to render emails in the Node.js runtime. The cause is React's: react-dom can't render with the React that React Server Components use there. Catch the error and you'll see it:

```ts
// src/app/edge/route.ts
import React from "react";
import { render } from "@hyper-elements/react";
import WelcomeEmail from "@/emails/welcome-email";

export const runtime = "edge";

export async function GET() {
  try {
    const { html } = await render(
      React.createElement(WelcomeEmail, { name: "Ada", plan: "Pro", dashboardUrl: "https://example.com/dashboard" })
    );
    return new Response(html, { headers: { "Content-Type": "text/html; charset=utf-8" } });
  } catch (error) {
    return Response.json({ error: (error as Error).message });
  }
}
```

> **Note:** Next.js 14 can't bundle Elements for the edge runtime. For emails, the Node.js runtime is the safe default on every version.

## An OpenGraph image from a template

A page's social card can be a [template](https://www.hyperelements.dev/docs/templates) drawn by `@hyper-elements/react/image` in an `opengraph-image.tsx` route: the pages `generateStaticParams` names are drawn when the app builds, any other when it's asked for. The template's check runs before anything is drawn. A title past the template's `maxLength` fails the request with the template's diagnostics instead of drawing a broken card.

```tsx
// app/blog/[slug]/opengraph-image.tsx
import { readFile } from "node:fs/promises";
import { join } from "node:path";
import { renderImage } from "@hyper-elements/react/image";
import { Card } from "@/lib/card"; // a template: template({ id: "acme.Card", root: "Canvas", fields: { title: … }, … })
import { posts } from "@/lib/posts";

export const size = { width: 1200, height: 630 };
export const contentType = "image/png";

export function generateStaticParams() {
  return posts.map((post) => ({ slug: post.slug }));
}

export default async function Image({ params }: { params: Promise<{ slug: string }> }) {
  const { slug } = await params;
  const post = posts.find((p) => p.slug === slug);
  const font = await readFile(join(process.cwd(), "assets/Inter-Regular.ttf"));
  const { image } = await renderImage(<Card title={post?.title ?? "Not found"} />, { fonts: [{ family: "Inter", src: font }] });
  return new Response(new Uint8Array(image), { headers: { "content-type": "image/png" } });
}
```

The image engines load a native module at run time, so they go in `serverExternalPackages: ["@resvg/resvg-js", "satori"]` in `next.config.ts`. With Cache Components (Next.js 16), a route segment can't export `runtime` (the Node.js runtime is the default), and the drawing goes in a function with `"use cache"` that returns the PNG's bytes, so the pages `generateStaticParams` names are prerendered.

## Prerendering and Cache Components

Since Next.js 16, `create-next-app` turns on Cache Components. Pages and GET route handlers that read no request data are then prerendered when the app builds, and the build fails if one reads a random number or the current date.

Hyper Elements reads neither. A render never leaks into the next one, and the same input always gives the same output. So a route handler or Server Component like the ones above prerenders at build time with no `dynamic` flag and no workaround.

A handler or page that reads request data (a search param, a header) isn't prerendered, and renders per request as usual.

## Tested versions

CI builds a real Next.js app on each version and checks that the route handler and the Server Component each come out as a real email (email tables, not a web layout, with the words in the HTML and the plain text) and as a builder design with its rows:

| Next.js | React | What's checked |
|---|---|---|
| 14 | 18 | Route handler, Server Component |
| 15 (Turbopack) | 19 | Route handler, Server Component, edge route |
| 16, Cache Components on | 19 | Route handler and Server Component, prerendered at build |

---

# AI agents

Source: https://www.hyperelements.dev/docs/guides/ai-agents

If an agent writes your designs, Hyper Elements is built so its first try works more often, and so a wrong try tells it exactly what to fix. You don't read HTML to find out. In [our benchmark](https://www.hyperelements.dev/docs/benchmark), an agent reached a passing email faster with Hyper Elements than with MJML (1.3×), hand-written HTML (1.8×) or React Email (2.6×).

## Why the API suits agents

- **One way to write each thing.** Styles go in `style={{ }}`, never as props. Space between blocks is the parent's `gap`; there are no margins. Text is elements, not HTML. An agent doesn't have to guess which of three equivalent forms you meant.
- **Errors say where and what to do.** Every problem comes back with a `code`, a `path` into the design and a `message` that names the fix.
- **Layout without HTML.** `outline()` prints the laid-out design as text: each block, its width, its words. An agent checks that two columns sit side by side by reading a few lines, not nested email tables.
- **The guide ships with the package.** `GUIDE.md` is written from the elements' own definitions, so it matches the version you installed.

## Give your agent the guide

### As a skill

Install the guide as an agent skill. It works in Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, Copilot and other agents, and before Hyper Elements is installed:

```bash
npx skills add hyper-elements/hyper-elements
```

The skill tells the agent to install `@hyper-elements/react` where the project doesn't have it. Once the package is installed, the agent checks the skill against the package's own `GUIDE.md`, which is written for the version you installed: both carry an id made from the guide's text, and where the ids differ the agent reads `GUIDE.md` and follows it. A skill installed months ago can't steer the agent wrong after an upgrade.

It offers two skills: `hyper-elements`, the guide, and `email-testing`, which tells an agent how to preview and check any email (a design, or HTML from MJML, React Email or a builder) in Outlook, Gmail, Apple Mail, Yahoo Mail and AOL Mail. `npx skills add hyper-elements/hyper-elements --skill email-testing` installs that one alone.

In Claude Code, both are plugins as well, in the repository's plugin marketplace:

```text
/plugin marketplace add hyper-elements/hyper-elements
/plugin install hyper-elements@hyper-elements
/plugin install email-testing@hyper-elements
```

### As a rule, in CLAUDE.md or AGENTS.md

Without the skill, add this to `CLAUDE.md` (Claude Code), `AGENTS.md` (Codex, Cursor and others) or a rule:

```text
Designs use Hyper Elements (@hyper-elements/react). If it isn't installed, install it with react and react-dom.
Before writing a design, read node_modules/@hyper-elements/react/GUIDE.md.
```

In a project that already has the package, Claude Code can load the guide into every session with an import in `CLAUDE.md`: `@node_modules/@hyper-elements/react/GUIDE.md`. Claude Code skips an import of a file that doesn't exist without a word, so before the package is installed, the agent gets nothing from that line: use the skill or the rule above until it is.

### For any model, from the web

The site serves the docs in plain text for language models:

- [`https://hyperelements.dev/llms.txt`](https://hyperelements.dev/llms.txt): an index of the docs.
- [`https://hyperelements.dev/llms-full.txt`](https://hyperelements.dev/llms-full.txt): the docs in one file.

Every docs page also has a **Copy page** button that copies it as Markdown, ready to paste into a chat.

> **Tip:** `GUIDE.md` is the short guide: how a design is written, the common mistakes, every element on a line. `REFERENCE.md`, next to it in the package, has every prop and style in full, with defaults.

### In a browser, with nothing installed

An agent with a browser can render a design in the [playground](https://www.hyperelements.dev/playground), read its diagnostics, and hand you a link to the result:

- **A link.** `https://www.hyperelements.dev/playground#code=<base64url of the code>` opens the page with the design rendered. Add `&view=pdf`, `&device=phone` or `&layout=preview`.
- **JavaScript.** `await hyperElementsPlayground.render(code, { root: "Page" })` resolves with `{ ok, root, html, text, outline, diagnostics, error }`. `hyperElementsPlayground.help()` lists every method.
- **WebMCP.** Where the browser has it, the page registers `render_hyper_elements`, `show_hyper_elements_preview`, `get_hyper_elements_reference` and `get_playground_code`.

The code runs in a sandbox in the tab: it isn't sent to a server.

## The loop

Point your agent at this loop. Each step is cheap, and only the last two write HTML.

### 1. Write

The agent writes a design with the elements from `@hyper-elements/react`.

### 2. Validate

`validate()` runs every check `render()` runs, without rendering and without throwing:

```tsx
import { formatDiagnostics, validate } from "@hyper-elements/react";

const { valid, diagnostics } = validate(<Welcome />);
console.log(formatDiagnostics(diagnostics));
```

Here's what comes back for `<Email backgroundColor="#fff">` with a `Text` styled `marginBottom: 16`:

```text
error prop/unknown at root.props.backgroundColor: An Email has no prop "backgroundColor": it's a style, style={{ backgroundColor: … }}
error style/unknown at root.children[0].style.marginBottom: "marginBottom" isn't a style a Text takes: use the parent's gap, or padding. See Text in @hyper-elements/react/GUIDE.md
```

Each line is a fix the agent can apply without asking you. Warnings and notes leave a design valid; only errors make `valid` false. With `@hyper-elements/email-clients`' plugin (`validate(email, { plugins: [await emailClients()] })`), a problem with email clients names them and says what to change:

```text
warning email/font-fallback at root.children[0].style.fontFamily: This font stack ends with the web font "Inter": where it doesn't load (Gmail, classic Outlook) the email client picks its own font [gmail, outlook] Fix: end it with a font the client has: "Inter, Arial, sans-serif"
```

With [lint](https://www.hyperelements.dev/docs/lint)'s plugin (`validate(email, { plugins: [lint()] })`, from `@hyper-elements/lint`), it also hears what makes the email hard to read, each with its fix: a link that says "click here", an image's alt that's a file name, faint or small text, headings out of order, merge syntax typed into the copy. `npx hyper-elements check` runs it already.

### 3. Outline

`outline()` prints the design as laid out on desktop, and says whether each `Row` stacks on phones:

```tsx
import { Column, Email, Heading, Text, Row, outline } from "@hyper-elements/react";

console.log(outline(
  <Email width={600}>
    <Heading level={1}>Your order</Heading>
    <Row style={{ gap: 16 }}>
      <Column style={{ width: 180 }}><Text>Shipping to</Text></Column>
      <Column><Text>Ada Lovelace</Text></Column>
    </Row>
  </Email>
));
```

```text
Email 600px
  Heading h1 600px "Your order"
  Row 600px: 2 side by side, stacked on phones
    Column 180px
      Text 180px "Shipping to"
    Column 404px
      Text 404px "Ada Lovelace"
```

The agent compares this against what you asked for. Wrong width, wrong nesting, missing words: all visible here. `outline()` throws an `ElementsError` if the design has errors, so validate first.

### 4. Render

```tsx
import { render } from "@hyper-elements/react";

const { html, text, diagnostics } = await render(<Welcome />);
```

A design with errors rejects with an `ElementsError` whose `diagnostics` hold the same `code`, `message` and `path` as `validate()`. `diagnostics` on success holds warnings. A few checks need the written output, such as an email's size against Gmail's limits, so they only run here.

### 5. Check it in the email client emulator

An agent with a browser can see the email as each email client shows it, free and locally, with no screenshot service account or API, in the email client emulator that comes with Hyper Elements: `renderInEmailClients()` from `@hyper-elements/email-clients` returns an HTML preview per client, which the agent can open, screenshot or save, and each lists what that client changed, as JSON the agent reads.

The `email-testing` skill gives an agent these steps for any email. To have an agent install it and test an email, give it this prompt:

```text
Install the email-testing skill
(npx skills add hyper-elements/hyper-elements --skill email-testing -y,
or read https://www.hyperelements.dev/skills/email-testing.md)
and follow it to preview [my email: an HTML file or a design]
in Outlook, Gmail, Yahoo Mail and Apple Mail, light and dark.
Show me each client's screenshot and what it changed.
```

```tsx
import { mkdir, writeFile } from "node:fs/promises";
import { renderInEmailClients } from "@hyper-elements/email-clients";

const { previews } = await renderInEmailClients(<Welcome />);
await mkdir("previews", { recursive: true });
for (const preview of previews) await writeFile(`previews/${preview.filename}`, preview.html);
```

Open each file, wait for `<html data-email-client-ready>`, and read `#email-client-findings`. See [Email client emulator](https://www.hyperelements.dev/docs/email-client-emulator).

## The loop from the shell

An agent that can run commands can do the same loop without writing a script, with [`@hyper-elements/cli`](https://www.hyperelements.dev/docs/cli) (`npm install -D @hyper-elements/cli`). Each design is a module whose default export renders the root, with its `PreviewProps` as props:

```bash
npx hyper-elements check emails/welcome.tsx --json     # 2. validate, with the email client checks
npx hyper-elements outline emails/welcome.tsx          # 3. the layout as text
npx hyper-elements render emails/welcome.tsx           # 4. out/emails/welcome.html and out/emails/welcome.txt
npx hyper-elements describe Button --root Email        # what an element takes, before writing it
```

With `--json`, stdout holds one line per design, with its `status` and `diagnostics`, then a summary line. The exit code is `0` when every design is free of errors, `1` when one has errors, and `2` when the command couldn't run as asked (a usage error; no designs, such as a file whose default export isn't a component). A design that doesn't load has an `error` instead: for a syntax error, its file, line, column and reason.

To test an email in the email clients from the shell, the agent uses what it has:

1. **Where the CLI finds a Chromium:** `npx hyper-elements preview emails/welcome.tsx --findings --json`. Each preview comes back with its `ready` and its `findings`: what that client removed or changed, what was missing, and text it draws on more lines. It needs `playwright-core` beside the CLI (`npm install -D playwright-core`), and `npx hyper-elements preview --install-browser` downloads a Chromium.
2. **Where it finds none** (exit `2`, `"browser": null, "reason": "no-browser"`, or `"no-playwright-core"`), the preview files are still written. An agent with a browser of its own opens each one, or the URLs `preview --serve` prints, waits for `<html data-email-client-ready>`, and reads the JSON in `#email-client-findings`.
3. **With no browser at all,** `check`'s diagnostics are what it has: each email client problem with the clients it's about and what to change.

## Common mistakes

Each of these made an agent's first try fail:

- `<Email backgroundColor="#fff">` → `<Email style={{ backgroundColor: "#fff" }}>`. Styles never go as props.
- `<Email style={{ width: 600, padding: 24 }}>` → `<Email width={600}>`, with the padding on a `Column` (a card) or a `Section` (a band) inside it. A root's width is a prop, and a root has no padding.
- `items={[{ text: "Home", link: "/" }]}` → `items={[{ text: "Home", href: "/" }]}`. A `Menu`'s items are `{ text, href }`, a `Social`'s icons `{ name, href }`.
- `style={{ marginBottom: 16 }}` → `gap: 16` on the parent. There are no margins.
- `ColumnLayouts`, `layout`, `headingType`, `altText`, `html` are props of Unlayer Elements' components, not these: use a `Row` of `Column`s, `level`, `alt`, and text as children.
- `<Image src="https://example.com/logo.png">` → `src={{ src: "https://example.com/logo.png", width: 240, height: 80 }}`, the file's size. Without it Outlook shows the image at its file's size, and Hyper Elements warns.
- `mobile={{ fontSize: 20 }}`, `hover={{ … }}`, `_hover` or `md: { … }` → `style={{ fontSize: 24, mobile: { fontSize: 20 }, hover: { … } }}`. Phone and hover styles are blocks of `style`, and there's one breakpoint: phones.

## Rules worth giving your agent

- Read `GUIDE.md` before writing a design.
- Check each design you write with `npx hyper-elements check <file> --json` (or `validate()`), and fix every error before you render it.
- A design has one root: `Email`, `Page`, `Document` or `Canvas`. The root decides the output.
- Raw tags such as `<b>`, `<br>` or `<div>` are errors. Use `Span`, `LineBreak` and the layout elements.
- Build reusable trees with a plain synchronous function that returns the root. Fetch data first: a component that is async or suspends is an error.
- Pass dynamic values as children or props, which Hyper Elements escapes. Only put markup you trust in an `Html` block.
- To move React Email templates, run `npx @hyper-elements/migrate` instead of rewriting them by hand. It keeps their logic and checks the result. Exit code `2` means a template failed to convert or lost content: report it, with the file and the reason. Don't pass `--force` to hide it. See [From React Email](https://www.hyperelements.dev/docs/migrate/react-email).

## A complete receipt-email walkthrough

For a worked example with Claude Code, order data, a diagnostic repair and a test send, follow [Build and validate React emails with Claude Code](https://www.hyperelements.dev/blog/react-emails-claude-code).

# Agent benchmark

Source: https://www.hyperelements.dev/docs/benchmark

We gave a coding agent five email briefs and five image briefs to build with Hyper Elements and other approaches. Each result was done when it passed the same checks for its brief. We timed how long that took and counted the output tokens.

[Email results](#results) · [Image results](#image-results)

The email comparison uses Hyper Elements, MJML, React Email and hand-written HTML. The image comparison uses Hyper Elements, Playwright and Canvas 2D.

## Results

16 runs per approach. Every run reached a passing email.

[![Agent benchmark comparing Hyper Elements, MJML, hand-written HTML, and React Email on median time, output tokens, and first-check passes. Full results follow in the table.](https://www.hyperelements.dev/img/hyper-elements-agent-benchmark.svg)](https://www.hyperelements.dev/img/hyper-elements-agent-benchmark.svg "Open the benchmark chart at full size")

| | Hyper Elements | MJML | Hand-written HTML | React Email |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Median time to a passing email | **33s** | 43s | 60s | 86s |
| Median output tokens | **1,831** | 2,762 | 4,903 | 6,215 |
| Passed the checks the first time they ran | **16 of 16** | **16 of 16** | 6 of 16 | 12 of 16 |
| Median turns | 9 | 9 | 8.5 | 18 |

- **Fastest.** Hyper Elements was 1.3× faster than MJML, 1.8× faster than hand-written HTML and 2.6× faster than React Email at the median, and the fastest on four of the five briefs (MJML was faster on the launch email). Within a brief it was faster in 40 of 52 pairings with MJML (one-sided Mann–Whitney, p < 0.01), 48 of 52 with HTML and 51 of 52 with React Email (p < 0.001 for each).
- **Fewest output tokens.** 1.5× fewer than MJML, 2.7× fewer than HTML and 3.4× fewer than React Email. The agent writes a short design; the engine writes the tables.
- **Right the first time.** Every Hyper Elements and MJML email passed the first time the agent ran the checks, against 6 of 16 hand-written HTML emails and 12 of 16 React Email ones.

How Hyper Elements differs from React Email and MJML beyond speed (layout, checks, email client previews, themes) is on [Hyper Elements vs React Email](https://www.hyperelements.dev/compare/react-email) and [Hyper Elements vs MJML](https://www.hyperelements.dev/compare/mjml).

## The emails

Five briefs, each with the exact copy, links and images, and its layout:

| Brief | What makes it hard |
|---|---|
| Password reset | A sized logo, a button, a preview text |
| Product launch | A hero image, three feature columns that stack on phones |
| Order receipt | Line items with the price on the right, two address columns |
| Newsletter | Two stories, each an image beside text, stacked on phones |
| Event invite | Three detail columns, a button with a hover color |

## The checks

Every approach was held to the same checks, run in headless Chromium at 800px and at 375px wide:

- the copy, the links and the preview text (present, and hidden);
- each button's link, color, size and hover color;
- each image loaded, with alt text, at its size;
- a table layout with no flex or grid, content 600px wide, and no sideways scroll on a phone;
- columns side by side on desktop and stacked on a phone, and line items on one line.

## How it ran

Each run started in a fresh directory with the brief, a `CLAUDE.md` of conventions and the checker, and the same prompt: "Build the email described in BRIEF.md, following CLAUDE.md. It's done when `node tools/check.mjs` passes." The agent could edit files and run `node`, `tsc`, `ls` and `cat`, with no web access.
