Across a Column it places what has its own size (a Button, an Image, an Svg, a box with a width); a block of text fills the width, so its words move with its textAlign.

## PageBreak

Source: https://www.hyperelements.dev/docs/elements/pagebreak

In a Document, where a page ends: what follows starts the next page.

Holds: nothing. Only in a Document.

## PageHeader

Source: https://www.hyperelements.dev/docs/elements/pageheader

In a Document: drawn at the top of every page, inside its margins.

Holds: Row, Column, Grid, Layer, Svg, Text, Heading, Link, Button, Image, Divider, List, Table, Video, Social, Menu, Html. Only in a Document.

`style`:
- `color`: *color* (inherited, Typography)
- `fontFamily`: *fontFamily* (inherited, Typography)
- `fontSize`: a length (a number of px) (inherited, Typography)
- `fontWeight`: *fontWeight* (inherited, Typography)
- `fontStyle`: one of "normal", "italic" (inherited, Typography)
- `lineHeight`: *lineHeight* (inherited, Typography)
- `letterSpacing`: a length (a number of px) (inherited, Typography)
- `textAlign`: one of "left", "center", "right", "justify" (inherited, Typography)
- `textTransform`: one of "none", "uppercase", "lowercase", "capitalize" (inherited, Typography)
- `padding`: *insets* (Spacing)
- `backgroundColor`: *color* (Background)
- `border`: *border* (Border)
- `gap`: a length (a number of px) (Spacing). Space between children.
- `alignItems`: one of "start", "center", "end", "stretch" (Layout). Where children sit across the layout's direction (vertically in a Row, horizontally in a Column), as CSS align-items. Across a Column it places what has its own size (a Button, an Image, an Svg, a box with a width); a block of text fills the width, so its words move with its textAlign.

## PageFooter

Source: https://www.hyperelements.dev/docs/elements/pagefooter

In a Document: drawn at the bottom of every page, inside its margins.

Holds: Row, Column, Grid, Layer, Svg, Text, Heading, Link, Button, Image, Divider, List, Table, Video, Social, Menu, Html. Only in a Document.

`style`:
- `color`: *color* (inherited, Typography)

- `fontStyle`: one of "normal", "italic" (inherited, Typography)
- `lineHeight`: *lineHeight* (inherited, Typography)
- `letterSpacing`: a length (a number of px) (inherited, Typography)
- `textAlign`: one of "left", "center", "right", "justify" (inherited, Typography)
- `textTransform`: one of "none", "uppercase", "lowercase", "capitalize" (inherited, Typography)
- `padding`: *insets* (Spacing)
- `backgroundColor`: *color* (Background)
- `border`: *border* (Border)
- `gap`: a length (a number of px) (Spacing). Space between children.
- `alignItems`: one of "start", "center", "end", "stretch" (Layout). Where children sit across the layout's direction (vertically in a Row, horizontally in a Column), as CSS align-items. Across a Column it places what has its own size (a Button, an Image, an Svg, a box with a width); a block of text fills the width, so its words move with its textAlign.

## ListItem

Source: https://www.hyperelements.dev/docs/elements/listitem

An item of a List: text, and a List of its own to nest one.

Holds: text; PageNumber, Span, Link, LineBreak, MergeTag, List.

Props:
- `dir`: one of "ltr", "rtl", "auto". Its text's direction, where it differs from the design's; it starts on that side unless aligned otherwise.

`style`:
- `color`: *color* (inherited, Typography)
- `fontFamily`: *fontFamily* (inherited, Typography)
- `fontSize`: a length (a number of px) (inherited, Typography)
- `fontWeight`: *fontWeight* (inherited, Typography)
- `fontStyle`: one of "normal", "italic" (inherited, Typography)
- `lineHeight`: *lineHeight* (inherited, Typography)
- `letterSpacing`: a length (a number of px) (inherited, Typography)
- `textAlign`: one of "left", "center", "right", "justify" (inherited, Typography)
- `textTransform`: one of "none", "uppercase", "lowercase", "capitalize" (inherited, Typography)
- `textDecoration`: one of "none", "underline", "line-through" (Typography)

`style.mobile` (on phones): `fontSize`, `lineHeight`, `letterSpacing`, `textAlign`.

## TableRow

Source: https://www.hyperelements.dev/docs/elements/tablerow

A row of a Table. A header row's cells are header cells, in bold.

Holds: TableCell.

Props:
- `header`: true or false (default `false`). Its cells head the columns below them.
- `footer`: true or false (default `false`). It ends the table (printed, on each page the table runs to).

`style`:
- `color`: *color* (inherited, Typography)
- `fontFamily`: *fontFamily* (inherited, Typography)
- `fontSize`: a length (a number of px) (inherited, Typography)
- `fontWeight`: *fontWeight* (inherited, Typography)
- `fontStyle`: one of "normal", "italic" (inherited, Typography)
- `lineHeight`: *lineHeight* (inherited, Typography)
- `letterSpacing`: a length (a number of px) (inherited, Typography)
- `textAlign`: one of "left", "center", "right", "justify" (inherited, Typography)
- `textTransform`: one of "none", "uppercase", "lowercase", "capitalize" (inherited, Typography)
- `backgroundColor`: *color* (Background)
- `height`: a length (a number of px) (Size)

`style.mobile` (on phones): `fontSize`, `lineHeight`, `letterSpacing`, `textAlign`.

## TableCell

Source: https://www.hyperelements.dev/docs/elements/tablecell

A cell of a TableRow: text, and images. Its width sets its column's.

Holds: text; PageNumber, Span, Link, LineBreak, MergeTag, Image.

Props:
- `colSpan`: an integer from 1 (default `1`). How many columns it spans.
- `dir`: one of "ltr", "rtl", "auto". Its text's direction, where it differs from the design's; it starts on that side unless aligned otherwise.

`style`:
- `color`: *color* (inherited, Typography)
- `fontFamily`: *fontFamily* (inherited, Typography)
- `fontSize`: a length (a number of px) (inherited, Typography)
- `fontWeight`: *fontWeight* (inherited, Typography)
- `fontStyle`: one of "normal", "italic" (inherited, Typography)
- `lineHeight`: *lineHeight* (inherited, Typography)
- `letterSpacing`: a length (a number of px) (inherited, Typography)
- `textAlign`: one of "left", "center", "right", "justify" (inherited, Typography)
- `textTransform`: one of "none", "uppercase", "lowercase", "capitalize" (inherited, Typography)
- `textDecoration`: one of "none", "underline", "line-through" (Typography)
- `padding`: *insets* (Spacing)
- `backgroundColor`: *color* (Background)
- `border`: *border* (Border)
- `width`: a length (a number of px, %) (Size). Its column's width (of a cell spanning one column).
- `verticalAlign`: one of "top", "middle", "bottom" (Layout)

`style.mobile` (on phones): `fontSize`, `lineHeight`, `letterSpacing`, `textAlign`, `padding`, `border`.

## Rect

Source: https://www.hyperelements.dev/docs/elements/rect

A rectangle at x, y in its Svg, rounded by rx.

Holds: nothing. Not in an Email.

Props:
- `x`: a number (default `0`)
- `y`: a number (default `0`)
- `width`: a number from 0 (required)
- `height`: a number from 0 (required)
- `rx`: a number from 0

`style`:
- `fill`: *color* (default `"#000000"`, Background). Its inside ("transparent" for none).
- `stroke`: *color* (Border). Its outline's color.
- `strokeWidth`: a number from 0 (Border)
- `opacity`: a number from 0 to 1 (Effects)

## Circle

Source: https://www.hyperelements.dev/docs/elements/circle

A circle centered at cx, cy in its Svg.

Holds: nothing. Not in an Email.

Props:
- `cx`: a number (default `0`)
- `cy`: a number (default `0`)
- `r`: a number from 0 (required)

`style`:
- `fill`: *color* (default `"#000000"`, Background). Its inside ("transparent" for none).
- `stroke`: *color* (Border). Its outline's color.
- `strokeWidth`: a number from 0 (Border)
- `opacity`: a number from 0 to 1 (Effects)

## Ellipse

Source: https://www.hyperelements.dev/docs/elements/ellipse

An ellipse centered at cx, cy in its Svg.

Holds: nothing. Not in an Email.

Props:
- `cx`: a number (default `0`)
- `cy`: a number (default `0`)
- `rx`: a number from 0 (required)
- `ry`: a number from 0 (required)

`style`:
- `fill`: *color* (default `"#000000"`, Background). Its inside ("transparent" for none).
- `stroke`: *color* (Border). Its outline's color.
- `strokeWidth`: a number from 0 (Border)
- `opacity`: a number from 0 to 1 (Effects)

## Line

Source: https://www.hyperelements.dev/docs/elements/line

A straight line from x1, y1 to x2, y2 in its Svg (drawn by its stroke).

Holds: nothing. Not in an Email.

Props:
- `x1`: a number (default `0`)
- `y1`: a number (default `0`)
- `x2`: a number (default `0`)
- `y2`: a number (default `0`)

`style`:
- `fill`: *color* (default `"#000000"`, Background). Its inside ("transparent" for none).
- `stroke`: *color* (Border). Its outline's color.
- `strokeWidth`: a number from 0 (Border)
- `opacity`: a number from 0 to 1 (Effects)

## Polygon

Source: https://www.hyperelements.dev/docs/elements/polygon

A closed shape through its points ("0,0 40,0 20,30"), in its Svg.

Holds: nothing. Not in an Email.

Props:
- `points`: text (required)

`style`:
- `fill`: *color* (default `"#000000"`, Background). Its inside ("transparent" for none).
- `stroke`: *color* (Border). Its outline's color.
- `strokeWidth`: a number from 0 (Border)
- `opacity`: a number from 0 to 1 (Effects)

## Path

Source: https://www.hyperelements.dev/docs/elements/path

A shape drawn by an SVG path (d), in its Svg.

Holds: nothing. Not in an Email.

Props:
- `d`: text (required). SVG path data ("M0 0 L40 0 L20 30 Z").

- `fill`: *color* (default `"#000000"`, Background). Its inside ("transparent" for none).
- `stroke`: *color* (Border). Its outline's color.
- `strokeWidth`: a number from 0 (Border)
- `opacity`: a number from 0 to 1 (Effects)

# Automate Open Graph images for every page in Next.js

Source: https://www.hyperelements.dev/blog/automate-open-graph-images-nextjs

To give every page of a Next.js App Router site its own Open Graph image, make one card template with Hyper Elements, list your pages and their titles in one place, and serve the cards from a route handler that Next.js prerenders when it builds. Each page’s metadata points at its card, unless the page has an image of its own.

Nobody draws a card by hand, and no card is drawn when someone requests it: `next build` draws one PNG per page and fails if a title can’t fit. This tutorial builds that for a small fictional site, Northline, in a new Next.js app with Cache Components on, as `create-next-app` sets it up. For a single card from a standalone Node.js script, see [Open Graph images in Node.js with local fonts](https://www.hyperelements.dev/blog/node-open-graph-images-local-fonts). This post doesn’t repeat it.

## What does the finished setup do?

Five files do the work. The template holds the brand. A list of pages holds the titles. One route handler draws a card for each page without its own image, and one function writes each page’s metadata.

```text
fonts/
  Inter-Regular.ttf
  Inter-Bold.ttf
lib/
  og/card.tsx           the card template
  og/render.ts          checks a page's values and draws its card
  pages.ts              every page: path, title, section, own image
  metadata.ts           a page's title, description and og:image
app/
  og/[...path]/route.ts serves /og/<page>.png, prerendered
  layout.tsx            the site's base URL
next.config.ts
```

At build time, the route handler asks for one card per page. Each card’s values are checked against the template, then drawn with the fonts from `fonts/`. The PNGs are saved with the build, and each page’s `og:image` and `twitter:image` tags point at its own card.

## What do I need to install?

In an App Router project, install the elements and the two image engines. They are optional peer dependencies of `@hyper-elements/react`, so you add them yourself. Keep Satori in the range the [image docs](https://www.hyperelements.dev/docs/outputs/image#install) give.

```bash
npm install @hyper-elements/react satori@^0.33.5 @resvg/resvg-js
```

Put the two Inter files in `fonts/` at the project root. Use TTF, OTF or WOFF files: the image renderer doesn’t draw WOFF2, which is what most web font downloads give you. Inter’s [releases](https://github.com/rsms/inter/releases) include TTF files. Any font works if you have the right to use it and it has every character your titles use.

Then tell Next.js not to bundle the engines. Without this line, `next build` fails on resvg’s native addon (`non-ecmascript placeable asset`).

`next.config.ts`

```ts
import type { NextConfig } from "next";

const nextConfig: NextConfig = {
  cacheComponents: true,
  partialPrefetching: true,
  // Satori reads a WebAssembly file and resvg is a native addon:
  // load them from node_modules instead of bundling them.
  serverExternalPackages: ["@resvg/resvg-js", "satori"],
};

export default nextConfig;
```

The first two settings are the ones `create-next-app` writes. Only `serverExternalPackages` is new.

## How do I make the card template?

A [template](https://www.hyperelements.dev/docs/templates) is a design with a few named fields. The fields are the only things that change from one card to the next. The logo, colors, fonts and layout are written into the template, so no page can change them. This card has two fields: the page’s title and its section, one of five. The section picks the card’s colors from palettes the template owns, so a page chooses its section, never its colors.

`lib/og/card.tsx`

```tsx
import {
  Canvas, Circle, Column, Heading, Layer, Path, Rect, Row, Svg, Text, prop,
} from "@hyper-elements/react";
import { template } from "@hyper-elements/react/template";

// Each section's colors: a background, three accents and a soft tint.
const PALETTES = {
  Product: { bg: "#4338ca", a: "#f472b6", b: "#facc15", c: "#22d3ee", soft: "#c7d2fe" },
  Pricing: { bg: "#047857", a: "#a3e635", b: "#fde047", c: "#5eead4", soft: "#a7f3d0" },
  Docs: { bg: "#0f172a", a: "#38bdf8", b: "#a78bfa", c: "#f472b6", soft: "#94a3b8" },
  Blog: { bg: "#be123c", a: "#fb923c", b: "#fde047", c: "#f9a8d4", soft: "#fecdd3" },
  Company: { bg: "#7c3aed", a: "#fbbf24", b: "#34d399", c: "#f472b6", soft: "#ddd6fe" },
};
type Section = keyof typeof PALETTES;
const SECTIONS = Object.keys(PALETTES) as Section[];

// The logo: a white tile with a navy chevron pointing north.
const logo = (
  <Svg width={44} height={44} viewBox="0 0 44 44" title="Northline">
    <Rect x={0} y={0} width={44} height={44} rx={10} style={{ fill: "#ffffff" }} />
    <Path
      d="M12 27 L22 16 L32 27"
      style={{ fill: "transparent", stroke: "#0f1729", strokeWidth: 4.5 }}
    />
  </Svg>
);

// Shapes on the right of the card, in the section's accents.
const shapes = (p: (typeof PALETTES)[Section]) => (
  <Svg width={1200} height={630}>
    <Circle cx={1070} cy={140} r={200} style={{ fill: p.a }} />
    <Rect x={820} y={340} width={240} height={240} rx={56} style={{ fill: p.b }} />
    <Circle
      cx={1130}
      cy={520}
      r={100}
      style={{ fill: "transparent", stroke: p.c, strokeWidth: 28 }}
    />
    <Path
      d="M880 300 L990 190 L1100 300"
      style={{ fill: "transparent", stroke: "#ffffff", strokeWidth: 30 }}
    />
  </Svg>
);

export default template({
  id: "northline.PageCard",
  version: "1.0.0",
  label: "Page card",
  root: "Canvas",
  formats: { og: { width: 1200, height: 630 } },
  fields: {
    title: prop.text({ label: "Title", required: true, maxLength: 120 }),
    section: prop.choice(SECTIONS, { label: "Section", required: true }),
  },
  // Checked when the card is drawn: nothing past the edges,
  // a font for every character, and a title that fits.
  rules: {
    require: { core: ["image/fit", "image/overflow", "image/glyph"] },
  },
  example: {
    title: "Release notes your team will actually read",
    section: "Product",
  },
  render(v) {
    const p = PALETTES[v.section];
    return (
      <Canvas
        width={1200}
        height={630}
        title={v.title}
        lang="en"
        style={{ backgroundColor: p.bg, fontFamily: "Inter" }}
      >
        <Layer style={{ width: 1200, height: 630 }}>
          {shapes(p)}
          <Column
            style={{
              width: 800,
              height: 630,
              padding: [64, 0, 64, 80],
              justifyContent: "space-between",
            }}
          >
            <Row style={{ alignItems: "center", gap: 16 }}>
              {logo}
              <Text style={{ color: "#ffffff", fontSize: 30, fontWeight: 700 }}>
                Northline
              </Text>
            </Row>
            <Column style={{ gap: 24 }}>
              <Row style={{ alignItems: "center", gap: 12 }}>
                <Svg width={16} height={16} style={{ flex: "none" }}>
                  <Circle cx={8} cy={8} r={8} style={{ fill: p.a }} />
                </Svg>
                <Text
                  field="section"
                  style={{
                    color: "#ffffff",
                    fontSize: 22,
                    fontWeight: 700,
                    letterSpacing: 3,
                    textTransform: "uppercase",
                  }}
                >
                  {v.section}
                </Text>
              </Row>
              {/* The largest of these sizes that keeps the title to four lines. */}
              <Heading
                field="title"
                level={1}
                fit={{ sizes: [72, 64, 56, 48], maxLines: 4 }}
                style={{
                  color: "#ffffff",
                  fontWeight: 700,
                  lineHeight: 1.08,
                  letterSpacing: -1.5,
                }}
              >
                {v.title}
              </Heading>
            </Column>
            <Text style={{ color: p.soft, fontSize: 22 }}>northline.example</Text>
          </Column>
        </Layer>
      </Canvas>
    );
  },
});
```

Four parts of it do the checking:

- **`prop.choice(SECTIONS, …)`** takes only the five section names that have a palette. Any other section is refused before anything is drawn.
- **`maxLength: 120`** refuses a longer title the same way. It counts characters, not width, so it’s a limit on input, not a promise that the title fits.
- **`fit={{ sizes: [72, 64, 56, 48], maxLines: 4 }}`** measures the title with the real fonts and draws it at the largest size that keeps it to four lines. A short title is drawn at 72px; a long one steps down. See [fitted text](https://www.hyperelements.dev/docs/templates/fields#fitted-text).
- **`rules`** makes three measurements required: `image/fit` (the title fits at one of its sizes), `image/overflow` (nothing runs past the card’s edges) and `image/glyph` (the fonts have every character). A card that breaks one of them is an error, so it’s never drawn clipped or with empty boxes. The [rules page](https://www.hyperelements.dev/docs/templates/rules) lists the others.

The logo and the shapes are `Svg` elements in the template, stacked behind the words with a `Layer`, so there are no image files to load. The text column is 800px wide, so the words never run over the shapes. The `example` values are what the template is tested and described with.

## How do I draw a card from a page’s title?

This function takes a page’s title and section and returns PNG bytes. It checks the values with the template’s `check()`, then draws the snapshot it returns with `renderImage()` from `@hyper-elements/react/image`.

`lib/og/render.ts`

```ts
import { readFile } from "node:fs/promises";
import { join } from "node:path";
import { formatDiagnostics } from "@hyper-elements/react";
import { renderImage } from "@hyper-elements/react/image";
import Card from "./card";

const font = (file: string) => readFile(join(process.cwd(), "fonts", file));

export async function renderCard(values: { title: string; section: string }) {
  // Check the values first: a missing title or one past maxLength stops here.
  const checked = Card.check(values, { format: "og" });
  const snapshot = checked.snapshots.og;
  if (!checked.valid || !snapshot) {
    throw new Error(
      `Card for "${values.title}":\n${formatDiagnostics(checked.diagnostics)}`,
    );
  }

  // Draw what was checked. A title that fits at none of its sizes rejects here.
  const { image } = await renderImage(snapshot, {
    fonts: [
      { family: "Inter", src: await font("Inter-Regular.ttf"), weight: 400 },
      { family: "Inter", src: await font("Inter-Bold.ttf"), weight: 700 },
    ],
  });
  return image;
}
```

`check()` doesn’t throw. It returns `valid`, the diagnostics and one snapshot per format, so the function throws itself when the values are refused. The fit and the glyphs can only be measured with the fonts, so `renderImage()` measures them. A design made from a template is always drawn strictly, so a required rule that fails rejects with an `ElementsError` instead of returning a clipped image.

Nothing is fetched while drawing. The fonts are read from disk, and `fontFamily: "Inter"` in the template matches the `family` given here. Text in a weight with no file is an error in a strict design, so both weights the card uses are given.

## Where do the page titles come from?

The cards need each page’s title before any page is rendered, so the titles live in one list that both the pages and the card route read. In a real site, build this list from your CMS or Markdown files.

`lib/pages.ts`

```ts
export type SitePage = {
  path: string;
  title: string;
  description: string;
  section: string;
  /** The page's own social image. Without one, it gets a generated card. */
  image?: string;
};

// Every page on the site, in one list. Load blog posts from your CMS here.
export const pages: SitePage[] = [
  {
    path: "/",
    title: "Release notes your team will actually read",
    description: "Northline turns merged pull requests into release notes.",
    section: "Product",
  },
  {
    path: "/pricing",
    title: "Simple pricing for teams of every size",
    description: "Plans for one project or a hundred.",
    section: "Pricing",
  },
  {
    path: "/docs/quickstart",
    title: "Publish your first release notes in five minutes",
    description: "Connect a repository and publish your first notes.",
    section: "Docs",
  },
  {
    path: "/about",
    title: "About Northline",
    description: "Who builds Northline, and why.",
    section: "Company",
    image: "/images/team.jpg",
  },
  {
    path: "/blog/release-notes-checklist",
    title:
      "The release notes checklist: what customers, support and engineers " +
      "each need from every release",
    description: "What to put in release notes, and what to leave out.",
    section: "Blog",
  },
];

export function pageAt(path: string) {
  const page = pages.find((p) => p.path === path);
  if (!page) throw new Error(`No entry for ${path} in lib/pages.ts`);
  return page;
}

/** A page's card: /og/index.png, /og/pricing.png, /og/blog/<slug>.png */
export function cardPath(path: string) {
  return path === "/" ? "/og/index.png" : `/og${path}.png`;
}
```

The default is a generated card. A page gets one unless its entry has an `image`.

## How do I serve the cards from Next.js?

One catch-all route handler serves every card. `generateStaticParams` names a card for each page without its own image, so Next.js draws them all during `next build` and saves the PNGs with the build.

`app/og/[...path]/route.ts`

```ts
import { cacheLife } from "next/cache";
import { renderCard } from "@/lib/og/render";
import { cardPath, pages } from "@/lib/pages";

// A card for every page without its own image, drawn when the app builds.
export function generateStaticParams() {
  return pages
    .filter((page) => !page.image)
    .map((page) => ({ path: cardPath(page.path).split("/").slice(2) }));
}

async function card(path: string) {
  "use cache";
  cacheLife("max");
  const page = pages.find((p) => !p.image && cardPath(p.path) === path);
  return page ? renderCard({ title: page.title, section: page.section }) : null;
}

export async function GET(
  _request: Request,
  { params }: RouteContext<"/og/[...path]">,
) {
  const { path } = await params;
  const png = await card(`/og/${path.join("/")}`);
  if (!png) return new Response("Not found", { status: 404 });
  return new Response(new Uint8Array(png), {
    headers: { "Content-Type": "image/png" },
  });
}
```

<div style="display:grid;grid-template-columns:repeat(auto-fit,minmax(300px,1fr));gap:16px;margin:0 0 12px"><figure style="margin:0"><img src="https://www.hyperelements.dev/img/blog/nextjs-open-graph-card-home.png" width="1200" height="630" loading="lazy" style="display:block;width:100%;height:auto;border:1px solid var(--line);border-radius:10px" alt="A green Northline card with lime, yellow and teal shapes, the section PRICING and the title Simple pricing for teams of every size."><figcaption style="margin-top:6px;color:var(--text-2);font-size:13px;line-height:1.5"><code>/pricing</code> · Pricing · 38 characters, drawn at 72px</figcaption></figure><figure style="margin:0"><img src="https://www.hyperelements.dev/img/blog/nextjs-open-graph-card-docs.png" width="1200" height="630" loading="lazy" style="display:block;width:100%;height:auto;border:1px solid style="margin-top:6px;color:var(--text-2);font-size:13px;line-height:1.5"><code>/docs/quickstart</code> · Docs · 48 characters, drawn at 72px</figcaption></figure><figure style="margin:0"><img var(--line);border-radius:10px" alt="A rose Northline card with orange, yellow and pink shapes, the section BLOG and the title The release notes checklist: what customers, support and engineers each need from every release, in four lines."><figcaption style="margin-top:6px;color:var(--text-2);font-size:13px;line-height:1.5"><code>/blog/release-notes-checklist</code> · Blog · 95 characters, drawn at 48px in four lines</figcaption></figure></div>

<p style="margin:0 0 28px;color:var(--text-2);font-size:13px;line-height:1.6">The PNGs this route returned for four pages in the list: one template, four sections. The logo, type and layout are the same on every card; the section picks the colors, and the fit picks the title’s size.</p>

Here is what each part of the route does:

- **`"use cache"`** is what lets Cache Components prerender the response. Without it, `next build` lists the route as dynamic (`ƒ`) and draws each card on request.
- **`cacheLife("max")`** sets how long a cached card lasts. With no `cacheLife`, the default profile revalidates every 15 minutes. The cards only change when you deploy, so `max` is the better fit.
- **The 404** covers any path that isn’t a page’s card, including a page that has its own image. Nothing is drawn for those requests.
- **No `runtime` export.** Satori and resvg need the Node.js runtime, which is the default for route handlers. With Cache Components on, `export const runtime = "nodejs"` fails the build (`Route segment config "runtime" is not compatible with nextConfig.cacheComponents`). With `runtime = "edge"` the build fails too, because the route uses `node:fs`.

If your app doesn’t use Cache Components, delete the `"use cache"` and `cacheLife("max")` lines and their import. `generateStaticParams` alone prerenders the cards then.

`next build` lists each card it drew:

```text
├   /og/[...path]
│ ├ ● /og/index.png
│ ├ ● /og/pricing.png
│ └ ● /og/blog/release-notes-checklist.png
```

### Why not the `opengraph-image.tsx` file convention?

Next.js also generates images from an `opengraph-image.tsx` file in a route segment, and adds the tags for you. It’s a good fit for one dynamic route: `app/blog/[slug]/opengraph-image.tsx` with `generateStaticParams` works with the same `renderCard()`. But the image function receives only the route’s `params`, not the page’s title. Every static page, such as `/pricing`, would need its own file with its own title. A single route handler reading one list covers the whole site.

## How does each page point at its card?

Each page builds its metadata with one function. It uses the page’s own image if there is one, and its card otherwise. It also fills in the card’s size and alt text.

`lib/metadata.ts`

```ts
import type { Metadata } from "next";
import { cardPath, pageAt } from "./pages";

export function metadataFor(path: string): Metadata {
  const page = pageAt(path);
  // The page's own image if it has one; otherwise its generated card.
  const image = page.image
    ? { url: page.image }
    : { url: cardPath(path), width: 1200, height: 630, alt: page.title };
  return {
    title: page.title,
    description: page.description,
    openGraph: {
      type: "website",
      siteName: "Northline",
      title: page.title,
      description: page.description,
      url: path,
      images: [image],
    },
    twitter: { card: "summary_large_image", images: [image] },
  };
}
```

Social sites need absolute image URLs, so set your site’s address as `metadataBase` in the root layout. Next.js resolves the relative `/og/…` paths against it.

`app/layout.tsx`

```tsx
import type { Metadata } from "next";

export const metadata: Metadata = {
  metadataBase: new URL("https://northline.example"),
};

export default function RootLayout({ children }: LayoutProps<"/">) {
  return (
    <html lang="en">
      <body>{children}</body>
    </html>
  );
}
```

A static page passes its own path:

`app/pricing/page.tsx`

```tsx
import { metadataFor } from "@/lib/metadata";

export const metadata = metadataFor("/pricing");

export default function Pricing() {
  return <h1>Simple pricing for teams of every size</h1>;
}
```

A dynamic route builds the path from its params:

`app/blog/[slug]/page.tsx`

```tsx
import { metadataFor } from "@/lib/metadata";
import { pageAt, pages } from "@/lib/pages";

export function generateStaticParams() {
  return pages
    .filter((page) => page.path.startsWith("/blog/"))
    .map((page) => ({ slug: page.path.slice("/blog/".length) }));
}

export async function generateMetadata({ params }: PageProps<"/blog/[slug]">) {
  const { slug } = await params;
  return metadataFor(`/blog/${slug}`);
}

export default async function Post({ params }: PageProps<"/blog/[slug]">) {
  const { slug } = await params;
  return <h1>{pageAt(`/blog/${slug}`).title}</h1>;
}
```

The blog post’s `<head>` then has these image tags, among the title and description ones:

```html
<meta property="og:image" content="https://northline.example/og/blog/release-notes-checklist.png"/>
<meta property="og:image:width" content="1200"/>
<meta property="og:image:height" content="630"/>
<meta property="og:image:alt" content="The release notes checklist: what customers, support and engineers each need from every release"/>
<meta name="twitter:card" content="summary_large_image"/>
<meta name="twitter:image" content="https://northline.example/og/blog/release-notes-checklist.png"/>
```

Next.js merges metadata shallowly: a page that sets `openGraph` replaces its layout’s `openGraph` whole. That’s why `metadataFor()` returns the complete `openGraph` object, not only the image.

A page missing from the list fails the build when its metadata is read (`No entry for /changelog in lib/pages.ts`), so no page ends up without a card by accident.

## How does a page opt out of its card?

Give its entry an `image`. The `/about` page above has one, so `generateStaticParams` skips it, `/og/about.png` returns 404, and its tags point at its own file:

```html
<meta property="og:image" content="https://northline.example/images/team.jpg"/>
<meta name="twitter:image" content="https://northline.example/images/team.jpg"/>
```

Next.js doesn’t know that file’s size, so it writes no width or height tags. Add `width` and `height` to the image object in `metadataFor()` if you want them.

## What happens when a title is too long?

The build stops. A title the card can’t take fails while Next.js prerenders its card, and `next build` exits with status 1. Each case below is the real output of `next build` with that title in `lib/pages.ts`.

A 115-character title is within `maxLength`, but at 48px it takes five lines:

```text
Error occurred prerendering page "/og/blog/release-notes-checklist.png". Read more: https://nextjs.org/docs/messages/prerender-error
Error [ElementsError]: [Elements] The template has 1 error:
error image/fit at root.children[0].children[1].children[1].children[1]: This Heading doesn't fit: it takes 5 lines at 48px, its smallest size, and fits 4: cut about 23 characters (required by northline.PageCard) Fix: Shorten the text, or give the template a smaller size
…
Export encountered an error on /og/[...path]/route: /og/blog/release-notes-checklist.png, exiting the build.
```

A 133-character title is refused by `check()` before it’s measured:

```text
Error: Card for "The complete checklist for writing release notes that customers, support teams, account managers and engineers will all actually read":
error template/value at values.title: Title: is longer than 120 characters
```

An emoji in a title is a character Inter doesn’t have:

```text
error image/glyph at root.children[0].children[1].children[1].children[1]: No font given draws "✨" (emoji): it's drawn as an empty box. Give a font that covers it (required by northline.PageCard)
```

A section the template has no palette for:

```text
Error: Card for "Release notes that people read":
error template/value at values.section: Section: expected one of "Product", "Pricing", "Docs", "Blog", "Company", not "Careers"
```

You can fix it in three places. Shorten the title. Add a shorter `cardTitle` to that page’s entry and pass it to `renderCard()`. Or, if the brand allows it, add a smaller size to the template’s `sizes`. For a character the font lacks, add a font that has it. For a new section, add its palette to `PALETTES`. The “cut about 23 characters” is an estimate: rebuild to confirm the new title fits.

## How do I check the cards?

Look at them before you trust them. In `next dev`, open a card’s URL, such as `http://localhost:3000/og/pricing.png`. The dev server draws it on request, from the same code: the PNG `next dev` served was byte for byte the one `next build` saved.

Check your shortest and longest titles, and titles with accents, names and punctuation you actually publish. Look at one card from each section too, since each has its own colors.

After that, the build guards the rest. Every card is drawn and measured on every build, so a new page whose title can’t fit stops the deploy. It doesn’t publish a clipped image.

Once deployed, open a page’s HTML and confirm its `og:image` URL loads without signing in. Then paste the page’s link into the sharing preview of the site you care about.

## Frequently asked questions

### Do I need an image API or a screenshot service?

No. The cards are drawn inside your build by Satori and resvg, from fonts on disk. No browser is launched, nothing is fetched, and there’s no API key.

### Can this run on the edge runtime?

No. `@hyper-elements/react/image` runs in Node.js only, and the route reads fonts with `node:fs`. Leave the route on the default Node.js runtime.

### When does a card change?

When you change a title in `lib/pages.ts` and build again. Cards are drawn from the list at build time. Under `cacheLife("max")`, Next.js may also redraw a cached card on the server after 30 days, from the same code and fonts. The fonts are traced into the server build, and the engines stay installed as ordinary dependencies.

### Can a card show more than the title?

Yes. Add a field to the template, such as an author or a date, and pass it from the page’s entry. Each new field is something that can vary between pages, so give it its own limits, and keep anything that should look the same everywhere in the template.

Start with `lib/og/card.tsx`: change the colors, logo and fonts to your brand, list your pages, and run `next build` to see every card. The [Next.js guide](https://www.hyperelements.dev/docs/guides/nextjs) covers emails and other outputs in the App Router, and [templates](https://www.hyperelements.dev/docs/templates) covers fields, formats and rules in full.

---

# Check HTML emails in GitHub Actions without rewriting your templates

Source: https://www.hyperelements.dev/blog/html-email-checks-github-actions

You can check an existing HTML email in GitHub Actions with `@hyper-elements/cli`: install the CLI, pass it the exported HTML file, and let its exit status fail the job. Add `--max-warnings 0` when warnings should block a change. You don’t need to rewrite the email in React or move it out of MJML, React Email, or your current builder.


This tutorial checks one committed file, `emails/receipt.html`, in an existing npm repository on GitHub.com. The result is a workflow that reports compatibility and HTML lint findings, fails when your policy requires it, and keeps JSON Lines diagnostics for review. It does not send an email or certify its appearance in real inboxes.



## How do I check an existing HTML email?


Use Node.js 20.6 or later, the CLI’s documented minimum. The workflow below selects Node.js 24 explicitly. From the repository root, install the CLI as a development dependency:


```bash
npm install -D @hyper-elements/cli
npx hyper-elements check emails/receipt.html --max-warnings 0
```


Commit the changed `package.json` and `package-lock.json`. Local installation lets CI use your reviewed dependency lockfile instead of fetching a new CLI release on every check. Update that dependency through your normal review process so local development and CI move together.


Already have exported HTML? Use it directly. Otherwise, save this deliberately flawed receipt as `emails/receipt.html`. Its “Click here” link gives us a specific, documented lint warning to repair:


```html
<!doctype html>
<html lang="en">
  <head>
    <meta charset="utf-8">
    <meta name="viewport" content="width=device-width, initial-scale=1">
    <title>Your Northline receipt</title>
  </head>
  <body>
    <h1>Thanks for your order</h1>
    <p>Your receipt for order NL-1042 is ready.</p>
    <p><a href="https://example.com/orders/NL-1042">Click here</a></p>
  </body>
</html>
```


Run the check command above. Hyper Elements’ [link-text rule](https://www.hyperelements.dev/docs/lint#link-text) warns about generic link labels because screen readers can list links by their words alone. HTML lint diagnostics use codes such as `lint/link-text`, with a line and column rather than a React component path.


Replace only the anchor’s words:


```html
<a href="https://example.com/orders/NL-1042">View your receipt</a>
```


Check the file again and address any remaining findings. Changing the words resolves that specific issue; it is not a claim that the destination exists, the receipt total is correct, or every inbox renders the message identically. Keep the `example.com` address in this fixture, and use your real receipt URL in production.



## What goes in the GitHub Actions workflow?


Create `.github/workflows/check-email.yml` with the following complete workflow. It checks the committed HTML file, so it needs no template-build command, browser installation, sending credentials, or React dependency.


```yaml
name: Check email HTML

on:
  pull_request:
  push:
    branches: [main]

permissions:
  contents: read

jobs:
  check-email:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - name: Check out the repository
        uses: actions/checkout@v7
        with:
          persist-credentials: false

      - name: Set up Node.js
        uses: actions/setup-node@v7
        with:
          node-version: '24'
          package-manager-cache: false

      - name: Install locked dependencies
        run: npm ci --include=dev

      - name: Check the exported email
        shell: bash
        run: |
          mkdir -p reports
          status=0
          npx hyper-elements check emails/receipt.html \
            --max-warnings 0 --json \
            > reports/email-check.jsonl || status=$?
          cat reports/email-check.jsonl
          exit "$status"

      - name: Keep the diagnostic report
        if: ${{ !cancelled() }}
        uses: actions/upload-artifact@v7
        with:
          name: email-check-diagnostics
          path: reports/email-check.jsonl
          if-no-files-found: warn
          retention-days: 7
```


<figure style="margin:0 0 28px"><img src="https://www.hyperelements.dev/img/blog/html-email-ci-reporting.png" width="1600" height="1008" loading="lazy" alt="A zero check status passes and a nonzero status fails; either path can upload available diagnostics without changing the check result." style="display:block;width:100%;height:auto;border:1px solid var(--line);border-radius:14px"><figcaption style="margin-top:10px;color:var(--text-2);font-size:13px;line-height:1.6">The diagnostic upload is a separate step. Saving a report must not hide a failed email check.</figcaption></figure>


Change `main` if your default branch has another name. The pull-request event checks proposed changes; the push event rechecks changes that land on that branch. There are no path filters to maintain while you establish the check.


[npm ci](https://docs.npmjs.com/cli/v11/commands/npm-ci) requires a lockfile consistent with `package.json`. `--include=dev` makes the CLI available even if the environment would otherwise omit development dependencies. Run this workflow from the npm project root, or adapt the paths and working directory for a nested project.


The workflow requests only repository-content read access and disables persisted checkout credentials. Don’t add sending-service secrets: checking this HTML file doesn’t require them. Use fictional order data in committed fixtures; diagnostic excerpts and retained artifacts can contain email content. The example uses GitHub-hosted Ubuntu runners, not a self-hosted runner configuration.



## Why capture the exit status before uploading the report?


GitHub Actions runs an explicitly selected Bash shell with error handling and `pipefail`. A command that fails can stop the step before later commands run. The `|| status=$?` branch records the CLI’s failure without abandoning the step; `cat` prints the report, and `exit "$status"` returns the original check result.


That distinction matters more than whether the report looks tidy. Don’t add `|| true` to the check, and don’t set `continue-on-error` just to get an artifact. Either would weaken the failure signal you added CI to obtain.


The upload step uses `!cancelled()`, so it can run after a failed check without trying to continue a canceled job. If dependency installation failed before the report existed, `if-no-files-found: warn` reports its absence; it doesn’t replace the earlier failure with a pass. The artifact expires after seven days, subject to the repository’s retention limits. GitHub documents the status-function behavior in its [expression reference](https://docs.github.com/en/actions/reference/workflows-and-actions/expressions#status-check-functions) and the artifact settings in [upload-artifact](https://github.com/actions/upload-artifact).


Saving an artifact is not guaranteed: an upload can itself fail, and an interrupted run may leave no useful report. Read the failing step first. Also, a failed workflow is not automatically a merge prohibition; configure the email-check job as a required status check in your repository’s branch protection or ruleset if that is your policy.



## How do I know the workflow is enforcing the policy?


Use the same receipt fixture to review both outcomes. In a pull request, leave the link as “Click here” and confirm that the check fails with a link-text warning. Then change it to “View your receipt,” push the repair, and inspect the next run. If other findings remain, fix those too rather than assuming this one edit should make the entire job green.


Review the artifact as well as the status: does it name the file you intended to check? Can a teammate find the offending markup from the diagnostic? This small failure-and-repair exercise checks the workflow’s wiring and makes the warning policy visible to reviewers. It is not a visual regression test. Keep future changes to the warning policy as deliberate as changes to the email itself.


## Which findings should fail the check?


The CLI documents these exit statuses. Treat any nonzero status as a failed CI check rather than assuming every failure means the email itself is invalid:


<table><thead><tr><th>Exit status</th><th>How to interpret it</th></tr></thead><tbody><tr><td><code>0</code></td><td>The command completed without errors or exceeding its warning limit.</td></tr><tr><td><code>1</code></td><td>The check found errors, exceeded the warning limit, or encountered a documented processing failure.</td></tr><tr><td><code>2</code></td><td>The command couldn’t perform the requested operation, such as a usage error or no usable input.</td></tr></tbody></table>


Lint findings are warnings or informational notes, not errors. Without a warning limit, a warning can leave the command successful. `--max-warnings 0` makes warnings fail the run; informational notes still don’t become failures merely because you chose that flag. See the [CLI exit-code reference](https://www.hyperelements.dev/docs/cli#json-and-exit-codes) for the full list.


For an existing collection of emails, decide which warnings must be fixed before making the job required. Keep any rule changes narrow and intentional. Lint configuration belongs under `hyperElements.lint` in the project’s `package.json`; don’t disable all lint just to get a green check. The [lint options](https://www.hyperelements.dev/docs/lint#options) list supported rule severities.



## How do I read the saved diagnostics?


`--json` writes one JSON line per checked input followed by a summary line. This is JSON Lines, not one JSON array: parse each nonempty line separately if you build tooling around it. Standard error remains separate, so an installation or command-launch problem may be visible in the Actions log rather than the report.


For HTML lint findings, use the diagnostic code to identify the rule, then the line, column, message and suggested fix to locate the markup. Follow the rule’s documentation link when present. Use the summary line to understand the overall result rather than treating an individual diagnostic as the whole check.


After a failed run, open its job log or download `email-check-diagnostics` from the workflow run. Reproduce the same command locally, repair the source that generates the HTML, regenerate it when necessary, and commit the updated file. Editing only an exported file is temporary if the next export restores the problem.



## Why didn’t a folder check my exported HTML?


Hyper Elements deliberately doesn’t discover HTML files when given a folder: template folders often contain generated HTML beside their sources. For existing HTML, name the file explicitly as this tutorial does, or give the documented shell pattern `emails/*.html`. Don’t replace the filename with `emails/` and assume the same inputs were checked.


If your repository generates email HTML during CI, add its existing build step before this check and point at the generated file. That build remains your generator’s responsibility. This tutorial intentionally keeps one committed file as the contract so you can establish the check without combining several framework setups.



## Does this replace Outlook or Gmail inbox testing?


No. The CLI checks documented compatibility concerns and runs the HTML lint rules; passing those checks does not prove visual correctness, delivery, personalization, or accessibility. HTML lint doesn’t check contrast, text size, or merge syntax, because it lacks the template information those checks need. Outlook conditional comments are skipped by HTML lint.


For another review layer, the [email client emulator](https://www.hyperelements.dev/docs/email-client-emulator) creates local, modeled client previews. Those are not screenshots captured from real inboxes. Keep actual client testing and a test send for the clients and content that matter to you. Browser-based preview collection is deliberately outside this basic CI job.



## Frequently asked questions


### Do I need to migrate from React Email or MJML?


No. Hyper Elements’ CLI accepts an existing `.html` or `.htm` file regardless of how it was generated. This workflow checks the output, not the generator’s component source.


### Do I need Playwright or a browser in CI?


Not for the `check` command shown here. Collecting browser-drawn preview findings is a separate workflow with additional requirements documented under [preview](https://www.hyperelements.dev/docs/cli#preview).


### Will warnings block a pull request?


`--max-warnings 0` makes warnings fail the job. To block merging, also make that job a required check in your repository settings. Informational findings are not warnings.


### Where should I start if I’m writing a new React email?


Follow [Build and validate React emails with Claude Code](https://www.hyperelements.dev/blog/react-emails-claude-code) for the authoring and repair loop, then return here to check exported HTML in CI. If the same order needs a PDF, the [Node.js invoice tutorial](https://www.hyperelements.dev/blog/node-pdf-invoices-without-chrome) covers that separate output.


Start with one representative email and a pull request that demonstrates a warning and its repair. Once reviewers understand the failure and report, apply the same explicit policy to the rest of your exported emails.

---

# Generate Open Graph images in Node.js with local fonts and a logo

Source: https://www.hyperelements.dev/blog/node-open-graph-images-local-fonts

To generate an Open Graph image in Node.js, write a React template rooted in `Canvas`, read your font and logo files into memory, and pass them to Hyper Elements’ `renderImage()`. It returns PNG bytes you can write to disk. The renderer uses Satori and resvg without launching a browser or fetching your assets.

This tutorial builds one branded card from a post’s title and author. It stays in a standalone Node.js script: no API route, screenshot service or framework integration. You’ll also add a conservative diagnostics policy and a review checklist, because a fixed-size image can clip text even when a template passes its checks.

## What do I need to generate a card?

Start with a maintained Node.js installation and an empty project directory. Install the React components, image engines and a runner for TypeScript with JSX:

```bash
npm init -y
npm install @hyper-elements/react satori@^0.33.5 @resvg/resvg-js react react-dom
npm install -D tsx
```

The Satori range is intentional: it is the compatibility range in the [image renderer’s installation docs](https://www.hyperelements.dev/docs/outputs/image#install), not a pin to an old Hyper Elements release. Keep that engine requirement aligned with the current docs when upgrading. Image rendering is a separate entry point; the ordinary element import does not load these engines.

Add `"type": "module"` to `package.json`, preserving its other fields. Create `tsconfig.json` with the following content. In an existing project, merge this JSX setting rather than replacing its configuration.

```json
{
  "compilerOptions": {
    "jsx": "react-jsx"
  },
  "include": ["card.tsx", "scripts/**/*.tsx"]
}
```

Place two font files and your logo in this structure. The logo in this example is a PNG whose intrinsic size is 240 by 80 pixels; change the template’s dimensions if yours differs. Use fonts and artwork you have permission to distribute.

```text
fonts/
  Inter-Regular.ttf
  Inter-Bold.ttf
images/
  logo.png
scripts/
  render-card.tsx
card.tsx
```

[tsx](https://tsx.is/getting-started) runs the script; it does not type-check it. Keep a separate TypeScript checking step if your project needs one.

## How do I turn post data into a React image template?

Save this as `card.tsx`. A [Canvas](https://www.hyperelements.dev/docs/elements/canvas) has explicit pixel dimensions. Its children stack vertically, and `justifyContent: "space-between"` spreads them through the available height. Text belongs in `Heading` and `Text`, not loose HTML elements.

`card.tsx`

```tsx
import {
  Canvas,
  Heading,
  Image,
  Text,
} from "@hyper-elements/react";

export const logoKey = "https://example.com/brand/logo.png";

export type CardData = {
  title: string;
  author: string;
};

export function assertCardData(data: CardData) {
  if (!data.title.trim() || data.title.length > 90) {
    throw new Error("Use a non-empty card title of at most 90 code units.");
  }
  if (!data.author.trim() || data.author.length > 60) {
    throw new Error("Use a non-empty byline of at most 60 code units.");
  }
}

export function PostCard({ title, author }: CardData) {
  return (
    <Canvas
      width={1200}
      height={630}
      style={{
        backgroundColor: "#101827",
        color: "#ffffff",
        fontFamily: "Inter, sans-serif",
        padding: 64,
        gap: 24,
        justifyContent: "space-between",
      }}
    >
      <Image
        src={{ src: logoKey, width: 240, height: 80 }}
        alt="Northline"
        style={{ width: 120 }}
      />
      <Text
        style={{
          fontSize: 20,
          fontWeight: 700,
          letterSpacing: 2,
          color: "#b8c6da",
        }}
      >
        NORTHLINE NOTES
      </Text>
      <Heading
        level={1}
        style={{ fontSize: 64, fontWeight: 700, lineHeight: 1.1 }}
      >
        {title}
      </Heading>
      <Text style={{ fontSize: 28, color: "#b8c6da" }}>
        {author}
      </Text>
    </Canvas>
  );
}
```

<figure style="margin:0 0 28px"><img src="https://www.hyperelements.dev/img/blog/node-open-graph-card-output.png" width="1200" height="630" loading="lazy" style="display:block;width:100%;height:auto;border:1px solid var(--line);border-radius:14px" alt="A dark Northline Notes card with a coral geometric logo, the title Ship a smaller JavaScript bundle and the byline Morgan Lee · Engineering."><figcaption style="margin-top:10px;color:var(--text-2);font-size:13px;line-height:1.6">The template rendered as a PNG with local Inter font files, a fictional Northline logo and the sample post data used below.</figcaption></figure>

The URL in `logoKey` is a lookup key, not a download instruction. The render script will associate that exact string with local image bytes. A plausible URL alone is not enough to render the logo.

The title and byline limits are application policy, not layout guarantees. JavaScript’s `length` counts UTF-16 code units, not visible characters or rendered width. A short unbroken identifier can be harder to fit than a longer sentence. Use a dedicated, concise card title when the full article headline does not fit.

## How do I load local fonts and write the PNG?

Save this second file as `scripts/render-card.tsx`. Run it from the project root so the relative asset paths resolve to the files above. Assets load before rendering, and the template receives plain post data.

`scripts/render-card.tsx`

```tsx
import { mkdir, readFile, writeFile } from "node:fs/promises";
import {
  ElementsError,
  formatDiagnostics,
  validate,
} from "@hyper-elements/react";
import { renderImage } from "@hyper-elements/react/image";
import { assertCardData, logoKey, PostCard } from "../card";

async function main() {
  const [regular, bold, logo] = await Promise.all([
    readFile("fonts/Inter-Regular.ttf"),
    readFile("fonts/Inter-Bold.ttf"),
    readFile("images/logo.png"),
  ]);

  const assets = {
    fonts: [
      { family: "Inter", src: regular, weight: 400 },
      { family: "Inter", src: bold, weight: 700 },
    ],
    images: { [logoKey]: logo },
  };

  const data = {
    title: "Ship a smaller JavaScript bundle",
    author: "Morgan Lee · Engineering",
  };
  assertCardData(data);
  const element = <PostCard {...data} />;

  const checked = validate(element);
  if (checked.diagnostics.length) {
    console.warn(formatDiagnostics(checked.diagnostics));
  }
  if (!checked.valid || checked.diagnostics.some((d) => d.severity === "warning")) {
    throw new Error("Resolve template errors and warnings before rendering.");
  }

  const { image, width, height, diagnostics } = await renderImage(element, assets);
  if (diagnostics.length) console.warn(formatDiagnostics(diagnostics));
  if (diagnostics.some((d) => d.severity === "warning")) {
    throw new Error("Resolve image warnings before saving the card.");
  }

  await mkdir("output", { recursive: true });
  await writeFile("output/card.png", image);
  console.log(`Wrote output/card.png (${width} × ${height})`);
}

main().catch((error: unknown) => {
  if (error instanceof ElementsError) {
    console.error(formatDiagnostics(error.diagnostics));
  } else {
    console.error(error);
  }
  process.exitCode = 1;
});
```

```bash
npx tsx scripts/render-card.tsx
```

The [Node.js file API](https://nodejs.org/api/fs.html#promises-api) reads the assets as buffers, creates the output directory and writes the returned bytes. Open `output/card.png` to inspect the actual image. If a run fails, do not publish a leftover file from an earlier run; only consume the output after the script succeeds.

## Why do font weights and image keys matter?

Hyper Elements’ image renderer fetches nothing. Each image must be supplied in the `images` map under the exact key its template uses, or embedded as a data URI. Supported image files are PNG, JPEG, GIF and SVG. Keep the asset paths fixed in your build configuration rather than letting external post data choose arbitrary local files.

Fonts are matched by family, weight and style. The template asks for Inter at regular and bold weights, so the script supplies both files under the same family name. Supplying only regular does not give the renderer the bold file: it uses the nearest supplied face and reports `image/font-weight`.

For image output, use TTF, OTF or WOFF bytes. **WOFF2 is not drawn.** A font declaration containing a web URL does not cause a download. The supplied fonts also need the actual glyphs you use; unsupported characters can appear as empty boxes. Check names, punctuation and the languages your posts contain, not just an English sample.

### What should I check when the logo or font is missing?

Separate file-loading failures from rendering diagnostics. If Node reports that `images/logo.png` does not exist, check your working directory and the local filename first. The renderer has not received that image yet. If the file loads but rendering reports `image/image`, compare the template’s `logoKey` with the map key character for character, then confirm the bytes belong to a supported image format.

For example, changing the template to `https://example.com/brand/mark.png` while leaving the map under `https://example.com/brand/logo.png` creates two different identifiers. Loading the right file under the wrong identifier does not satisfy the template. Share one exported constant, as this example does, instead of maintaining duplicate strings.

For a font problem, compare the template’s `fontFamily` with the family names in `assets.fonts`. They are your matching labels, not filesystem paths. Renaming a WOFF2 file to `.ttf` does not convert it. Supply an actual supported file and explicitly include the weight the heading asks for. When you change assets, inspect the newly generated PNG rather than assuming an earlier preview still represents the card.

## Does validation prove the card fits?

No. `validate()` can report unsupported template features and estimated Canvas overflow before rendering. It cannot check files it has not received. `renderImage()` adds font and image checks using the supplied bytes; errors reject with `ElementsError`.

| Finding | What to fix |
| --- | --- |
| `image/font` | Supply a usable font file; do not pass WOFF2. |
| `image/font-weight` | Supply the requested weight or change the template. |
| `image/image` | Check the exact lookup key, bytes and supported file format. |
| `canvas/overflow` | Shorten the content or change the layout, then inspect the PNG. |

The script refuses to save on warnings. That is a deliberately conservative policy for this example, not the renderer’s default behavior. A clean diagnostic list still does not certify that text fits: `canvas/overflow` is an estimate, and anything outside the fixed Canvas edges is cut off.

Before adopting the template, inspect a short title, your longest accepted title, an unbroken word, and representative accented or non-Latin text. Confirm the logo proportions, every line of the heading and the byline. If a title clips, rewrite it or reduce its font size and inspect again. Do not add unlimited user text: the renderer also lays out text beyond the visible boundary, consuming time and memory.

## How do I generate one card for each post?

Once the first PNG looks right, reuse the loaded `assets` for a small list of post records. Replace the single-card block in `main()`, from `const data` through the final `console.log`, with this loop. It writes sequentially and keeps the same warning policy.

```tsx
const posts = [
  {
    slug: "smaller-bundles",
    title: "Ship a smaller JavaScript bundle",
    author: "Morgan Lee · Engineering",
  },
  {
    slug: "useful-build-logs",
    title: "Make build logs useful",
    author: "Morgan Lee · Engineering",
  },
];

await mkdir("output", { recursive: true });
for (const post of posts) {
  if (!/^[a-z0-9]+(?:-[a-z0-9]+)*$/.test(post.slug)) {
    throw new Error("Use a plain lowercase slug for each output filename.");
  }
  assertCardData(post);
  const element = <PostCard {...post} />;
  const checked = validate(element);
  if (checked.diagnostics.length) {
    console.warn(formatDiagnostics(checked.diagnostics));
  }
  if (!checked.valid || checked.diagnostics.some((d) => d.severity === "warning")) {
    throw new Error(`Fix template diagnostics for ${post.slug}.`);
  }
  const result = await renderImage(element, assets);
  if (result.diagnostics.length) {
    console.warn(formatDiagnostics(result.diagnostics));
  }
  if (result.diagnostics.some((d) => d.severity === "warning")) {
    throw new Error(`Fix image warnings for ${post.slug}.`);
  }
  await writeFile(`output/${post.slug}.png`, result.image);
}
```

Use unique slugs, or later records overwrite earlier files. This small script is not a transactional publishing system: if a later record fails, earlier PNGs remain. Only publish the completed set after the whole command succeeds.

## How does the card become a link preview?

Generating a PNG does not attach it to a page. Publish the chosen file at a public HTTPS URL, then add Open Graph metadata to that page’s HTML `<head>`. Replace these example URLs with your real page and image addresses:

```html
<meta property="og:type" content="article">
<meta property="og:title" content="Ship a smaller JavaScript bundle">
<meta property="og:url" content="https://example.com/blog/smaller-bundles">
<meta property="og:image" content="https://example.com/og/smaller-bundles.png">
<meta property="og:image:type" content="image/png">
<meta property="og:image:width" content="1200">
<meta property="og:image:height" content="630">
<meta property="og:image:alt" content="Northline Notes: Ship a smaller JavaScript bundle, by Morgan Lee.">
```

The [Open Graph protocol](https://ogp.me/) defines the page title, type, canonical URL and image URL, plus the image’s optional dimensions, type and description. The local filename is not a public image address. Check that the deployed page contains your tags and that the image URL opens without authentication before testing a shared link.

## Frequently asked questions

### Can I use a Google Fonts stylesheet instead of font bytes?

Not as the image renderer’s font input. Hyper Elements needs supported font file bytes or supported data URIs. Download and supply the required TTF, OTF or WOFF files with the correct family, weight and style.

### Can I export SVG instead of PNG?

Yes. Pass `format: "svg"` to `renderImage()` and write the returned bytes to a `.svg` file. Text is drawn as paths. This tutorial uses PNG for the published card; changing the file extension alone does not change the output format.

### Can I render this template in an Edge runtime?

The documented Hyper Elements image entry is Node.js-only. Keep this script in a Node.js build step rather than assuming the native image engine works in an Edge or browser runtime.

### Will the title shrink automatically to fit?

This template does not implement automatic text fitting. Its title has a fixed font size and the Canvas clips at its edges. Keep a bounded, editorially chosen card title and inspect the actual PNG with your longest inputs.

Start with the single-card script: replace the sample data, logo and font files, then inspect your first PNG. The [image output reference](https://www.hyperelements.dev/docs/outputs/image) covers other formats and diagnostics. For other server-side outputs, try [PDF invoices in Node.js](https://www.hyperelements.dev/blog/node-pdf-invoices-without-chrome); for an agent-led template repair loop, see [React emails with Claude Code](https://www.hyperelements.dev/blog/react-emails-claude-code).
