# Generate PDF invoices in Node.js without headless Chrome

Source: https://www.hyperelements.dev/blog/node-pdf-invoices-without-chrome

Use a React `Document` template and `renderPdf()` to write an invoice PDF directly in Node.js. Supply fonts and images as bytes, define each page explicitly, and inspect the result before sending it.

This tutorial uses Hyper Elements for the template and its `@hyper-elements/react/pdf` entry for PDF output. You do not launch a browser or fetch assets during rendering. You also do not get a browser’s full CSS model or automatic pagination. The example deliberately separates the invoice and payment terms into two pages.

## How do I create the first invoice PDF?

Start in an empty directory with Node.js and npm available. Install the PDF engine explicitly: it is an optional peer dependency, not something the main Hyper Elements entry loads for you. These commands follow the [PDF installation guide](https://www.hyperelements.dev/docs/outputs/pdf) and the [tsx project setup](https://tsx.hirok.io/installation).

```bash
npm init -y
npm install @hyper-elements/react @react-pdf/renderer react react-dom
npm install -D tsx
```

In `package.json`, add `"type": "module"` as a top-level field, keeping the existing fields. This makes the example run as ESM; without it, the CommonJS path can fail on the PDF engine’s dependency exports. This setting affects other JavaScript and TypeScript files in the package too, so use this isolated tutorial directory rather than changing an existing application blindly. See [tsx’s module-format guide](https://tsx.hirok.io/modules).

Create this configuration so JSX uses React’s automatic runtime. The `.tsx` extension enables JSX syntax; the [JSX configuration](https://tsx.hirok.io/typescript#jsx) selects how it is transformed. This is a small execution setup, not a complete TypeScript checking configuration.

tsconfig.json

```json
{
  "compilerOptions": {
    "jsx": "react-jsx"
  }
}
```

Before running the script, create `fonts/` and `images/`. Put licensed Inter Regular and Bold TTF files at the paths below, and supply a PNG logo with a 3:1 aspect ratio. Use your own assets; no download script or remote CDN is required.

```text
fonts/Inter-Regular.ttf
fonts/Inter-Bold.ttf
images/logo.png
invoice.tsx
tsconfig.json
```

Save this complete example as `invoice.tsx`. The order is fictional. It uses two items, no tax and a single currency so the PDF workflow stays visible. Replace those business rules with your own before making a real invoice.

invoice.tsx

```tsx
import { readFile, writeFile } from "node:fs/promises";
import {
  Document, ElementsError, Heading, Image,
  PageFooter, PageHeader, PageNumber,
  Table, TableCell, TableRow, Text,
  formatDiagnostics, validate,
} from "@hyper-elements/react";
import { renderPdf } from "@hyper-elements/react/pdf";

const order = {
  number: "INV-2705",
  customer: "Morgan Lee",
  issued: "10 November 2026",
  due: "10 December 2026",
  items: [
    { id: "shirt", name: "Linen shirt", quantity: 2, unitCents: 4800 },
    { id: "bag", name: "Canvas bag", quantity: 1, unitCents: 2400 },
  ],
};

const money = (cents: number) =>
  new Intl.NumberFormat("en-US", {
    style: "currency", currency: "USD",
  }).format(cents / 100);

const totalCents = order.items.reduce(
  (sum, item) => sum + item.quantity * item.unitCents, 0,
);

// This is an application limit, not a renderer fit guarantee.
if (order.items.length > 6) {
  throw new Error("Review and split this invoice into explicit pages.");
}

const logo = "https://assets.example.com/invoice-logo.png";

function Invoice() {
  return (
    <Document
      size="A4"
      margin={48}
      title={`Invoice ${order.number}`}
      style={{ fontFamily: "Inter, sans-serif", fontSize: 14 }}
    >
      <PageHeader style={{ padding: [0, 0, 20, 0] }}>
        <Image
          src={{ src: logo, width: 240, height: 80 }}
          alt="Northline Supply"
          style={{ width: 120 }}
        />
      </PageHeader>
      <PageFooter>
        <Text style={{ fontSize: 10, textAlign: "right" }}>
          Page <PageNumber /> of <PageNumber total />
        </Text>
      </PageFooter>
      <Document.Page style={{ gap: 16 }}>
        <Heading level={1}>Invoice {order.number}</Heading>
        <Text>Bill to: {order.customer}</Text>
        <Text>Issued: {order.issued} · Due: {order.due}</Text>
        <Table style={{
          cellPadding: [8, 4],
          rowBorder: "1px solid #dedede",
        }}>
          <TableRow header>
            <TableCell>Item</TableCell>
            <TableCell style={{ textAlign: "right" }}>Qty</TableCell>
            <TableCell style={{ textAlign: "right" }}>Unit</TableCell>
            <TableCell style={{ textAlign: "right" }}>Amount</TableCell>
          </TableRow>
          {order.items.map((item) => (
            <TableRow key={item.id}>
              <TableCell>{item.name}</TableCell>
              <TableCell style={{ textAlign: "right" }}>
                {item.quantity}
              </TableCell>
              <TableCell style={{ textAlign: "right" }}>
                {money(item.unitCents)}
              </TableCell>
              <TableCell style={{ textAlign: "right" }}>
                {money(item.quantity * item.unitCents)}
              </TableCell>
            </TableRow>
          ))}
        </Table>
        <Text style={{ fontWeight: 700, textAlign: "right" }}>
          Total due: {money(totalCents)}
        </Text>
        <Text>Payment instructions are on the next page.</Text>
      </Document.Page>
      <Document.Page style={{ gap: 16 }}>
        <Heading level={2}>Payment terms</Heading>
        <Text>Please pay by {order.due}.</Text>
        <Text>Use {order.number} as the payment reference.</Text>
        <Text>Contact your account representative for payment details.</Text>
      </Document.Page>
    </Document>
  );
}

async function main() {
  const element = <Invoice />;
  const check = validate(element);
  if (check.diagnostics.length) {
    console.warn(formatDiagnostics(check.diagnostics));
  }
  if (!check.valid || check.diagnostics.some(
    (d) => d.severity === "warning",
  )) {
    throw new Error("Review template diagnostics before writing a PDF.");
  }

  const { pdf, diagnostics } = await renderPdf(element, {
    fonts: [
      { family: "Inter", src: await readFile("fonts/Inter-Regular.ttf") },
      {
        family: "Inter", src: await readFile("fonts/Inter-Bold.ttf"),
        weight: 700,
      },
    ],
    images: { [logo]: await readFile("images/logo.png") },
  });
  if (diagnostics.length) console.warn(formatDiagnostics(diagnostics));
  if (diagnostics.some((d) => d.severity === "warning")) {
    throw new Error("Review PDF warnings before saving the file.");
  }
  await writeFile("invoice.pdf", pdf);
}

main().catch((error: unknown) => {
  if (error instanceof ElementsError) {
    console.error(formatDiagnostics(error.diagnostics));
  } else {
    console.error(error);
  }
  process.exitCode = 1;
});
```

<figure style="margin:0 0 28px"><img src="https://www.hyperelements.dev/img/blog/node-pdf-invoice-output.png" alt="Actual invoice PDF output showing fictional Northline Supply invoice INV-2705 for Morgan Lee, with two line items and a total due of $120.00." width="953" height="560" loading="lazy" style="display:block;width:100%;height:auto;border:1px solid var(--line);border-radius:14px"><figcaption style="margin-top:10px;color:var(--text-2);font-size:13px;line-height:1.6">Actual PDF output from the example, using local Inter font files and a fictional Northline Supply logo. Cropped to the invoice body; the page-number footer and separate terms page are not shown.</figcaption></figure>

Run the file from the project root so the relative asset paths resolve:

```bash
npx tsx ./invoice.tsx
```

If the render succeeds without warnings, the script writes `invoice.pdf` in that directory. The two explicit pages contain the invoice and its terms, with the same logo and page-number footer.

## Why keep order data outside the template?

The template should describe the document, not fetch the order or decide which prices are authoritative. Load and authorize the order first, then pass trusted data into your rendering code. The example keeps everything in one file so you can see the whole path.

Prices are stored as integer cents and line amounts are calculated before currency formatting. Do not add formatted currency strings. This deliberately narrow example assumes USD, whole item quantities and no discounts or taxes; it is not a general accounting library. Keep your existing tax, rounding and invoice-number rules in the business layer.

Likewise, the six-item guard is an editorially chosen input bound, not a measurement of A4 capacity. Even one very long description can wrap into too much space. Validate incoming field lengths and quantities for your application, then review the longest real data you permit. Do not silently truncate a description or discard a line to make the page fit.

## How do local fonts and images work?

The logo URL is an identifier used to match the template’s image to bytes in `images`. The renderer does not download that URL. The [Node.js file API](https://nodejs.org/api/fs.html#fspromisesreadfilepath-options) supplies those bytes from disk, and `writeFile()` saves the PDF bytes. Deploy the asset files with your application and resolve their locations deliberately.

Supply each font weight you use. Here, regular text uses Inter Regular and the total uses Inter Bold. Hyper Elements accepts TTF, OTF or WOFF for PDF fonts, not WOFF2. Raster images must be PNG or JPEG; an external SVG image is not drawn as an image. An `Svg` element is a separate vector option.

For text outside Western European characters, provide a font with the necessary glyphs. Standard PDF fallback fonts are limited, and the renderer does not check that your supplied file contains every character. Inspect the actual customer names and symbols you support. A font’s presence alone is not a text-correctness test.

## Will a long invoice create more pages automatically?

No. [`Document.Page`](https://www.hyperelements.dev/docs/elements/document-page) defines a page; it does not spill its children onto another one. Alternatively, `PageBreak` splits a run of content into explicit pages. A header and footer repeat on each page inside the document’s margins.

Choose page boundaries in your application. For larger invoices, prepare page-sized groups, repeat the table heading in each page’s table and put the grand total where you intend it. A fixed number of rows is only a starting policy: variable descriptions, font sizes and header heights change the space required.

The `document/overflow` diagnostic is an estimate, not a text measurement or a promise that every row is visible. The absence of that warning must not be your acceptance criterion. If automatic flow for arbitrary documents is a requirement, this explicit-page approach is not the right fit without additional pagination work.

## When is a browser-based PDF still the better choice?

Choose this workflow when you can express a bounded document using the supported elements and want assets supplied explicitly. It is not an HTML-to-PDF compatibility layer. Reusing an existing application screen may be a different problem from building an invoice template.

For example, [RisingStack’s Puppeteer tutorial](https://blog.risingstack.com/pdf-from-html-node-js-puppeteer/) uses headless Chrome to print an existing, heavily styled React report with SVG visualizations. That approach preserves a browser-rendered page, but introduces browser setup and deployment concerns. Neither approach is universally better: decide whether you need a browser page printed or a document assembled from a constrained template.

Also separate “no network during rendering” from “no network in the application.” An application may fetch an authorized order before it creates the template. Here, rendering receives already-loaded data and asset bytes. Keeping that boundary explicit makes missing files and missing order data different failures, rather than a remote asset request hidden inside document generation.

## Which diagnostics should stop the export?

The script checks the template first, then checks PDF-specific diagnostics after rendering. `validate()` can report unsupported features and estimated overflow, but font and image checks need the actual files and happen in `renderPdf()`. A `valid: true` result can still contain warnings.

This example treats every warning as a reason to stop before saving. That is an application policy, stricter than the renderer’s default. Keep stable diagnostic codes in automated checks and show the message to the developer. Catch ordinary application and file errors too; they are not all template diagnostics.

<table><thead><tr><th>Diagnostic</th><th>What to review</th></tr></thead><tbody><tr><td><code>pdf/root</code></td><td>Use a Document root, not an Email or Canvas.</td></tr><tr><td><code>pdf/image</code></td><td>Supply the matching image bytes and a supported format.</td></tr><tr><td><code>pdf/font</code> / <code>pdf/font-weight</code></td><td>Provide the requested family, file format and weight.</td></tr><tr><td><code>document/overflow</code></td><td>Shorten or split the content explicitly, then inspect every page.</td></tr></tbody></table>

The [diagnostics reference](https://www.hyperelements.dev/docs/diagnostics) explains severities and paths. PDF errors reject with `ElementsError`; warnings and notes accompany the rendered bytes. Do not hide those messages simply because a file exists.

## What should I check before sending an invoice?

Open the generated PDF, not only a browser rendering of the JSX. Review every line item, the total, logo proportions, page numbers, page edges and the last line on each page. Copy a customer name and an amount into a text editor, then search for them in the PDF. A page can look correct while its text layer is wrong.

Test a sequence of invoices in the same process, including accented names followed by ordinary Latin names, because the current text-layer issue is process-dependent. Use the largest descriptions and item counts you allow. These checks are regression cases, not a substitute for a released fix.

For an application integration, keep the PDF bytes until your review/export policy passes, then hand them to your existing download, storage or attachment code. Do not log private billing data. If you also need a transactional email, our [React receipt-email tutorial](https://www.hyperelements.dev/blog/react-emails-claude-code) covers a separate Email template; share order data, not a promise that one layout fits both outputs.

## Frequently asked questions

### Does this turn arbitrary HTML into a PDF?

No. It renders the supported Hyper Elements element model under a Document root. For an existing browser page that depends on full browser CSS or JavaScript, a browser-based print workflow may be more appropriate. This tutorial does not replace that workflow.

### Can I preview the document as HTML?

Yes. `render()` from the main package returns print-ready HTML for a Document. The [print HTML guide](https://www.hyperelements.dev/docs/outputs/pdf#print-html) describes it. HTML font loading and PDF font bytes are separate configurations; an HTML preview is not a substitute for inspecting the final PDF.

### Does tsx check TypeScript types?

No. It transforms and runs TypeScript. Add a separate TypeScript check to your project if you need one; [tsx documents that workflow](https://tsx.hirok.io/typescript). Runtime template diagnostics and static types answer different questions.

### What should I try next?

Replace the fictional order and local assets, generate one bounded invoice and inspect both pages. Then add your longest permitted data and review the current PDF release notes before connecting it to a billing workflow. Start with the complete example, not an unbounded table and an assumption that pagination will handle it.

---

# Build and validate React emails with Claude Code

Source: https://www.hyperelements.dev/blog/react-emails-claude-code

To build a React email with Claude Code, give it the guide shipped with your installed renderer, ask for a template, then make it check that template before sending. With Hyper Elements, that loop is `validate()` for template problems, `outline()` for text-based layout inspection, and `render()` for HTML and plain text. A passing check is useful feedback—not proof that every inbox looks right.

This tutorial takes a fictional shop's receipt through that loop. You'll keep order data separate from presentation, repair an unsupported style, and prepare a test send with Resend. Hyper Elements renders the message; your email provider delivers it. You don't need to change providers to use this authoring workflow.

## What does the complete receipt template look like?

Start with this template in `emails/receipt.tsx`. The example uses fictional data and a reserved example-domain link; replace the link and merchant details before a real send.

```tsx
// emails/receipt.tsx
import {
  Button, Column, Email, Heading, Table, TableCell,
  TableRow, Text,
} from "@hyper-elements/react";

export type Order = {
  number: string;
  customer: string;
  items: { name: string; quantity: number; unitPrice: number }[];
  delivery: number;
  orderUrl: string;
};

const money = (cents: number) => `$${(cents / 100).toFixed(2)}`;

export function Receipt({ order }: { order: Order }) {
  const subtotal = order.items.reduce(
    (sum, item) => sum + item.quantity * item.unitPrice, 0,
  );

  return (
    <Email
      previewText={`Receipt for order ${order.number}`}
      style={{
        backgroundColor: "#f4f4f5",
        fontFamily: "Helvetica, Arial, sans-serif",
        gap: 16,
      }}
    >
      <Text style={{ fontWeight: 700 }}>Northline Supply</Text>
      <Column style={{ backgroundColor: "#ffffff", padding: 24, gap: 16 }}>
        <Heading level={1} style={{ fontSize: 24, mobile: { fontSize: 20 } }}>
          Thanks for your order, {order.customer}
        </Heading>
        <Text>We've received order {order.number}. Here's your receipt.</Text>
        <Table style={{ cellPadding: [8, 0], rowBorder: "1px solid #e4e4e7" }}>
          <TableRow header>
            <TableCell>Item</TableCell>
            <TableCell style={{ textAlign: "right" }}>Amount</TableCell>
          </TableRow>
          {order.items.map((item, index) => (
            <TableRow key={index}>
              <TableCell>{item.quantity} × {item.name}</TableCell>
              <TableCell style={{ textAlign: "right" }}>
                {money(item.quantity * item.unitPrice)}
              </TableCell>
            </TableRow>
          ))}
        </Table>
        <Text>Subtotal: {money(subtotal)}</Text>
        <Text>Delivery: {money(order.delivery)}</Text>
        <Text style={{ fontWeight: 700 }}>
          Total paid: {money(subtotal + order.delivery)}
        </Text>
        <Button href={order.orderUrl} style={{ backgroundColor: "#111827" }}>
          View your order
        </Button>
      </Column>
      <Text style={{ fontSize: 12, color: "#52525b" }}>
        Northline Supply · Fictional shop for this example
      </Text>
    </Email>
  );
}

export const exampleOrder: Order = {
  number: "NL-1042",
  customer: "Ada",
  items: [
    { name: "Field notebook", quantity: 2, unitPrice: 1200 },
    { name: "Pencil set", quantity: 1, unitPrice: 600 },
  ],
  delivery: 500,
  orderUrl: "https://example.com/orders/NL-1042",
};
```

<figure style="margin:0 0 28px"><img src="https://www.hyperelements.dev/img/blog/claude-code-receipt-email.png" alt="Rendered Northline Supply receipt for order NL-1042: two field notebooks and one pencil set, a $30 subtotal, $5 delivery, $35 total paid, and a View your order button." width="1360" height="1060" loading="lazy" style="display:block;width:100%;height:auto;border:1px solid var(--line);border-radius:14px"><figcaption style="margin-top:10px;color:var(--text-2);font-size:13px;line-height:1.6">Browser screenshot of the complete template above, rendered with the fictional example order. This is not an inbox compatibility test.</figcaption></figure>

The prices are integer cents, with a deliberately simple USD formatter. Production totals should come from your trusted order system, including its tax, discount and currency rules. Don't turn an email template into a second billing engine.

Two columns keep the item table compact. Quantity lives beside the item name instead of becoming a third narrow column. Spacing belongs to the containing `Column`'s `gap`, and padding belongs inside that card. These are Hyper Elements' [layout rules](https://www.hyperelements.dev/docs/layout), not arbitrary CSS conventions.

## How do you set up the project and Claude Code?

Use a server-side Node.js project. In an existing app, keep its package manager and configuration. For a new folder, create a `package.json` first, then install the renderer and its React peers:

```bash
npm init -y
npm install @hyper-elements/react react react-dom
npm install -D tsx
```

The [quickstart](https://www.hyperelements.dev/docs/quickstart) documents the renderer installation and requires React and React DOM 18 or later. This tutorial uses [tsx's project installation](https://tsx.hirok.io/installation) to execute the TypeScript/JSX scripts. It isn't an email preview service or a type checker.

For the fresh project, add `"type": "module"` to `package.json`, keeping its other fields. Create a `tsconfig.json` containing:

```json
{
  "compilerOptions": {
    "jsx": "react-jsx"
  },
  "include": ["emails/**/*.tsx", "scripts/**/*.tsx"]
}
```

In an existing TypeScript app, merge the JSX setting into its configuration rather than replacing it. The [tsx TypeScript guide](https://tsx.hirok.io/typescript) explains transformation settings and the separate role of type checking.

Put this import on its own line in a project-root `CLAUDE.md`:

```text
@node_modules/@hyper-elements/react/GUIDE.md
```

Use the bare line, not a fenced code block inside the actual file. Claude Code's [memory documentation](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/memory) says imports resolve relative to the file containing them; imports inside code spans or fences are skipped. If your `CLAUDE.md` lives elsewhere, adjust the relative path.

The guide is generated from the element definitions and matches the package you installed. That's more useful than asking an agent to reconstruct an API from remembered examples. After an upgrade, use the new package's guide rather than an old copy pasted into your instructions.

## What should you ask Claude Code to do?

Give the agent a brief with both the desired result and the checks it must show. For example:

```text
Read the installed Hyper Elements GUIDE.md before changing the template.
Build a receipt email using emails/receipt.tsx and its Order type.
Keep order data outside the template. Use a two-column item table,
a clear total, a real customer name and one View your order button.
Use the elements from @hyper-elements/react, not raw HTML tags.
Run validate(), report errors and warnings, and fix template errors.
Then show outline(), render HTML and plain text, and inspect both.
Don't send anything or use credentials until I ask.
```

This makes the acceptance criteria visible. A polished screenshot alone can't tell you whether the plain text lost a total, whether the button points to the right order, or whether an unsupported property was used.

Load order data before rendering and pass it as props. Hyper Elements doesn't wait for async or suspending template components. Keep database access and provider calls in your server-side workflow, outside `Receipt`.

## How do you check and render the email?

Save the following as `scripts/render-receipt.tsx`. It is the complete local inspection step; it doesn't send an email.

```tsx
// scripts/render-receipt.tsx
import { mkdir, writeFile } from "node:fs/promises";
import { formatDiagnostics, outline, render, validate } from "@hyper-elements/react";
import { exampleOrder, Receipt } from "../emails/receipt";

async function main() {
  const email = <Receipt order={exampleOrder} />;
  const checked = validate(email);
  if (checked.diagnostics.length) {
    console.warn(formatDiagnostics(checked.diagnostics));
  }
  if (!checked.valid) throw new Error("Fix the template errors before rendering.");

  console.log(outline(email));
  const { html, text, diagnostics } = await render(email);
  if (diagnostics.length) console.warn(formatDiagnostics(diagnostics));

  await mkdir("preview", { recursive: true });
  await writeFile("preview/receipt.html", html);
  await writeFile("preview/receipt.txt", text);
}

main().catch((error) => {
  console.error(error);
  process.exitCode = 1;
});
```

Run it from the project directory:

```bash
npx tsx scripts/render-receipt.tsx
```

Open `preview/receipt.html` in a browser and read `preview/receipt.txt` separately. The HTML includes its head styles; don't strip them before sending. The text version comes from the same template, but still deserves a human check for readable order, facts and destinations.

`validate()` reports template diagnostics without writing output. `render()` is asynchronous and rejects invalid templates with an `ElementsError`. Our outer error handler also catches unexpected failures in your code; don't assume template validation makes application exceptions impossible.

## How does the agent repair an unsupported style?

A common mistake is adding a margin to a text block. The [diagnostics reference](https://www.hyperelements.dev/docs/diagnostics) uses this intentionally invalid example:

```tsx
import { Email, Text, validate } from "@hyper-elements/react";

const result = validate(
  <Email>
    <Text style={{ marginBottom: 16 }}>Hi</Text>
  </Email>
);
```

TypeScript flags `marginBottom` as an unsupported style before runtime. For JavaScript or generated input that reaches validation, the documented result is `valid: false`, code `style/unknown`, and path `root.children[0].style.marginBottom`. The message tells you to use the parent's gap or padding.

Repair the layout relationship instead of substituting another margin:

```tsx
<Column style={{ gap: 16 }}>
  <Text>We've received your order.</Text>
  <Text>We'll email you when it ships.</Text>
</Column>
```

Don't paste the deliberately invalid snippet into the finished receipt. Use it to understand the feedback, then ask the agent to rerun the checks on the corrected template. Match diagnostic codes in automation and show the explanatory messages to people.

Also distinguish severity from success. An error makes the template invalid. A warning can leave `valid` true while reporting an output limitation; an info note can describe a difference such as classic Outlook's square corners. Review the trade-off instead of blindly deleting all styling until the list is empty.

## What should you look for in outline()?

`outline()` describes the laid-out template as text: blocks, desktop widths, words and links. It can also say whether a `Row` stacks on phones. It is not a screenshot, a mobile simulation or an inbox capture.

For this receipt, check the content rather than copying a supposedly universal outline transcript:

- The customer's name and order number are present.
- The table has an item and an amount column, with every line item.
- Subtotal, delivery and total are present in a sensible reading order.
- The button's destination matches the order you passed in.

Then inspect the browser preview at wide and narrow widths. Long product names, more items and larger prices are better stress cases than the shortest possible example. An outline can make structure inspectable, but it doesn't certify visual quality.

## How do you send a test with Resend?

Install Resend's Node SDK, following its [Node.js guide](https://resend.com/docs/send-with-nodejs):

```bash
npm install resend
```

Save this as `scripts/send-receipt.tsx`. Configure `RESEND_API_KEY`, `EMAIL_FROM` and `EMAIL_TO` in the server process before running it. Use a sender on your verified domain and your own test inbox. Never commit the key or put it in a browser bundle.

```tsx
// scripts/send-receipt.tsx
import { Resend } from "resend";
import { render } from "@hyper-elements/react";
import { exampleOrder, Receipt } from "../emails/receipt";

async function main() {
  const { RESEND_API_KEY, EMAIL_FROM, EMAIL_TO } = process.env;
  if (!RESEND_API_KEY || !EMAIL_FROM || !EMAIL_TO) {
    throw new Error("Set RESEND_API_KEY, EMAIL_FROM and EMAIL_TO on the server.");
  }
  const resend = new Resend(RESEND_API_KEY);
  const { html, text } = await render(<Receipt order={exampleOrder} />);
  const { data, error } = await resend.emails.send({
    from: EMAIL_FROM,
    to: EMAIL_TO,
    subject: `Your receipt for order ${exampleOrder.number}`,
    html,
    text,
  });
  if (error) throw new Error(`Resend: ${error.message}`);
  console.info("Resend accepted:", data?.id);
}

main().catch((error) => {
  console.error(error);
  process.exitCode = 1;
});
```

After replacing the example merchant details and link and reviewing the files, run:

```bash
npx tsx scripts/send-receipt.tsx
```

Provider acceptance isn't proof of inbox delivery or correct rendering. Send tests to the clients your readers use and verify the HTML and plain-text parts. The [sending guide](https://www.hyperelements.dev/docs/guides/sending) also covers using other providers with the same rendered output.

## What should you review before a real send?

Use a short, repeatable review instead of asking the agent whether the result is “good.” First compare the receipt with the source order: names, quantities, delivery charge and the destination URL. Then read the plain text without looking at the HTML. A customer should understand the same purchase and next action in either version.

Next try a longer customer name and a long product label. Look for awkward wrapping at a narrow browser width, but don't describe that browser view as an Outlook or Gmail test. Finally, send to your own inboxes and open the message in the clients you support. Record any difference you accept deliberately, rather than making the agent chase a different design on every pass.

For a team workflow, keep these review criteria beside the template. The agent can repeat structural checks; the owner still decides whether the receipt says the right thing and is ready for customers.

## What does validation not prove?

A valid template isn't a universal email-client guarantee. Browser layout, a diagnostic derived from support information, and a real message opened in an inbox are different checks. Use all three where they matter.

Some checks need the written HTML: Gmail-related HTML and stylesheet size diagnostics arrive during `render()`, not the earlier `validate()` step. Don't stop at the first green result. Check mobile readability, links, plain text and the clients that actually receive your messages.

## FAQ

### Can Claude Code send the email for me?

The template workflow doesn't grant permission to send. Keep credentials on the server and require an explicit sending step. Start with your own test inbox, not a customer list.

### Does valid: true mean there are no warnings?

No. It means no template errors were reported. Read warnings and notes, and inspect render-time diagnostics as well.

### Do I need Resend?

No. This tutorial uses it for a concrete test send. Hyper Elements writes HTML and plain text; a provider such as SES, Postmark, SendGrid or Nodemailer can deliver those bodies too.

### What's the next step?

Adapt `exampleOrder`, replace the fictional merchant and example-domain link, and repeat the check–inspect–render loop. Keep the [quickstart](https://www.hyperelements.dev/docs/quickstart), [agent guide](https://www.hyperelements.dev/ai) and [rendering reference](https://www.hyperelements.dev/docs/rendering) alongside the template as you make it your own.
